News.title: ‘I can’t use my arms or legs but sailed 3,000 miles across the Atlantic using a straw’
News.content:
With a simple sip and puff, Natasha Lambert sailed her 46 foot long catamaran 3,000 miles across the Atlantic. Aged just nine when the aspiring mariner said she wanted to sail, after a family activity holiday, her dad Gary was determined to make her dream come true.

But it was no mean feat. Born with cerebral palsy, Natasha, now 29, from the Isle of Wight, can’t use her arms or legs and struggles to speak. Her breath control, however, is top notch - giving her dad a cunning plan.

Her younger sister, Rachel, 19, explains: “Growing up, it was never a ‘no’ for Tash, but an ‘ok, how can we make this happen’. Our parents encouraged her to have a go at all sorts - like abseiling. When she expressed an interest in sailing, Tash wanted to not just be a passenger. She wanted to be in control of the boat. But when we did some research near our home in Cowes, the technology just wasn’t there.

“Dad is an electrician by day, but a mad inventor by night. Off he went into his shed and he created a custom ‘sip-and-puff’ breath-control system for Tash, so that she could independently skipper and steer sailing boats.”

‌



View 6 Images Rachel, dad Gary, mum Mandy and Natasha Lambert

The sip-and-puff proved life-changing for Natasha, giving her a level of independence and control normally made impossible by her condition. A small tube shaped like a straw is held securely in her mouth via a modified helmet.

Sipping (inhaling) on the tube turns the boat right, while puffing (blowing) turns it left. A tongue-operated LED light beam switch inside the straw lets her move between different modes using a toggle, in order to control the sails.

Rachel says: “Tash can easily drink from a straw, so that was the basis of it. They started with a model boat that she could control on a pond, then upgraded and upgraded until it became a full size boat. Then Tash got on board.”

‌



Gary’s ingenious invention was a game-changer. Natasha says: “I loved it.” Rachel continues: “Even when people are pushing Tash's wheelchair, they'll just push her out across the road without saying, ‘we're turning now.’ On the boat, it's all Tash. She decides where we're going and when we're going.”

View 6 Images Sailing sisters: Natasha with her sister Rachel

The family started by getting Tash to sail on rivers. Aged 11, it was time to tackle the Solent, the strait of water separating the Isle of Wight from the mainland. Rachel says: “She sailed across, no fear, all by herself. We were sailing besi

de her on another boat. She was supposed to stop and let the instructor on, but instead she turned around and kept sailing straight back across.

‌



“There’s a stigma around disabilities and, because Sasha is in a wheelchair, people assume there's a mental disability as well. But in Tash's case, that's not at all true - there's an awful lot going on up here. She has the same hopes, dreams and wants as anyone else. And she’s as determined as hell.

For her first charity challenge, in September 2012, Natasha sailed her boat, MissIsle Too, around the Isle of Wight, raising more than £17,000, which was shared between the Ellen MacArthur Cancer Trust, RNLI and Scope.

The following year, she completed a solo cross-Channel voyage from Boulogne in France, to Dover. And in 2014, she navigated in stages along the south coast of Britain up to Wales. She was then named Young Sailor of the Year.

View 6 Images Rachel says of her sister Natasha: "She has the same hopes, dreams and wants as anyone else. And she’s as determined as hell."

‌



In 2015, Natasha and her family set up the Miss Isle School of Sip and Puff Sailing, based in Cowes, and registered as a charity. It utilises the ‘sip-and-puff’ breath-control technology developed by Gary, to teach other young people with severe physical disabilities how to independently sail and skipper boats.

Later that year, Natasha was awarded a British Empire Medal for her charity work - but she is always seeking greater challenges. So, when Dame Ellen MacArthur, who broke the world record for the fastest solo non-stop circumnavigation of the globe in 2005 and lives on the Isle of Wight, gave Tash a pilot guide to the Atlantic - it was her green light to sail across the ocean.

Rachel says: “She signed it, ‘Here’s to the next one, Tash’.” Two years of research followed before the family opted for a 46 foot catamaran called Blown Away. Rachel says: “A catamaran is a much more stable platform for Tash's wheelchair and for moving around the boat. There's a little bit more room.

“Then we started adapting it, which was another two years. Dad tore bits apart, took things out. We made doorways bigger, added track, so that Tash could be in a sling in rough weather to go up and down stairs.”

‌



View 6 Images The Blown Away catamaran, on which the Lambert family crossed the Atlantic

Of course, Tash’s sip-and-puff was added, too. Mum Mandy was the brains of the operation. Natasha says: “She was the backbone.” Rachel continues: “Mum pushed it all forwards. Then it was about training, getting used to the boat, getting used to living on it, how that all worked for us.”

The family of four set sail on 22 November 2020. Natasha was the skipper, supported by a five-person team including Rachel, Gary and Mandy. Midway, they encountered a ferocious storm, but Natasha was fearless.

Rachel says: “One of the most amazing things about sailing, about being on boats, being on the water, is that the weather, the ocean, doesn't care if you're in a wheelchair or not. It's going to be the same for everybody. It’s about skill - and Tash has that in spades.”

‌



Sailing from Gran Canaria, Natasha and family travelled 3,000 miles to Saint Lucia in 18 days, 21 hours, 39 minutes and eight seconds. Part of the ARC event, more than 50 boats and 300 sailors took part.

View 6 Images Natasha on the boat's treadmill

Natasha finished 28th and, aged just 23, became the first person to sail across the Atlantic using the sip-and-puff system. Rachel laughs: “Tash wanted to carry on when we got there. One of the first things she said was, ‘now let’s do the Pacific’.

But, tragically, this year Mandy died from cancer, after being diagnosed last September. So, while they wait for the right moment to tackle the Pacific, in November, the sisters and their dad will cross the Atlantic again in her memory.

‌



Rachel says: “We miss her every day. It’s been really hard. We were such a team. Most families can’t say they’ve crossed an ocean together. But Mum is still with us and she’ll be with us on the boat. One of the last things she said to us was, ‘keep having adventures. Keep seeing the world’. So we will - we’re doing it for her.”

They are hoping to raise £30,000 for 3 charities - the Ellen MacArthur Cancer Trust, RNLI (where Rachel volunteers) and the Calvert Lakes (where Natasha first tried sailing).

Sailing together has forged an incredibly close bond between the sisters, too. Rachel, who is currently on her gap year after finishing sixth form, says: “We squabble like siblings, but when it matters we’re a pretty formidable team. I’m incredibly proud of Natasha. We both have our roles. Tash has the determination, the tenacity. This is her dream, and her dream is the catalyst to everything we do. We support, facilitate, and make it happen.”

For Natasha, sailing means liberty. She says: “I don’t have a disability on the water. I feel free.”

‌

News.title: Widdecombe police reopen investigation into incident at Farage's home, BBC understands
News.content:
Counter-terrorism police investigating the killing of Ann Widdecombe have reopened an inquiry into an incident at Nigel Farage's south London home, the BBC understands.

It is understood to relate to what the Reform UK leader described as a "lit incendiary device" being pushed through his letterbox in April 2025.

Counter Terrorism Policing (CTP) London said it was looking into an "attempted burglary" at a property as part of the Widdecombe murder investigation, but did not confirm the home was linked to Farage or why it might be connected to the killing of the former MP.

CTP London has also referred itself to the police watchdog over how the initial investigation into the Farage incident was handled.

Police said at the time that "damage was caused to a door but nothing was stolen".

Both CTP London and the Metropolitan Police were involved in enquiries. No arrests were made and the investigation was closed.

But on Friday, CTP London said a new line of inquiry had been identified that was not "pursued by them at the time".

The Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) said it had "decided to independently investigate the conduct of a Counter Terrorism Policing London staff member following a referral received earlier [on Friday]".

A statement continued: "The conduct relates to an allegation the individual failed to identify and pursue a line of enquiry relating to an attempted burglary reported in April 2025."

CTP London said it would "full engage" with the watchdog's investigation, adding: "The victims and families in both investigations have been updated today, and we continue to support them."

Ann Widdecombe, the 78-year-old former Conservative minister and Reform UK spokeswoman, was found dead at her home in Devon last month with serious injuries.

Joshua Kerry, from Rotherham in South Yorkshire, was later charged with her murder.

Kerry was initially arrested on suspicion of murder on 11 July, before being additionally arrested on 13 July on suspicion of the commission, preparation or instigation of acts of terrorism.

Widdecombe had served as Tory MP for Maidstone in Kent for 23 years and was appointed to ministerial roles in Sir John Major's government in the 1990s.

News.title: Infantino denies claims Uefa paid off alleged 'lover' when he was general secretary
News.content:
Gianni Infantino's alleged lover was given a severance payment over the affair by Uefa while he was its general secretary, according to a Daily Telegraph investigation, external.

A spokesman for the now Fifa president was reported to have told the paper Infantino "strongly denies these categorically untrue allegations".

Uefa, for whom Infantino was general secretary from 2009 to 2016, issued a statement confirming "a departure payment was made to the individual in question".

The allegations come as Infantino fights for his future as Fifa president following his aborted plans to sell off stakes in the World Cup to private investors.

BBC Sport has contacted Fifa and Infantino for comment.

The Telegraph reported that Uefa paid a six-figure sum to the woman, who had an alleged relationship with Infantino, who is married, during his time at European football's governing body.

"Fifa president Gianni Infantino strongly denies these allegations, and they are categorically untrue. Any insinuation of inappropriate conduct or violation of statutes or regulations is defamatory," a Fifa spokesman told the Telegraph.

"No employee at Uefa and Fifa has ever raised a complaint regarding Mr Infantino's behaviour because there never was an incident where he was involved."

Uefa confirmed a payment was made to the woman in question and that it covered the fees for her to complete an MBA course at a local business school.

It said all payments were in line with regulations at the time, but those regulations have since been tightened and "reflect those found in a modern, high-profile organisation".

News.title: Hunter Biden tells BBC his pardon was 'not good' for America or his father's legacy
News.content:
Hunter Biden has told the BBC he is "the most privileged person there is" after receiving a presidential pardon from his father, former US President Joe Biden, acknowledging it was not a good choice for America or his father's legacy.

In a wide-ranging interview with the BBC's Newsnight, Hunter Biden defended the controversial pardon, revealed his father's "painful" cancer has spread, ruled out seeking elected office and spoke about helping others recover from addiction.

Asked about the 2024 pardon, he said he understood the criticism but noted: "What would you have thought of my dad if he did not do that for me."

"It's something that is easily criticised and for good reason," he added.

"It's not fairâ¦ All I know is that I'm grateful that he did it for me," he said, acknowledging the pardon was "not good" for the American people, the Constitution - or his father's legacy.

He argued to the BBC that his father ultimately acted out of concern that he would become a target under Donald Trump's incoming administration.

"I was the only one in the world that could have gotten what I got from the only person in the world who could give it, my father."

Hunter Biden also insisted he and his father had never discussed the possibility of a pardon before it was granted.

"There is no way that you can have those kinds of discussions that would not become public," he said.

President Biden granted his son a full and unconditional pardon in December 2024, despite repeatedly saying beforehand that he would not use the powers of the presidency to intervene in his son's legal cases. In announcing the decision, the former president said his son had been "selectively and unfairly prosecuted".

The pardon covered his son's federal gun conviction, a tax case he'd pled guilty to and any federal offences committed between 2014 and 2024.

News.title: Police officers investigated over handling of sex offender who murdered two women
News.content:
Met Deputy Assistant Commissioner Kevin Southworth has acknowledged that failures to remand Levy in custody during court hearings in May and June 2025 left him free to commit further offences.

BTP confirmed two officers have been moved to other roles due to "incompetence" in handling investigations into Levy's transport assaults.

Crime and policing minister Sarah Jones said the situation "raises serious questions".

"The fact that Levy was able to inflict such devastating harm after being freed by police and the courts is deeply concerning."

Lisa Ramsarran, chief crown prosecutor for the CPS, said: "Our actions fell short of the standards that victims, families and the public are entitled to expect.

"In particular, there were points where we could and should have taken a more robust approach to representations about bail, based on the information available."

Victims' Commissioner for London Andrea Simons called for a "multi-agency review" over the "litany of failures to manage such a prolific offender".

She told BBC Breakfast that public services "have to get better at recognising patterns of offending" before attackers become "emboldened".

She continued: "There was a lack of restrictions that could have been placed on him and a failure to monitor him appropriately - so all of those things, I think, we need answers to now."

Lisa Squire, whose daughter Libby was murdered by a man who had previously committed a string of sex crimes, told the BBC that a "catalogue of disasters" had led to Levy's murders.

She told BBC Radio 4's Today programme "the patterns were there, he was flying those red flags", and said there were "precursor offences" for which he could have stopped by police.

"At the moment, the message going out, in my opinion, is that women's safety is not important," she continued.

ZoÃ« Billingham, a former independent police inspector who pushed for reforms on how violence against women in girls is policed, said that "too often in cases like this the dots aren't being joined up".

She added: "It's not one or two missed opportunities that could have brought him to justice, that could have had him locked up and behind bars and no longer a threat to women and girls. It was an extraordinary succession."

News.title: Fifth heatwave of the year likely next week as temperatures could hit 35C
News.content:
Temperatures on Saturday will begin to climb above average again, reaching the mid- to high 20s Celsius in most of England and Wales.

It will be cooler in Scotland and Northern Ireland at 17 to 21C with more cloud, a bit of rain and a blustery wind.

By Sunday and into next week temperatures will rise even further with many parts of the UK exceeding their heatwave threshold temperature of 25 to 28C, depending on location.

With this hotter weather expected to last well into the week, many locations will have the three consecutive days needed to declare the fifth widespread heatwave of the year.

It has already been a remarkable summer in the United Kingdom with multiple records broken.

July has been the sunniest month on record for the UK, as well as the driest July on record for England and Wales.

There have so far been 33 days this year when temperatures have exceeded 30C in the UK. Next week, it is likely the record of 34 days, set in 1995, will be broken.

For the first time ever, a temperature of 35C has also been recorded somewhere in the UK on the three consecutive months of May, June and July.

It is possible August will join that list by the end of next week as some forecast models suggest 35C in central and south-east England.

News.title: I went for a full body MOT and the results came as a shock
News.content:
Annabel Mason-Thompson went for a Neko Health scan in September last year, knowing she had a suspicious-looking mark on her back - but it wasn't flagged by the technology.

"I felt a bit let down if I'm honest," the 50-year-old says. "Their AI scanner failed to pick up any of my four cancerous lesions.

"It was only when I went into the doctor's room after the scan and I pointed out my red mark did they take a look at it."

Further examination confirmed the mark was suspicious, so Neko Health contacted Annabel to say she would need treatment and wrote a letter to her private dermatologist to say the "lesion requires evaluation with a view to possible excision".

Her dermatologist found three more cancerous marks which needed urgent treatment.

"Luckily," she says, "they were all slow-growing basal cell carcinomas. I had to have two cut out and two taken off via cryotherapy."

Neko Health says "member safety and clinical excellence are at the heart of everything" it does. The company said its clinical team did identify a "lesion of concern" and it was reviewed by two of its dermatologists before a referral was made for potential treatment.

"We know that no one system is foolproof," Nilsonne says, "which is why we have multiple lenses - it is crucial that the technology and human expertise work together."

His company's latest data shows that of the 4,362 scans carried out on clients who visited Neko Health's Stockholm headquarters last year, 1.2% discovered life-threatening conditions such as melanoma and leukaemia. A further 4% spotted significant health conditions that required further treatment, and 1.2% flagged conditions that could be reversed such as pre-diabetic blood sugar levels.

While the figures are not representative of the population and only account for those who can afford to pay for this kind of preventive healthcare, Nilsonne says this is an indicator of how medicine should look in the future.

But GPs disagree. Prof Victoria Tzortziou Brown, president of the Royal College of GPs (RCGP), says they haven't seen "convincing evidence" private broad screening tests "improve health outcomes".

She says the results from these private scans can also place an additional strain on the NHS as clients come back for further tests and potential treatment, even "where the findings prove to be clinically insignificant".

News.title: He's been frozen on Everest for 30 years, now 'Green Boots' may finally be coming home
News.content:
For 30 years, a dead body known as "Green Boots" has been lying in the snow, nestled under an overhanging rock, not far from Mount Everest's summit.

The lime mountaineering boots worn by an Indian climber who died in 1996 have been a grim trail marker for many climbers on their way up the world's highest peak ever since.

Now India is looking for a specialist high-altitude recovery team to undertake a complex and risky mission to retrieve what they say is Dorje Morup's body â arguably the most famous of the hundreds whose bodies have been left frozen on the mountain.

They hope they are on the cusp of returning his remains to friends and family who never gave up hope he'd come home.

"On some days, before I went to sleep, I would think that there'd be a knock on the door tonight and that when I opened, he would be there," Morup's wife told the BBC.

"When he comes home, I will ask him: 'Where were you all these years?'"

Warning: This story contains a picture of a dead body.

News.title: Digital cameras and wired earphones are back and 'a bit more real'
News.content:
Luckily I'm out with my photography-loving best friend, who helps adjust the settings on the camera and gets snapping while I'm otherwise engaged on the dancefloor.

The mere sight of us pulling out the camera and squinting through its tiny viewfinder draws attention â "I've not seen one of these in years", a man remarks.

He's right â digital cameras had their heyday in the late 1990s and early 2000s, just before smartphones took off.

There are currently 42 million active film camera users globally, more than a third of these aged 18â30 and largely influenced by social media trends, according to a market research report, external last year.

So why, when we're surrounded by more advanced tech here in 2026, are they seemingly making a resurgence?

For Lily Redman, a 26-year-old content creator from South Wales, digital cameras "capture a quality that my phone just can't replicate".

She's been taking one on nights out and to concerts and feels the flash on her phone "is grainy and too high definition" compared to the "more smooth" finished product on a digital camera.

"I think people are looking for a bit of grit or something that feels a bit more real," she says.

That may also explain why low exposure photos taken on iPhones and Androids â where people dodge ready-made filters to artificially crank down the exposure setting and produce a darker image â are also popular on socials right now.

With digital cameras offering an element of surprise when you plug in the memory card reader to your computer at home, digital cameras capture a moment in time.

"If I look back at photos my mum took when I was two, they look so old but when I look at photos I took five years ago, they look like they were taken yesterday," says Redman.

"Phone photos have warped our perception of time."

News.title: Strictly dancers Ola and James Jordan separate after 23 years of marriage
News.content:
Former Strictly Come Dancing stars James and Ola Jordan have confirmed they have separated after more than 20 years of marriage.

The former professional dancers were regulars on the show for several series after first featuring in 2006.

The couple's manager Vickie White confirmed the split, which was first reported by the Sun newspaper, external.

She said in a statement: "It is with great sadness that I can confirm that James and Ola began a trial separation some time ago.

"Their shared priority remains co-parenting their daughter, Ella, and they are committed to putting her wellbeing first.

"They would greatly appreciate your understanding as they navigate this difficult time."

Ola Jordan won the Open Polish Championship in 1999 when she was 17 years old and became James' dance partner shortly afterwards in March 2000.

She moved to England a month later and the pair got married in October 2003.

James appeared on Strictly from 2006 to 2013 while Ola appeared on the show until 2015.

Ola's celebrity partners included wildlife presenter Steve Backshall and Welsh sprinter Iwan Thomas, while James danced with former international gymnast and broadcaster Gabby Logan, as well as The One Show presenter Alex Jones.

News.title: Bristol Airport disruption a 'shambles' as flights restart
News.content:
Disruption because of a runway defect at Bristol Airport continues, as flights start to depart.

Hundreds of passengers were stranded on Friday evening after the decision was made to close the runway shortly after 18:00 BST. All flights were suspended until 08:00 on Saturday.

Flights have since restarted amid delayed take offs and diversions.

In a short statement on the airport website, a spokesperson said: "There will be some disruption to some flights today. We apologise for any inconvenience caused."

News.title: Woman attacked by bed bugs during Travelodge stay
News.content:
Thirteen days after Hannah Stephenson stayed a night in a Travelodge hotel, she is still itching with red lumps over her body - a nightmare she would not wish on her "worst enemy".

The 31-year-old from Bassingbourn had been out with friends in Cambridge and decided to book a one-night stay at the hotel on Newmarket Road on 26 July to save money instead of getting a taxi home.

The next morning, she woke up to a "horrible realisation", feeling itchy with red lumps over her body and blood spots smeared on the bedding â the tell-tale signs of bed bugs, she said.

A Travelodge spokesperson said: "We are deeply sorry for Ms Stephenson's experience and how distressing an incident like this can be."

Stephenson said a lovely evening with friends had turned into a horrible morning.

"It was just a lovely wholesome time of Cambridge sightseeing and pubs, and now it is tarnished by these bedbug bites," she said.

"It wasn't until I saw the blood and the bugs that I realised what had happened."

News.title: Man guilty of fatal shooting of teen outside club
News.content:
A man has been found guilty of fatally shooting an 18-year-old outside a Wembley nightclub.

Tyrece Balcha was found with gunshot wounds outside the Crystal Club in Atlantic Crescent at about 05:30 GMT on 21 September 2025. He was taken to hospital, where he died four days later.

A jury at the Old Bailey found Ashley Wallace, 40, of Shenley Road, Southwark, guilty of murder and possession of a firearm with intent to endanger life.

At the same trial, two men were found not guilty of murder. A woman was cleared of possession of a firearm, possession of a firearm with intent to endanger life, and perverting the course of justice. The jury did not reach a verdict on a fourth man.

CCTV footage showed that Balcha had been involved in an altercation inside the club before being followed outside and shot.

Wallace fled the scene in a vehicle and was arrested on 25 September after police traced the car to south-east London.

A revolver carrying Wallace's DNA was found inside the vehicle, and investigators established that the bullet recovered from the murder scene had been fired from the gun.

News.title: How asylum protests brought disorder to Thetford
News.content:
It is normally a quiet residential street but on Wednesday night, Clover Way erupted.

Residents later described their shock at seeing hundreds of people converging on an address where they believed asylum seekers were being housed.

It was one of five locations across the Norfolk town of Thetford that saw sporadic violence and disorder over three consecutive evenings, beginning on Tuesday.

Two police officers were taken to hospital, including one who had been bitten, and there were arrests on suspicion of offences including public order, harassment and possession of an offensive weapon.

Andy Symonds, the chair of the Norfolk Police Federation, said Friday night had been "much calmer", although "a number of people" had been dispersed using powers from Section 35 of the Anti-Social Behaviour, Crime and Policing Act 2014.

"We are on watch for tonight, it's the weekend. We will be dispersing people from the area," he told the BBC.

News.title: Man charged after four killed in lamp-post crash
News.content:
A man has been charged in connection with a crash that killed four people.

James Diggle, 27, of Alundale Road in West Derby, Liverpool, faces four counts of aiding and abetting causing death by dangerous driving.

The charge follows the deaths of four men, Jack Diggle, 23, Benjamin Dooley, 23, Andrew Roberts, 24, and Craig Shackleton-Brady, 26, who were killed when the black Cupra they were travelling in hit a lamp-post in Huyton, on Merseyside, on 24 July.

Merseyside Police said Diggle would be appearing at Liverpool Magistrates' Court later.

News.title: How mum joined ‘rising number of hidden homeless’ after fleeing with daughter
News.content:
When Jodie and her daughter had to flee their hometown, they could only take what they could carry - two black bin bags filled with their belongings.

Jodie, then aged 30, found herself in Margate, Kent, with a seven-year-old child to take care of and no place to live.

"I had to leave everything," Jodie said. "The bags were mainly my daughter's clothes and her dolls."

Having left after feeling threatened, she chose the seaside town where they had been on summer and half term holidays, although it meant leaving her family and friends behind.

"I wanted to go somewhere that wasn't very alien for my daughter," said Jodie, now 42.

"It was still scary, but I had to be the strong one and protect her. I had to do it so that my daughter could have a life."

After a brief stay in council emergency accommodation, she said they spent a year sleeping on the sofas and floors of people she had met in Margate.

News.title: The 101-year-old who created a dolls' house museum with her childhood toys
News.content:
Val Ripley may be 101 but she still enjoys playing with dolls' houses.

She was given her first by her parents when she was eight, in Christmas 1932, and remembers waking up and seeing a huge parcel all wrapped up.

"I remember thinking 'they can't have bought me that one', and it was my pride and joy my whole childhood."

More than 30 years later, Val and her sister rediscovered what she thought had been lost while clearing out her parents' attic and decided to create a museum.

News.title: Audience label Amanda Knox’s show at Edinburgh Fringe ‘respectful’ to Meredith Kercher’s memory
News.content:
An audience member called Amanda Knox’s controversial comedy show at Edinburgh Fringe “respectful” and “authentic” after watching the opening night on Friday, August 7.

“I thought it was really authentic – [Knox] came across as quite powerful and carried the room,” said Nigel, from London.

Knox, who was falsely imprisoned in 2009 for the murder of her roommate Meredith Kercher, performed her show Cartwheel following unsuccessful calls for it to be banned.

Kercher’s sister, Stephanie Kercher, had called for the show to be cancelled, claiming that it “normalises and trivialises violence against women.”

Kercher, an exchange student from the University of Leeds, was killed aged 21 in Perugia, Italy, in 2007.

News.content:

Joe Biden’s son has admitted that his presidential pardon was “not good” for America or his father’s reputation.

Hunter Biden was granted clemency in 2024 after having been convicted of three federal gun charges related to his purchase of a firearm in 2018. He also pleaded guilty to nine federal tax charges.

His conviction marked the first time a sitting US president’s child was found guilty of a crime, and was facing up to 25 years in prison and fines of up to $750,000 at his sentencing.

In a BBC Newsnight interview, Mr Biden defended the controversial pardon, saying: “What would you have thought of my dad if he did not do that for me?"

"I was the only one in the world that could have gotten what I got from the only person in the world who could give it, my father."

open image in gallery In 2024, Hunter Biden was granted clemency after having been convicted of three federal gun charges related to his purchase of a firearm in 2018 ( AFP/Getty )

However, he admitted the pardon was “not good” for American people, the Constitution, or his father’s reputation.

President Biden granted his son a full pardon in December 2024, retracting on his previous vow to “accept the outcome” of the judicial process.

Mr Biden said he and his father never discussed the possibility of a pardon before it was granted.

At the time it was granted, the former president said: “I hope Americans will understand why a father and a president would come to this decision.”

open image in gallery President Biden granted his son a full pardon in December 2024 ( Getty )

The president has the authority to grant a pardon to anyone convicted in federal court or by a military court martial. A pardon blocks any further punishment for the forgiven offense and effectively prevents any further consequences of a criminal conviction. The president does not have the authority to grant pardons on state-level convictions.

A pardon does not include an expungement of a criminal record, but it will restore most legal disabilities, including voting rights and the ability to sit on a jury and possess a firearm. However, it also does not signify innocence.

In the BBC interview, Mr Biden spoke emotionally about the struggles of watching his father’s battle with prostate cancer.

He revealed that the cancer has “metastasised into his bones and further. It's very painful”.

Praising his father, he said he is, “to this day, the centre of our family”.

He added: "He's the best father, the best husband, the best grandfather.

"The only thing that I say about my dad, about his health right now, is I wish he would complain more."

News.title: Transfer news LIVE: Arsenal identify Vinicius Jr alternatives and Liverpool agree Barcelona defender deal
News.content:
Why Arsenal Want Bruno Guimaraes So Badly

Arsenal have moved on from their chase of Vinicius Jr after he signed a contract extension with Real Madrid and the Gunners have now reignited their interest in Atletico Madrid’s Julian Alvarez while PSG’s Bradley Barcola is also on their list.

But Bruno Guimaraes has finally officially completed his £75m move from Newcastle United with the deal for the 28-year-old midfielder representing a key piece of business of Mikel Arteta ahead of Arsenal’s title defence.

Rodri looks set to leave Manchester City amid interest from Barcelona and Real Madrid. The World Cup winning captain is into the final year of his contract and favours a move to Barca – though an initial offer of £38m has been rejected.

Liverpool, meanwhile, also want to sign Barcola from Paris Saint-Germain and have lined up his teammate Ibrahim Mbaye in what could be a double swoop for Andoni Iraola’s side. The European champions may be willing to let them go, especially following Maghnes Akliouche signing from Monaco, while the Reds also look to have secured much-needed defender help with ex-Barcelona captain Ronald Araujo set for a loan deal, with an option to buy, at Anfield.

Elsewhere, Manchester United have added to their ranks by bringing in a teenage midfielder and they are exploring their options at left-back with Lewis Hall reportedly now set on a move to Old Trafford, but Newcastle are determined to stop the exodus and insist he is not for sale.

Pharmacies claim the amount of wasted medicines thrown away in England in just one year could fill 75 swimming pools.

The public has been told not to “over-order” medicine and instead only order a repeat prescription when it is needed after an estimated 3,400 tonnes worth of partially used medicines were disposed of in England in 2024/25, according to the National Pharmacy Association (NPA).

The NPA, which analysed data from local health bodies, estimates that wasted medicine costs the NHS at least £480 million a year.

“Wasted medicines cost the NHS significant sums of money every year that could be invested in better services for patients,” said Olivier Picard, chairman of the National Pharmacy Association.

“More than this, wasting medicines can have environmental and health consequences and we can do much more to tackle this growing problem.

“As soon as a medicine leaves a pharmacy, even if it is not used and is unopened, it must be disposed of, so it is important patients only get medicines they are sure they will use.”

An estimated 3,400 tonnes worth of partially used medicines were disposed of in England in 2024/25 ( PA )

The NPA, which represents 6,000 independent community pharmacies in the UK, is calling for patients with several repeat prescriptions to have more reviews so medicines that are no longer needed can be identified.

“We are urging patients only to request medicines if they really need them when ordering repeat prescriptions,” Mr Picard added.

“As well as this, patients who are prescribed multiple medicines should have these more regularly reviewed to ensure they are being fully utilised.

“If a patient has any concerns about their medicines, they should speak to their pharmacist who can help them get the most out of their medicines.”

Commenting, Dr Rasha Abdelsalam Elshenawy, senior lecturer in postgraduate medicine at the University of Hertfordshire, said: “Medicines waste isn’t only a financial and environmental problem – it’s a patient safety and resistance problem.

“Leftover antibiotics kept at home are often taken later without medical advice, which fuels antimicrobial resistance, one of the biggest threats to modern medicine.

“Regular medication reviews and only ordering what is needed protects patients, the NHS and the environment.”

Drugs for a common eye condition could one day be used to treat certain aggressive cancers, including breast cancer, melanoma and a type of blood cancer.

Scientists at The Institute for Cancer Research found these cancers rely on the same molecule to become aggressive and spread

Their study found existing drugs which block the molecule and are currently used to treat patients with glaucoma could be repurposed to help fight cancer. It also identified certain markers which could determine which patients may respond well to the drugs.

Experts said that the study “lays the foundations” for identifying suitable patients, and repurposing drugs which have already proven to be safe could mean they reach patients faster.

Lead author Victoria Sanz Moreno, professor of cancer cell and metastasis biology, said: “Some cancers are particularly aggressive, and once they spread they become very hard to treat.

“Catching these aggressive cancers and preventing their ability to move around the body is really crucial to our mission to keep more people living well with cancer.

“Our research has identified a shared weakness of aggressive cancer cells that could be targeted across many cancer types, wherever they originate in the body.

open image in gallery Scientists confirmed their findings in aggressive cancers such as breast cancer ( Getty/iStock )

“We confirmed our findings in aggressive cancers such as breast cancer, melanoma, and a type of blood cancer called acute myeloid leukaemia, but we believe this molecular fingerprint of cancer cells likely to die after treatment applies to many more cancer types.

“It’s reassuring to know that a treatment already exists – a drug currently being used safely in some patients could be adapted to treat these cancers.”

Researchers set out to find markers that could be used to identify which cancers would respond well to drugs that block a molecule called ROCK, also known as Rho kinase.

When cancer cells spread around the body, they cause advanced disease that is hard to treat, and these aggressive cells rely on ROCK.

The molecule keeps the scaffolding of cells tense, making the cells contract and become round, which generates force for the cancer cells to squeeze through tissue.

The study, published in the journal iScience, saw researchers look for markers that could be used to identify which cancers would respond well to drugs that block ROCK – which are already in use to treat glaucoma.

The team, working in the Breast Cancer Now Toby Robins Research Centre at the ICR, looked at information from a drug sensitivity database to identify which types of cancer cells responded to ROCK inhibitors.

Researchers found that breast cancer cells that responded to ROCK inhibitors had a particular gene that was not working properly, called E-Cadherin.

In melanoma, the database showed that cells that respond to ROCK inhibitors tended to have a more rounded shape and high activity of a signalling pathway called NFKB.

And acute myeloid leukaemia cells that responded well to ROCK had a specific subset of gene alterations.

The findings were then turned into lab experiments on tumour samples and studies in mice.

open image in gallery The study found that patients who may respond well to the drugs can be identified with certain markers ( Getty/iStock )

The researchers hope that in the future a biopsy of a patient’s cancer showing these markers could indicate whether ROCK inhibitors would work well for the patient.

Dr Simon Vincent, chief scientific officer at Breast Cancer Now, said: “With around 11,500 women tragically dying from breast cancer every year in the UK, research like this is vital to finding more effective treatment options.

“This study helps to lay the foundation for understanding who among those with certain cancers, including breast cancer, might benefit most from existing drugs. Finding new uses for existing treatments, which we know people can safely take, is easier and faster than developing new cancer drugs from scratch.

“It’s encouraging that these drugs may be especially effective in targeting cancer cells that are more likely to spread and resist treatment.

“While this research is still at an early stage and clinical trials are needed, it’s an important step towards more personalised breast cancer treatments in the future.”

First author of the study, Jaume Barcelo, postdoctoral research fellow at The Institute of Cancer Research, London, now based at the Barts Cancer Institute at Queen Mary University of London, added: “Our study has identified a specific pattern of features that is consistent across many cancer types, and that can be used to match the right patients to this treatment.

“The next stage for this research will be to test how these drugs that inhibit ROCK work in combination with other treatments, to maximise the benefit for patients.

“As ROCK inhibitors are already approved to treat glaucoma, I hope that our findings can be used to progress the drugs into clinical trials to treat cancer in the near future.”

Susanna Daniels, chief executive officer of the charity Melanoma Focus, said: “Despite major advances in melanoma treatment over the past decade, too many people still die from the disease each year, and not every patient responds to the treatments currently available.

“Every new discovery improves our understanding of how melanoma grows and survives, bringing us closer to treatments that are more effective, more targeted and have the potential to improve survival.

“While these findings are still at an early stage and will need to be tested in clinical trials, they offer an encouraging direction for future melanoma research and the development of more personalised treatments.”

News.title: Nigel Farage ‘horrified’ Ann Widdecombe murder detectives probing firebombing on his home
News.content:
The Way Back. Read our Privacy notice

Nigel Farage is “horrified” that counter-terror police probing the alleged murder of Ann Widdecombe have reopened a year-old investigation into a “firebomb” attack at his house.

Officers said the incident, which The Telegraph described as a “lit incendiary device” being posted through the Reform UK leader’s letterbox, happened at an address in Greater London and was reported in April 2025.

The Metropolitan Police and Counter Terrorism Policing (CTP) London said they investigated an “attempted burglary”, but no arrests were made at the time and the case was closed pending any new lines of inquiry.

Mr Farage, who was not home at the time of the attack and found the damage when he returned home, earlier described the alleged attack as an “outright arson attempt”.

“Luckily it had burned itself out on the porch,” he told The Telegraph in April this year.

Reopening their probe, CTP London said they had identified a line of inquiry “which may have been relevant” but was “not identified and pursued by them at the time”.

The police watchdog, the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC), is now investigating the “conduct” of a CTP London staff member, following an allegation that the employee “failed to identify and pursue a line of inquiry” related to the attempted burglary.

The Independent understands that Mr Farage is “horrified” that the attack on his home in 2025 is being reinvestigated by detectives investigating Ms Widdecombe’s murder.

A source said: “There has been a very serious policing error which is why counter terror have referred themselves to IOPC, which is unprecedented.”

Reform UK spokesperson and former Tory minister Ms Widdecombe, 78, died on 8 July after she was hit over the head with a hammer 21 times at her home in Haytor on Dartmoor, Devon, a court heard.

Counter-terror police investigating the death of former MP Ann Widdecombe have reopened a year-old probe into an alleged firebomb attack at Nigel Farage’s home ( PA )

Joshua Kerry, 28, was charged with her murder on 20 July. He has not yet entered a plea and has been remanded in custody until his next court appearance.

Reform UK MPs were given round-the-clock security protection, paid for by the party, after Ms Widdecombe’s death over fears of similar attacks.

Mr Farage has previously raised concerns about MPs’ security, including his own, and said after her death: “And I do fear that for anybody in public life, or especially the political space, things have become even more dangerous to them.”

Confirming the reopened probe following the attack on Mr Farage’s home, senior national co-ordinator for Counter Terrorism Policing, Vicki Evans, said: “As part of the ongoing investigation led by Counter Terrorism Policing South East into the murder of Ann Widdecombe, officers have reopened an investigation into an incident reported to police last year.

She added: “Given the nature of this matter and the significant public interest in the investigation into Ann Widdecombe’s death, it was of critical importance for us to provide this update.”

CTP London said it made a “mandatory conduct referral” to the police watchdog on Friday.

An IOPC spokesperson said on Friday: “We can confirm that the IOPC has decided to independently investigate the conduct of a Counter Terrorism Policing London staff member following a referral received earlier today.

“The conduct relates to an allegation the individual failed to identify and pursue a line of enquiry relating to an attempted burglary reported in April 2025.

“Counter Terrorism Policing London has been notified of our decision, and no further information is available at this early stage.”

Typhoon Dolphin lashed Japan's southern Okinawa ​prefecture on Saturday, injuring six people and cutting power to more than 50,000 buildings, while China shut ports and ‌halted ferries ahead of the storm's expected arrival on its east coast.

At least five elderly people, three of whom fell due to strong winds, suffered non-life-threatening injuries in Okinawa while another person was injured in Kagoshima prefecture, authorities said.

Nearly 39,000 buildings were without power in Kagoshima while just over 12,000 were affected in Okinawa. Domestic airlines, ANA and Japan Airlines, cancelled flights to and from Okinawa. The typhoon had maximum sustained winds ⁠of 162 kph (90 mph) with gusts reaching 216 kph.

Okinawa and Amami island in Kagoshima prefecture are the main areas expected to be affected in Japan.

In China, where the typhoon is expected to make landfall between late Sunday and early ⁠Monday, authorities have designated Dolphin as an orange-category typhoon — the second-highest level.

Worried about the risk of flooding and landslides, authorities also raised the emergency response level for Dolphin by one notch to level III, the second-lowest level.

The typhoon is most likely to make landfall between Zhoushan city in Zhejiang province and Fuding city in Fujian province and is expected to have winds of 38-45 metres per ‌second (85-101 mph) near its centre, according to China's National Meteorological Center.

open image in gallery A satellite image shows Typhoon Dolphin approaching Japan's Okinawa ( Reuters )

China's National Marine ‌Forecasting Center on Saturday maintained its highest, red-level warning for waves, forecasting 5-to-8m (16-to-26ft) waves in coastal waters off Zhejiang through Sunday afternoon.

open image in gallery Map from Japanese Meteorological Agency (JMA) shows path of Typhoon Dolphin ( JMA )

Under an orange-level warning, waves in coastal waters off Shanghai and northern Fujian could be 3 to 5.5m.

Rain and strong winds are ⁠expected to affect eastern China through August 12, including parts of Shanghai and neighbouring provinces. Some areas of eastern Zhejiang could receive more than 600mm (23.6in) of rain, according to forecasters.

Zhejiang raised its coastal typhoon alert to its highest level and halted port operations. Authorities in eastern and southern China also suspended ferries, halted some construction work and ordered fishing boats back to port.

Ningbo Lishe International Airport in Zhejiang said it will suspend all flights on Sunday. Shanghai's Yangshan port had been cleared of vessels by late Friday, while some rail services in the Yangtze River Delta ‌will be suspended from Sunday.

Beijing authorities have said they are monitoring the typhoon's path and are preparing flood-control and evacuation plans for the capital.

In Taiwan, 78 flights, mostly international, were cancelled because of ‌the typhoon, the government said.

Heavy rain was expected ⁠in northern parts of the island over the weekend, though authorities had not ordered evacuations as of ⁠Saturday. China has ordered that, due to the typhoon, ships passing through the Taiwan Strait must heed its traffic control instructions — measures that Taipei denounced as "ridiculous", saying ‌that Beijing has no right ​to restrict access to international waters.

China views democratically governed Taiwan ‌as its own territory and claims the strategic strait. ​Both Taipei and Washington reject that claim.

News.content:

It is an image that somehow captures the crisis of Europe’s present and future: a smouldering wildfire burning on grassland just two miles from a nuclear plant.

More than 100 firefighters were called in to tackle the blaze sweeping through Dunwich Heath on the Suffolk coast at the end of July, which lies just north of the Sizewell B nuclear plant that powers up to 2.5 million British homes. The fire tore through the equivalent of 210 football pitches on the Suffolk coast before it was extinguished.

Across the continent, wildfires have been much more severe and widespread. Spain and France have seen tens of thousands of acres of land scorched over the last month, and nearly a quarter of a million people were forced from their homes. The Independent saw first-hand how communities have been torn apart as France recorded its hottest July on record.

It has left Europe in a bind. The continent urgently needs nuclear power to combat climate change; but extreme heat, drought and wildfires pose huge challenges for the transition.

As climate change brings hotter and more deadly summers, nuclear plants drawing water from drying rivers are struggling to keep their low-carbon nuclear fleets fully operational, resulting in outages and desperate moves to import electricity at a premium.

open image in gallery Scorched land following a wildfire at Dunwich Heath on 31 July, with the Sizewell nuclear power station in the background ( AFP/Getty )

Heatwaves shut down nuclear plants

France had to close three reactors just last week after drought conditions cut flows in its rivers, while record-low waters levels on the Danube pushed Hungary to shut its sole nuclear plant, stretching power supply capacity to its limits.

Romania, meanwhile, blew up huge rocks and sank weighted barges in an effort to divert cooling water towards its nuclear plant on the Danube, after having to close one of two reactors last week. And Slovenia began reducing reactor output due to high temperatures and low flows on the Sava River. Serbia saw output at its largest hydropower plant fall to just 20 per cent of capacity, pressing the government to import electricity from abroad.

Experts say that while nuclear energy remains one of the most reliable and cost effective means of energy production, heat and drought linked to the climate crisis will create challenges for European nations to tackle in order to ensure a resilient grid ready for the future.

The European Union depends on nuclear power for about one quarter of its electricity needs and a third of its low-carbon electricity. That share has steadily risen since 2022, growing by nearly five per cent between 2023 and 2024 alone. And in March, the EU announced a further €330 million of investment to accelerate fusion energy and support nuclear technologies and skills.

open image in gallery Romanian Navy blasts rocks in controlled explosions on the Bala channel to divert the Danube water flow toward the Cernavoda nuclear power plant ( Reuters )

It has taken decades for the continent to ease public concern about nuclear power. Incidents such as the Three Mile Island meltdown in 1979 and Chernobyl in 1986 encouraged caution and anti-nuclear movements in countries like Germany, which phased out its fleet in favourable of renewables, leaving a space for Russian energy imports until the invasion of Ukraine.

Steadily, opposition to nuclear power has grown quieter in Europe and stations today span from Torness, east of Edinburgh, to Odesa in Ukraine, and Almaraz in central Spain to Loviisa in Finland. That pivot has helped deliver a relatively cost-effective and continuous source of power with a low carbon footprint. But rising temperatures in Europe, driven by the climate crisis, still creates obstacles for swathes of the European fleet.

Why drought hits nuclear plants so hard

“We need abundant carbon-free electricity to limit climate change, even as climate change makes some of that electricity harder to produce,” explained Dr Katy Huff, professor of nuclear engineering at the University of Wisconsin-Madison.

Dr Huff, who served as assistant secretary for the Office of Nuclear Energy under the Biden administration, told The Independent that the problem brought by climate change is twofold.

First, low river levels brought by drought mean that nuclear plants struggle to take as much water as they need to cool down. Second, when temperatures are already high, there are restrictions on how much warm water the plants can discharge back into the river to avoid making it hotter.

open image in gallery A sunken Nazi warship from World War II was exposed due to low Danube River levels caused by drought and extreme heat in Prahovo, Serbia, last week ( Reuters )

“The latter limits can sometimes be relaxed temporarily with ecological monitoring, but regulatory waivers can’t fix a lack of water volume,” she said.

Rest assured, nuclear power stations will not go into meltdown if gets too hot, and a reactor cannot detonate like a bomb. But turning them off in countries such as Hungary, which depends on its station for 40-50 per cent of its power, can result in drastic consequences like limits on consumption and importing expensive electricity from outside.

Dr Huff said that these conditions are not unique to nuclear power: heat impacts fossil fuel plants in much the same way as it does nuclear reactors. In Serbia, water shortages have created problems at cooling systems in coal plants. Drought also affects hydropower and heatwaves affect the efficiency of solar panels and wind turbines.

open image in gallery Satellite images shows reduced water levels along the sandbanks of the Danube River near Vukovar, Croatia (top) August 1, 2026, and water levels at the same location last year (bottom), August 1, 2025 ( European Union/Copernicus Sentinel-2 )

What can Europe do?

In the future, reactor cooling will have to account for heatwaves driven by climate change, says Henry Preston, spokesperson for the World Nuclear Association. He pointed to the UAE’s adoption of a special deep sea water intake to ensure year-round cool temperatures. Others already use liquid sodium instead of water as a coolant.

Volodymyr Kholosha, president of the Ukrainian Nuclear Society and former minister of emergencies, told The Independent that Ukraine - also situated on thousands of rivers - has developed resilience by investing in cooling ponds and reservoirs, such as in Khmelnytskyi and Zaporizhzhia, and evaporative cooling towers.

He said these changes “significantly mitigate” the impact of seasonal heatwaves compared to the standard river-cooled facilities seen in Europe.

open image in gallery Hungary turned off lights at Budapest landmarks on Wednesday to reduce energy due to the power crisis stemming from its nuclear plant not getting enough water ( Reuters )

Mr Kholosha said that while high summer temperatures do not pose safety risks to plant operations, sustained heatwaves can affect performance, adding that “climate adaptation remains an important priority for the long-term development and modernisation of Ukraine’s nuclear sector”.

“In my view, climate adaptation is becoming one of the fundamental prerequisites for long-term energy independence in Europe,” he said.

“If generation assets cannot operate at capacity during extreme weather events, energy independence becomes fragile, exposing countries to volatile spot markets or unwanted dependency on external suppliers during critical supply pinches.

open image in gallery A sandbar exposed by the low water level of the Danube River near Novi Sad, Serbia, on August 7 ( AFP/Getty )

“Ultimately, climate adaptation for both nuclear power and renewables is an essential component of overarching energy security. By insulating generation capacity from weather extremes and hydrological deficits, European nations can maintain generation reliability and avoid weather-driven reliance on energy imports.”

Europe is getting warmer as a result of a changing climate. Nuclear has a role to play in ensuring power generation does not contribute to that shift. But it too now faces a direct challenge from hotter summers - leaving the continent in a bind.

To avoid a doom-spiral of wildfires and heatwaves leading to an energy crisis every summer, politicians will have to act.

News.title: Gomes scores for Aston Villa in defeat by Bayern Munich in Hong Kong
News.content:
Aston Villa 1 Bayern Munich 2

Aston Villa’s tour of the Far East ended in defeat as they lost 2-1 to German champions Bayern Munich in a pre-season friendly at the Kai Tak Sports Park in Hong Kong on Friday.

Bayern took the lead inside the final 10 minutes of the first half, with defender Kim Min-jae heading in from Tom Bischof’s sublime free-kick. Villa goalkeeper Marco Bizot made a string of saves in the second half to keep Bayern’s lead at one goal until former Liverpool forward Luis Díaz smashed in Bayern’s second off the underside of the bar.

Just as the game appeared to be out of reach for Aston Villa, who had struggled to create much going forward for most of the game, Unai Emery’s side showed some life late on. Summer signing João Gomes’s goal from the edge of the box gave them hope before Tammy Abraham nearly brought them back onto level terms, only to be denied by a fine save from 40-year-old Manuel Neuer.

Aston Villa are next in action in six days’ time when they take on Paris St-Germain in the Uefa Super Cup before kicking off their Premier League campaign at Brighton. Bayern have one more friendly to come against RB Leipzig before the DFL-Supercup against Borussia Dortmund. They then kick off the defence of their Bundesliga crown against Stuttgart at home on August 28.

News.title: Suspected Ebola case on packed Congo river boat sparks testing rush
News.content:
Congolese health authorities have intercepted and detained a river boat on its way to the capital after a suspected Ebola case onboard.

Authorities have set up a mobile clinic to test more than 200 passengers after one of them disembarked and died earlier on the voyage.

The boat travelling from the northeastern commercial hub of Kisangani was stopped and held in Maluku, some 40 miles from Kinshasa.

Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) is dealing with its worst ever outbreak of the viral haemorrhagic fever, which has seen nearly 4,000 cases and killed around 1,801 people according to the latest government figures.

Samuel Roger Kamba, the health minister, said a 32-year-old man had disembarked in Pimu in Mongala province, before developing ‌suspected Ebola symptoms and dying.

“We did not say it was Ebola. We said there was a suspected case for which we are being cautious,” the health minister told a press conference, according to MediaCongo, a local news site.

He said there had been no other reports of deaths among travellers.

The virus has so far spread to five provinces, though more than 90 per cent of cases have been recorded in the north eastern Ituri region.

News.title: The best luxury hotels in the Cotswolds
News.content:
From gracious old farmsteads and magnificent manor houses to an ancient coaching inn creaking with Tudor character, the top luxury hotels in the Cotswolds combine a wonderful sense of history with contemporary style and outstanding modern British cuisine. Whether near picturesque Broadway in the north of the region or close to Bath in the south, location is a key attribute to them all: some offer serene escapes in acres of their own rolling parkland; others sit amid superb gardens; and several take over classic honey-stone villages that look as if they have been beamed in from a halcyon era of the past.

They all excel in providing creature comforts, whether crackling fires by kick-back sofas, canopy beds with soft throws, or suites with terraces and hot tubs. Facilities are top-notch too, ranging from beautiful bars and quiet terraces to blissful spas with inviting pools and even an opportunity for equine adventures. Read on to discover our pick of the best luxury hotels in the Cotswolds.

News.title: El Nino could cause explosion of rabid seals, animal health experts warn
News.content:
This year’s El Nino weather event risks propelling an outbreak of rabid seals around the world, the world’s animal health body has warned.

Countries in South America and Australasia are being urged to look for signs the deadly infectious disease has reached their waters, only two years after it was first confirmed in South Africa.

The 2024 discovery of rabies in South Africa’s Cape fur seals was the first significant outbreak ever found in marine mammals and has been described as a “significant shift in rabies ecology”.

More than 100 cases have been confirmed in South Africa and Namibia since then, raising fears that aggressive rabid seals could infect humans, pets and other wildlife.

Changing patterns in fish stocks caused by the El Nino phenomenon now potentially risk widening the spread, as uninfected seal populations migrate for food and come into contact with rabid colleagues.

Scientists believe warming sea temperatures off Antarctica could send seal populations northwards into Southern African waters, where they could be exposed to rabies.

They could then return to their home waters, taking the virus with them and infecting other seal populations.

News.title: ​Arteta’s ‘dynasty’ dream collides with Arsenal’s harsh reality
News.content:
Arsenal 1 Real Betis 3

Mikel Arteta says he wants to create a “dynasty” at Arsenal as he threw down the gauntlet to his players to retain their Premier League title and reach a “different level”.

Arsenal are on the verge of completing a £75m deal for Brazil midfielder Bruno Guimãraes from Newcastle and have not given up hope of landing Real Madrid winger Vinícius Júnior, who has been offered an improved contract by the Spanish giants.

The Premier League champions slumped to a 3-1 defeat to Real Betis in Dublin on Wednesday night, when they paid the price for individual errors and a lethargic, sloppy defensive display.

But that did little to quell Arteta’s ambitions for the new season. “I’m even more excited [about this season], and we’re going to go and attack every possible title because that’s the ambition that we have,” he said.

“We know that we have the ability. We will go from a strength to a strength as well, whether it’s with the players that we have to take them to a different level, and with the market that is still open to recruit as well, so we are very optimistic about it.

“All the work that we’ve done – that I’ve done through the summer – is to understand what we need to do to win again and to create a dynasty in this football club. That’s the aim.”

Despite Arteta’s bullishness, he conceded Arsenal would have to be a lot better than they were against Betis. When asked about the mood in the dressing room, he said: “Very upset, given a hard time. They are fuming, but this is good. That’s what we need.”

Telegraph Sport analyses some of the talking points from a disappointing evening at the Aviva Stadium.

No Saliba a concern

The importance of goalkeeper David Raya and centre-backs William Saliba and Gabriel Magalhães to Arsenal hardly needs overstating. Their title success was built on the foundations provided by that triumvirate at the back.

Raya has yet to report back from holiday after Spain’s World Cup triumph and Saliba is facing an extended spell on the sidelines with a back injury. Gabriel did appear for the second half but, watching this, Arteta is unlikely to have been dissuaded from the belief he needs another top defender to compensate for the loss of Saliba.

It may have been only Arsenal’s second game of pre-season, so a degree of legginess was understandable.

But the ease with which they were cut open and overloaded by the Spanish side, and the volume of individual errors, did not sit comfortably with Arteta with just over a fortnight until they kick off their title defence at home to newly promoted Coventry City.

Only once in 63 matches last season did Arsenal concede three goals in a single game but they were fortunate Betis did not score more. “In the first half there are two different things: to play well and to compete,” said Arteta, who saw his side trail 3-1 at the interval.

News.title: Ebola outbreak outpacing containment effort, WHO chief warns
News.content:
Caused by the rare Bundibugyo strain of Ebola, for which there are no vaccines or treatments, it has been extremely difficult to contain, according to experts on the ground.

“The outbreak is spreading faster than our scale-up of the response, with new cases doubling in some hotspots over the past week alone,” Dr Tedros said on X.

Part of the difficulty is that the virus was circulating undetected for weeks before the outbreak was formally declared in mid-May, leaving health officials even now racing to catch up with the spread.

Prof Placide Mbala, director of research, clinical trials and innovation at Africa CDC, told the Telegraph: “It’s mostly the fact we arrived a bit late. It took us some time before we detected this virus outbreak. And when we detected the outbreak, we already had a total of I can say more than 200 suspected cases. It’s been difficult to catch up. That’s where we are.”

While the DRC has a wealth of experience in tackling haemorrhagic fever outbreaks, the effects of that initial delay are still being felt.

Prof Mbala said: “We have some experience dealing with the cases, the labs, the communication, the infection prevention and control.

“We have some experience... But my observation is that we were very slow, and it’s why we’re in this situation.

“We are slow detecting the people, slow responding, we are slow deploying people, we are slow to recruit the community healthcare workers to improve contact tracing, we are slow to deploy the safe burials.”

DRC’s largest outbreak had previously been from 2018 to 2020, when 3,481 cases were recorded.

The West Africa outbreak recorded 28,616 cases and 11,310 deaths according to the WHO.

Prof Mbala said insecurity was also severely hampering attempts to curb the virus. The outbreak epicentre is in Ituri province, which has been wracked by ethnic strife for decades and is also home to militias competing to control mining.

He said: “There are many, many mining groups controlling most of the mining places. We have a big issue with those places, because they are places where the response team cannot go.”

Medics and aid workers have also been undermined by violent public distrust of their efforts.

Locals in the area have either doubted the existence of the virus, or have accused health teams of deliberately spreading the infection, or somehow benefiting from it.

More than a dozen health facilities have been set alight and several health workers have been killed.

Prof Mbala said: “The local people, they also sometimes are very upset, because they believe that it’s a kind of a business, and people who are coming here, they are getting a lot of money, [so] don’t want this disease to stop.”

He said he hoped that immunity was starting to rise in some areas and this would start to curb transmission.

However there was also a risk that people fleeing the outbreak would spread the virus further afield.

He said: “The second scenario is the fact we are seeing people moving from the affected area to new areas, to run away from the response team because they do not want to go to the treatment centre.

“And in complicity with their family members living in other areas, they are now the ones who are spreading the disease to new areas

“So we’ll see new places affected because people are moving around from the affected zone to the non-affected zone.”

News.title: Mykhailo Mudryk returns as Chelsea slip to Juventus defeat
News.content:
Chelsea 0 Juventus 1

Mykhailo Mudryk made his first Chelsea appearance since November 2024 as Xabi Alonso’s team succumbed to their second pre-season defeat.

Mudryk replaced Nicolas Jackson in the 82nd minute against Juventus, marking his return to competitive football after a long doping ban that was resolved this week thanks to changes in Wada regulations.

There were a couple of crosses delivered from the left flank by the Ukrainian winger, who could yet leave Chelsea on loan or on a permanent basis before the close of the transfer window.

Juventus were the victors though, thanks to a sumptuous 68th-minute goal by Kosovo winger Edon Zhegrova.

Alonso had 21 players on his bench, and made 12 second-half substitutions.

Levi Colwill and Cole Palmer featured in the defeat by 10-man Spurs on Saturday, but sat this game out as they continue to build fitness. Danny Welbeck did start though, reunited with former Brighton team-mate Joao Pedro up top.

Chelsea scored just one goal against Spurs and Juventus, but the thrust provided by right-back Marco Palestra in tandem with first Geovany Quenda and then Estevao was a bright spot for Alonso.

Chelsea continue their pre-season against AC Milan on Saturday, before they host Real Sociedad at Stamford Bridge on August 15.

They begin their Premier League campaign at Fulham in the Monday night slot on the opening weekend.

News.title: The underground lab where ‘princess mosquitoes’ are treated like royalty
News.content:
Beneath the grand Art Deco headquarters of the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine lies a vast labyrinth inhabited by weird and wonderful creatures.

In this maze of subterranean labs, store rooms and corridors live colonies of disease-bearing insects and arachnids from all over the world, from bed bugs, sand flies and microscopic dust mites to the so-called kissing bugs that spread Chagas disease – a sinister condition that can cause its victims to drop dead of heart failure without warning, albeit decades after the first (silent) infection.

Behind a series of doors, contained in stacks of mesh boxes, you can even find the flies that spread trachoma, the Dickensian eye disease that is still a leading cause of blindness around the world. But be warned: entering the room is not for the faint of heart – the flies feed on human excrement and the smell is impossible to forget.

There are also many varieties of mosquito, including several species of the Anopheles genus that spread malaria, Culex and Aedes mosquitoes that are also vectors for human and animal diseases, and even Toxorhynchites, perhaps better known as the elephant mosquito, a friendly giant which doesn’t bite people but preys on other mosquitoes.

These animals have been studied intensely since the insectaries were established in the building’s vaults in the 1960s, underpinning many breakthroughs in the control, surveillance, and understanding of vector-borne diseases in the developing world.

LSHTM researchers are now looking closer to home. They have established the UK’s first laboratory colony of Aedes vexans mosquitoes, a species native to the British isles, to study whether they could harbour diseases like West Nile virus, Rift Valley fever, Zika or Japanese encephalitis.

Sports.title: Bruno Guimaraes reveals he joined Arsenal to ‘make history’ as he completes £75million transfer from Newcastle
Sports.content:
ARSENAL have signed Bruno Guimaraes from Newcastle for £75million.

The Gunners confirmed the Brazilian’s arrival on Saturday, almost exactly a month after he asked to leave St James’ Park.



Guimaraes, 28, signed a four-year deal with an option to extend until 2031 after completing his medical on Thursday.

Newcastle had been reluctant to sell their skipper but they caved in after Arsenal offered to pay the full fee up front.



The North Londoners are long-standing admirers of Guimaraes, and Mikel Arteta was desperate to capture him in this window.

Former Gunners sporting director Edu started tracking him as a youngster at Athletico Paranaense and the club continued to keep tabs on him at Lyon and Newcastle.



Guimaraes said after his arrival: “Well, I feel good, I feel amazing. I’m glad for the opportunity. Since the first time I spoke to [Arsenal sporting director Andrea] Berta and Mikel [Arteta], I was excited.

“I just felt inside of me that I need a new challenge in my life and I think to be an Arsenal player is going to be an exciting challenge in my life.

“I’m so excited to join them, not only the Brazilians, we have an amazing squad here. I’m so excited to meet the other players, to start training. I just want to give my best.

“I want to win trophies, I want to make history and I think I’m in the right place to do it. I’m so excited to start.



BEST ONLINE CASINOS – TOP SITES IN THE UK

“We have tough games to play this season, so the squad is going to be very, very important and I’m hopeful we can achieve our dreams.

“[Declan] Rice sent me a message: ‘Come here and please no more fights, now we’re friends’. I was happy he messaged me, but the midfield we have here, in my point of view, is one of the best in Europe.

“Everyone is an amazing player, I’m so excited to start chatting and play, and know the players very, very well, but we have an amazing midfield.

“The message for me is thank you for everything you have done. All the messages you gave me, I’m so excited to join you. I will give you my best, I promise.

“Like I said, I’m your warrior, I’ll never give up. Hopefully we can create many, many good memories together.”



Berta welcomed Guimaraes to the Emirates and explained Arsenal went full on for his signature due to his versatility in midfield.

The Italian executive added the Brazil international will help Arteta further develop the North Londoners’ “playing style”.

Berta said: “We are delighted to welcome Bruno Guimaraes to our club. Bruno is a player with a great mentality and great quality, who will bring strong leadership to our squad.

“With Bruno joining us, we are further strengthening the heart of our team. As we have all seen, Bruno can play as a defensive midfielder and as a box-to-box player.

“He combines quality with quantity, and has provided goals and assists for his team every year.



“Bruno will allow Mikel to further develop our playing style and will also increase our internal competitiveness, which is essential for maintaining the standards required when we are aiming to win major trophies.”

This has been a painful transfer window for the Toon, who have lost a raft of key players and manager Eddie Howe.

Anthony Gordon and Sandro Tonali were both sold for big money, but the looming sale of Guimaraes was reportedly the “final straw” for Howe, who quit last week.

New boss Matthias Jaissle should have cash for a rebuild but about £7m of the Guimaraes fee will go to Lyon, who are entitled to 20 per cent of the Magpies’ profit.

Guimaraes broke down in tears as he said goodbye to his Newcastle team-mates.



He said in a statement to the Toon: “This is one of the toughest decisions of my life. When I arrived, the club was in a challenging position and I am incredibly proud of what we achieved together.

“I fell in love with this place. I really mean that. From my first day, the supporters, my teammates, Eddie and the staff, and everyone connected with the club made me and my family feel at home.

“I thank PIF, our chairman Yasir Al-Rumayyan and Jamie Reuben for everything they have done for me and for this football club. I also want to say thank you to David and Ross for the huge respect to me throughout this process. They did everything they could to keep me at Newcastle, and I am very grateful for our time together.

“This move is very tough because Newcastle means so much to me, but I wanted to experience something new in my life. I feel ready for a new challenge for myself and my family. I had a very positive conversation with Matthias Jaissle, and I leave knowing the club is in very good hands.

“To the supporters, thank you will never be enough, but I say it with all my heart. I will always be proud to have been part of this club’s journey. Thank you for everything.”



Arsenal had already signed Christos Tzolis and Illan Meslier this summer, as well as making Piero Hincapie’s loan move permanent.

But the signing of an established Premier League star in Guimaraes will take their squad to another level.

It will also relieve some of the burden from Declan Rice, who played over 60 matches for club and country last season and carried niggling injuries into the World Cup.

All-action Guimaraes, who scored nine league goals last term, can also bring an attacking flair to the midfield.

Josh Kroenke described Rice as a “plug-and-play” signing when Arsenal splashed £105m on him in 2023.

Guimaraes will be expected to make a similar impact at the Emirates.

And his arrival will make up for missing out on Vinicius Jr, who opted to sign a contract extension at Real Madrid after being courted by the Gunners.
