Several roads were submerged under water Image: Parveen Kumar/Hindustan Times/Sipa USA/picture alliance

On Friday, Delhi recorded record rainfall, India Meteorological Department (IMD) records show, making it the wettest first week of August in over a decade.

As the heavy rain lashed the city, several highways and streets were submerged under up to four feet of water, disrupting daily life.

The IMD issued a red alert for the city.

The waterlogged roads brought traffic to a standstill, especially in the adjoining Gurugram.

According to the IMD, the showers were triggered by multiple low-pressure systems passing through Delhi, southwest Uttar Pradesh and neighboring regions.

World.title: Typhoon Dolphin hits Japan as China braces for coming storm
World.content:
A typhoon is lashing Japan's south, causing injuries and blackouts. It is now headed for China, where ports have been closed in preparation.

Typhoon Dolphin raged over Japan's southern regions on Saturday, causing some injuries and blackouts.

Okinawa and Amami island in Kagoshima prefecture were the areas expected to be worst affected.

The storm is expected to move on to China, making landfall along its eastern and southern ‌coast between late Sunday and early Monday, with Chinese authorities shutting down ports and ferry services ahead of the storm.

What do we know about Typhoon Dolphin in Japan?

The typhoon has brought maximum sustained winds of 162 kilometers per hour (roughly 100 miles per hour) and ​gusts reaching ‌216 kph

Authorities in Okinawa prefecture said 240 people had taken shelter at evacuation centers in the region on Friday

Five elderly people were reported to have suffered non-life-threatening injuries

Japan Meteorological Agency forecast strong winds, heavy rain and high waves in the Okinawa region through Sunday

The Naha Airport on Okinawa Island said it closed on Friday, and all domestic and international flights in and out of Naha, the prefectural capital, have been canceled

Power was cut to some 14,000 buildings in Okinawa

What preparations is China making for Typhoon Dolphin?

The China National Meteorological Centre Typhoon Dolphin has said Typhoon Dolphin will probably make landfall between the city of Zhoushan in Zhejiang province and the city of Fuding in Fujian province.

Zhejiang has raised its coastal typhoon alert to its highest level, while ceasing port operations and suspending 162 passenger ferry routes.

The storm is expected to bring rain and strong winds to eastern China, including parts of Shanghai, through August 12.

Some parts of eastern Zhejiang could be in for a deluge, forecasters say, with more than 600 mm (23.6 inches) of rain possible.

Ningbo ⁠Lishe ​International Airport in Zhejiang said it will stop its operations from 11:30 ​p.m. (1530 GMT) on Saturday and suspend all flights on Sunday.

Fishing boats in Wenling in Zhejiang province have sought shelter ahead of the storm Image: Zhou Xuejun/Xinhua/AP Photo/picture alliance

Taiwan-China tensions over typhoon restrictions

Taiwan, where 63 international flights have been cancelled, is also expected to experience heavy rain in the north over the weekend.

New political friction between Taiwan and China has also arisen after Beijing ordered that ships passing through ⁠the Taiwan Strait must heed ​its traffic control

instructions amid the typhoon.

Taipei has slammed Beijing's injunctions as "ridiculous," saying that Beijing has no right to restrict access to international waters.

"The unreasonable and crude statement ‌by ​the relevant Chinese Communist departments reflects an ignorance, disregard, and trampling of international order and norms. It is utterly ridiculous!" Taiwan's Mainland Affairs Council said in a statement late ​on Friday.

China regards the democratically governed island as a breakaway territory of its own and also claims to own the strategic strait, a stance rejected by both Taipei and Washington.

World.title: Germany debates reintroducing mandatory civilian service
World.content:
Social organizations are skeptical about the government's ideas for a civilian service program that youths could choose as an alternative should Germany reinstate mandatory military conscription.

Germany's constitution, the Basic Law, guarantees that no person can be forced into armed military service. Should the government reinstate mandatory conscription, a civilian-service alternative would have to be established for people who invoke their right to refuse military service on moral grounds as conscientious objectors.

Germany's federal government is making arrangements for this. The Family Affairs Ministry, led by Karin Prien, of the conservative Christian Democrats (CDU), has confirmed that in recent months it reached out to 23 large associations and organizations to ask what capacities they had to offer if civilian service were reinstated. Of those, 22 indicated a general willingness to offer opportunities for civilian service participants.

Thorsten Frei, the parliamentary group leader of the center-right bloc of the CDU and Christian Social Union (CDU/CSU) in the Bundestag, told the German broadcasters RTL and ntv that it was "very clever and correct" for the Family Affairs Ministry to prepare in this way. However, Frei said, there are no new developments in the discussion surrounding the possible reinstatement of conscription.

Germany looks at conscription to boost military numbers To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Bundeswehr seeks soldiers

After lengthy negotiations, the coalition government of the CDU/CSU and the center-left Social Democrats (SPD) agreed that military service would remain voluntary in Germany for now. Whether this remains the case will depend on how many soldiers the German armed forces, the Bundeswehr, can recruit in the coming months and years.

The goal is to increase the number of troops from 185,000 to at least 260,000 by 2030 in order to strengthen national defenses and fulfill NATO requirements. Or, as German Chancellor Friedrich Merz (CDU) put it: The Bundeswehr should become the strongest conventional army in Europe.

The so-called new military service, which has been in force since the start of this year, is also expected to boost the recruitment effort. It combines improved conditions for volunteers with responsibilities applying to all 18-year-old men: They must fill out a questionnaire to answer if they would be prepared to serve in the army.

They are required to undergo medical examinations and to state whether they are interested in joining the armed forces. However, they maintain the constitutional right to refuse military service as conscientious objectors.

Bundeswehr applications increase

Even without reinstating compulsory military service, the recruitment drive is on track to reach its target for 2026, according to a June forecast by Germany's Defense Ministry. However, only about 530 young men have voluntarily signed up to the military as a direct result of the Bundeswehr questionnaire in 2026.

So, though a return to conscription is not currently expected, it remains an option for the government. Combined with civilian service, it was in place in Germany (starting in West Germany in 1956) until 2011, when it was suspended. However, it was not removed from the constitution. So, parliament can reactivate it by law if needed, for example if the country's security situation changes.

The alternative, mandatory civilian service (Zivildienst) usually involved working in a hospital or care home for several months.

This civilian service was replaced in 2011 by the Bundesfreiwilligendienst , or federal volunteer service, which is open to people of all ages and genders. Conscription only applied to men.

'Government-mandated cheap labor'

Major German welfare organizations have pledged their support should civilian service be relaunched. At the same time, they warn against false expectations. The general consensus is that civilian service is no fix for acute staff shortages in the social services sector. Instead of relying on obligation, the federal government should instead strengthen the optional engagement of young people.

"Our main wish is improved conditions for the voluntary services," Eva Maria Welskop-Deffaa, the president of the German Caritas Association , told the public broadcaster ARD. "And there is still a lot of room for improvement on that."



Imported care giver: Skilled, needed, stalled by bureaucracy To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Germany's opposition parties have also criticized a possible return to mandatory civilian service. According to the socialist Left Party, the state "should not dictate how young people spend a year of their lives," co-leader Ines Schwerdtner said. That applied to both military and civilian service. On the other side, young people should not serve as "stopgaps for a welfare state" which the government "has been systematically underfunding for years." Nursing care, emergency services and social institutions did not need "government-mandated cheap labor," Schwerdtner told the Funke media group.

In any case, the Family Affairs Ministry sees a need to revise and modernize the current civilian service law. It plans to present its proposals after Germany's summer recess.

This article was originally written in German.

World.title: Ceuta: Spain sets up border controls on travelers from Italy
World.content:
Spain had warned Italy it would impose entry checks on visitors unless Rome halts its controls by Sunday. Even though they don't share a land border, the countries entered a spat after the Ceuta border rush.

Spain's government on Friday moved to impose reciprocal entry checks on people traveling from Italy. The Spanish government had warned that it would do so unless Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni's governemnt lifted the border measures it has implemented against Spain.

Italy's right-wing government announced the checks at the height of the social media panic as tens of thousands of people gained entry into the Spanish exclave of Ceuta bordering Morocco last week.

The checks are essentially symbolic, given that Ceuta is not on the European mainland and Italy and Spain do not share a land border, meaning that the vast majority of people potentially affected are tourists on planes.

Nevertheless, the issue has turned into a point of dispute between two governments of different ideological persuasions with contrasting messaging priorities on migration policy.

Did Morocco instigate the Ceuta migrant incident? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

What did Spain say about checks on travelers from Italy?

The border controls on Italy will go into effect from midnight ‌on ⁠Saturday ⁠until September 7, the Spanish government said. Border agents will check passport, nationality and visas for Italian passengers and visitors from other ​countries arriving from Italy.

Spain had called Italy's decision to impose checks on people arriving from Spain "unjustified, contrary to the interests of the European Union and discriminatory against ​the Spanish population."

Madrid said there was no real risk of people who overwhelmed Ceuta's border controls reaching the European mainland, let alone Italy. It pointed to the vast majority of the estimated 72,000 people returning to Morocco within days. Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez also drew attention to the higher numbers of irregular migrants reaching Italian than Spanish territory in recent years.

"If [Italy] fails to [remove the entry checks] before Sunday, August 9, Spain will be forced to adopt proportionate measures to protect the interests and dignity of its citizens," the government said.

Italy replied later Friday that it would not accept "ultimatums ⁠or ⁠impositions" from Madrid, and that it would maintain the suspension of Schengen rules for non-EU nationals arriving from Spain until at least August 15.

Despite Spain's objections, an array of European countries, including Germany, and the European Commission all made comments about the importance of border security to the open-border Schengen Zoneamid the public uproar. Italy was among comparatively few to go so far as to frame the issue as "suspending" Spain's Schengen status, however.

Italy first made the announcement as images and footage of the border breach were going viral online Image: Atlas/REUTERS

What do we know about Italy's checks on travelers from Spain?

Details on precisely what checks, if any, Italy has actually implemented over the past week have been thin on the ground.

Migration analyst Gerald Knaus told DW earlier this week that the move was "pure populism" and a "completely bizarre" measure.

"They don't have a border, so it's only for a few flights," Knaus said. "It makes no sense in the high tourist season. And as Giorgia Meloni indicated, it shouldn't inconvenience travelers."

Knaus said the decision could only be understood in the context of domestic political appearances, not foreign policy realities.

"I think to understand it, you must understand that on [Meloni's] right, there is a radical right party in Italy that puts pressure on her. And so politicians everywhere in Europe, when they see these images which create fear, are looking for something to say — something to do that makes them look tough."

EU defends border response after Ceuta crossing To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Meloni and Sanchez: A clash of styles on migration

At least in terms of their stated positions and approaches, Italy and Spain have quite different stances on the issue of migration.

Meloni came to power in 2022 in Italy, after several years of much higher irregular migration rates and asylum applications caused in large part by the wars in Syria and Ukraine. She promised a tougher line on migration into one of the most common landing points in southern Europe.

Sanchez, meanwhile, has championed a more pro-migration stance during his two terms in office. He argues that Spain's economy needs migration and offered an amnesty and temporary residency permit process earlier this year to irregular migrants already in the country. Sanchez said it was better to grant residency and start collecting taxes than to keep people out of the formal labor market.

Migration expert Knaus, however, warned against overstating the practical differences between the two countries, saying Meloni faced similar economic requirements and was actually pursuing comparable policies — only with much less public fanfare.

"Italy is doing something very similar. Hundreds of thousands of people are brought in or are already in the country and are regularized for the Italian labour market under Giorgia Meloni," Knaus said. "And 1.6 million people were regularized under various Italian governments in the last 20 years."

World.title: Colombia: Trump ally De la Espriella takes office
World.content:
Conservative Abelardo de la Espriella was sworn in as Colombia's president, promising to crack down on armed drug gangs.

Abelardo de la Espriella was sworn in as Colombia's president on Friday, promising to boost ties with the United States and tackle armed groups linked to the drug trade.

The 48-year-old ex-lawyer lurches the Andean nation to the right, taking office after winning a close June 21 runoff against Sen. Ivan Cepeda, an ally of outgoing President Gustavo Petro.

Security was stepped up in case armed groups ambushed the occasion Image: Luis Acosta/AFP

What happened at the inauguration?

In a speech shortly after his swearing-in, De la Espriella vowed once again to wipe out "narcoterrorism" in the South American country.

"The option of dialogue is completely exhausted," he said, referring to his predecessor, who had promoted a peaceful resolution to the crisis.

De la Espriella then promised to restore "order, authority and freedom" to the South American nation.

"There will be no room for maneuvers that undermine the stability of the nation," said the hardline leader, who has spoken of opening mega-prisons to house captured rebels and drug dealers.

Instead of the capital Bogota, the inauguration took place at a university in the southwestern city of Cali.

Colombia’s third-largest city is located near major drug-trafficking corridors and the Pacific coast, and is a regular scene of violence by rival groups.

Among the VIP guests were King Felipe VI of Spain, acting US Attorney General Todd Blanche, FIFA President Gianni Infantino and Latin American presidents, including Argentina's Javier Milei, Ecuador's Daniel Noboa and Chile's Jose Antonio Kast.

Outgoing president Petro declined to attend the ceremony and called for mass protests Friday, claiming election fraud without providing evidence.

After the swearing-in, the new president was due to address troops at a military barracks Image: Matias Delacroix/AP Photo/picture alliance

Who is Abelardo de la Espriella?

The 48-year-old is a former lawyer and businessman who has never held public office.

He funded his campaign with the profits from his law firm and other business ventures in the agri-food, real estate and fashion sectors.

The self-styled "El Tigre" (The Tiger) plans to forge a military alliance with the US and Israel to aid his war on rebel groups, including remnants of the FARC guerrillas, who waged an armed conflict that peaked in the 1990s and 2000s.

De la Espriella won the backing of US President Donald Trump after committing Colombia to a US-backed coalition to fight drug trafficking, dubbed the "Shield of the Americas."

He has also offered to launch joint military operations with Washington and even host US troops on Colombian soil.

The millionaire has also announced plans to resume diplomatic relations with Israel and sever them with Cuba and Nicaragua.

De la Espriella's win is another point for right-wing politics in Latin America, after electoral victories from Chile to Costa Rica, having also promised to crack down on security issues.

World.title: Última hora de la entrada de inmigrantes a Ceuta, en directo | Primeros controles a viajeros desde Italia: “A los que no tenían DNI les han llevado a otra sala para identificarles”
World.content:
Primeros controles a viajeros desde Italia: "A los que no tenían DNI les han llevado a otra sala para identificarles"

Giovanni ha subido la mañana de este sábado a un avión en Roma con destino al aeropuerto del Prat en Barcelona. “Al llegar, la policía nos ha dividido en dos grupos. A los italianos nos han pedido la documentación. Espero que esta situación acabe lo antes posible”, admitía un tanto molesto en la zona de salidas de la T1 del aeropuerto catalán.

Fuentes de la Policía Nacional en la infraestructura aeroportuaria barcelonesa aseguraban este sábado: “Italia es un país caliente en materia de inmigración. Solo revisaremos a los pasajeros que sospechemos que han subido en algún avión pero son de procedencia extracomunitaria y quieren acceder a España”.

En la práctica, los controles en Barcelona se han hecho de forma totalmente aleatoria, concentrándose en un vuelo procedente de Roma. De hecho, la normalidad imperaba esta mañana en el aeropuerto. Jorge Villoslada es Español. Viaja muy a menudo y este sábado partió de Roma en dirección Barcelona. “Ha pasado algo muy raro. Al llegar, la policía nos ha preguntado qué hacíamos en España. Yo he enseñado mi DNI y me han dejado salir. A los que no tenían documentación española les han llevado a una sala para identificarles”, sostiene.

El vuelo procedente de Bolonia ha tenido mayor suerte en lo que a controles policiales se refiere. Libia es de Módena. Ha subido este sábado a un avión en Bolonia dirección a Barcelona. “Al llegar al Prat no hemos encontrado ningún control. Creo que el problema es más en Italia. Nicoletta es de Turín y ha aterrizado en el mismo vuelo. “Hemos llegado con el carné de identidad en la mano por si había problemas, pero nadie ha dicho nada”.

World.title: Ajax, ING and Ace & Tate hit by data breach
World.content:
Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Football club Ajax, bank ING and eyewear chain Ace & Tate have been caught up in the data breach at logistics firm CEVA Logistics, which came to light this week when Bol and De Bijenkorf warned customers their details may have been exposed.

CEVA handles deliveries for the companies and had access to the customer data needed to fulfil orders. The firm says it cannot rule out that personal details were leaked, although the companies affected say no payment details, usernames or passwords were taken.

Whether addresses, email addresses or phone numbers were exposed remains unclear.

At ING, the breach affects customers who ordered physical products through the bank’s rewards points scheme.

Ajax has advised supporters to be extra alert to phishing messages in the coming weeks. The club and Ace & Tate have both reported the breach to privacy watchdog AP, as Bol did earlier this week.

Ace & Tate has warned customers that current orders may be delayed, although online ordering is still running. CEVA said it would respond to the breach at a later stage.

World.title: Actor Peter Faber, star of Dutch cinema’s golden age, dies at 82
World.content:
Peter Faber, one of the best-known faces of Dutch film and theatre for half a century, has died at the age of 82.

Faber was admitted to hospital in early July with breathing difficulties related to untreatable heart problems, his family told news agency ANP.

He broke through in the 1970s, widely regarded as the golden age of Dutch cinema, with roles in Keetje Tippel and Paul Verhoeven’s wartime classic Soldaat van Oranje – the film that later spawned the long-running musical which closed last month after 16 years.

He also took the title role in the 1976 film of Max Havelaar, Multatuli’s classic novel about Dutch colonial rule, and appeared alongside Sean Connery and Anthony Hopkins in Richard Attenborough’s A Bridge Too Far.

Faber began his career as a co-founder of Het Werkteater, an Amsterdam collective set up in the early 1970s to shake up Dutch theatre with performances about ordinary people and recognisable emotions. He won the Louis d’Or, the top Dutch theatre prize for a male actor, twice.

He kept working into his eighties. His final film role came in 2023 in Sweet Dreams, the Dutch entry for the 2024 Oscars, in which he appeared alongside his son Jesse.

Faber often spoke about his difficult upbringing, part of which he spent living on the streets of Amsterdam as a teenager. In 2008 he set up the Peter Faber Foundation to help young people build confidence, and to “make the switch from destructive to creative energy”. Its motto is “I can do it, I want it, I’m doing it. Now!”

A public memorial service will be held at Het Zonnehuis in Amsterdam-Noord on Monday between 10am and midday.

World.title: Cabinet rules out compensation for drought-hit businesses
World.content:
Despite the country’s continuing water shortage, entrepreneurs feeling the squeeze won’t be receiving any help from the government any time soon.

“There are arrangements in place for the event of a natural disaster, such as the flooding in Limburg in 2021, but we are not there yet,” infrastructure and water management minister Vincent Karremans said while visiting Nijmegen on Thursday.

“We don’t have the money in the account either. We can’t help it that it isn’t raining.”

Maarten Ouboter, a technician for the Amstel, Gooi and Vecht water authority, told DutchNews: “The question is: how much is a government – the public – responsible for the weather? The minister was clear: droughts can happen.”

Low water levels are hurting everyone from inland vessels that can’t sail down dwindling rivers to houseboat owners on the Rhine who have effectively been marooned. Several locks have been closed, ferries have been cancelled and the economically important Twente Canal, reported broadcaster NOS, is also inaccessible.

And while Karremans estimates that the economic damage to businesses runs “into the tens, if not hundreds of millions of euros”, he views the water shortage as an “entrepreneurial risk, after all” – not a natural disaster.

A shortage but not a crisis

For now, the country’s water level remains at 2 – a shortage but not yet a crisis. That could change if the drought continues for another few weeks. But the government maintains its priorities are preserving the country’s dikes and ensuring enough available drinking water, not propping up businesses.

“We are now at a point that the rivers flowing into our low-lying delta have never been so low in August,” said Ouboter, who focuses on the Amsterdam area. “We are comparable to 1947, but that was in November.”

Using a football analogy, he said the drought “in June was ‘second league’; in July it was ‘first league’; in August, it’s Champions League.”

Boosting water storage

Karremans said more water must be stored for the future, including in places like the IJsselmeer and the Volkerak-Zoommeer. The cabinet is currently working on the Freshwater Delta Plan to ensure rainwater captured in the spring, for example, can be used in drier months.

In Amsterdam, an innovative system of wadis – dry water ditches – catches rainwater that can be distributed later where needed and also absorbs extra rainwater to prevent flooding.

“The way we think about water has changed,” said Ton Hilhorst, the chief garden designer at Amsterdam’s Artis zoo. “Water was always seen as the enemy, but now we must keep it in the country, not pump it out.”

Weather forecasters are predicting another warm and largely cloudless weekend, with rain unlikely in the current week.

World.title: Philip Morris rebuked over AI campaign against EU tobacco rules
World.content:
The Dutch advertising standards watchdog RCC has reprimanded tobacco behemoth Philip Morris for an AI-powered ad campaign that it says violated the country’s tobacco advertising ban.

As the EU prepares its biggest tobacco tightening rules in 15 years, the public was invited to share its views via comments.

But a recent investigation by broadcaster NOS and the journalism platform Pointer found that Philip Morris used AI to generate hundreds of fake “citizen” responses opposing tougher EU rules on vapes, which along with other cigarette alternatives like e-cigarettes and heated tobacco, now account for 40% of the company’s revenue.

Here’s how the campaign worked: Philip Morris put up yellow posters carrying QR codes in tobacco shops under the slogan “Your Voice Your Choice.” Scanning the code led to a tool that asked multiple-choice questions and then an option to write a first-person text, which users could then send to the Commission.

The investigation found that some 71% of responses from the Netherlands were written by AI, the second highest after Portugal.

The RCC had several problems with the campaign, including that the text generator was paid for and owned by Philip Morris. The company defended its actions by saying it contributed to the public debate.

“The fact that the statements are framed as a call for public consultation does not detract from their commercial character,” said the watchdog.

The written responses also portray alternative tobacco products positively, which the RCC says constitutes advertising and therefore violates the tobacco advertising ban.

Doctors

In June, a group of doctors and healthcare campaign groups made a formal complaint to the RCC, saying the “misleading” campaign used an AI tool to influence European decision-making on tobacco and nicotine products.

Lawyer Laura van Gijn, who represents the doctors, told NOS that violating the tobacco advertising ban is a criminal offence. “This decision is a clear signal to the tobacco industry that digital influence campaigns do not fall outside the scope of the advertising ban, even when packaged as citizen participation. This precedent is relevant for similar campaigns elsewhere in Europe.”

World.title: No more “shame lips”: Dutch dictionary adds new word for labia
World.content:
Women’s rights groups are applauding the latest addition to the definitive Dutch dictionary Dikke Van Dale of the word labia: vulvalippen, added alongside the word schaamlippen.

While both words mean labia, the old schaamlippen translates as “shame lips”, which the organisations say is stigmatising as compared to the more neutral “vulva lips”.

“We should just mention these parts in our education with children and young people,” artist Esther van der Valk told broadcaster NOS. “People now know that this is a normal word, and with that we can break the taboo.”

Van der Valk is a member of Dolle Mina, the women’s rights group that was founded in the Netherlands in 1969 and has been advocating for the inclusion of vulvalippen in the Dutch dictionary to counter stigmatisation. They’re joined by Schaamteloos, a more recent campaign seeking to change language and attitudes regarding female anatomy.

Body positive

While schaamlippen will remain in the dictionary, the addition of vulvalippen means the word gets official Dutch language status – proof, say the activists, that the normalisation of sexuality via language can be achieved if enough people want it.

Schaamlippen is not the only word where shame is embedded in its name. There’s schaamhaar – “shame hair” – which is the name for pubic hair, schaambeen (shame bone) for pubic bone and even schaamstreek (shame area) for pubic area.

But Schaamteloos says it had to start somewhere, so it picked schaamlippen. “Everyone has pubic hair, a pubic bone, and a pubic area,” says the group, but “only half of us have labia – or ‘shame lips’ … which adds to a disproportionately large amount of trouble due to the taboo on talking about this.”

While some doctors and even the media have taken to using vulvalippen, it’s not yet part of the everyday Dutch vernacular.

That may change when the new anatomically correct word is included in the Dikke van Dale. That’s expected to happen during its next online update, likely this Autumn.

World.title: Four arrested for death threat against Breda mayor
World.content:
Police have arrested four men suspected of threatening to kill Breda mayor Paul Depla, after a photograph found on a football supporter’s phone revealed new evidence for a case that had stalled.

A banner bearing the words “Depla Dood” (Depla dead) was hung on the front of a café in the city’s Meidoornstraat on March 8, when NAC Breda played Feyenoord. Depla reported the threat to the police, but in May prosecutors said the case had halted because the suspects could not be linked to the banner.

A breakthrough came when several NAC supporters were arrested over rioting around the club’s match against Heerenveen on May 10 and their phones were seized, police said. On one of them, officers found a photograph of the banner in which four men could be identified.

The four – three from Breda, aged 16, 32 and 34, and a 24-year-old from Oosterhout – were arrested on Thursday and will be questioned. Threatening a public official carries a maximum prison sentence of four years.

It is unclear what prompted the threat, but broadcaster NOS reported it may have followed a warning from the city council to a different café, which had planned to host a pre-match party for the club’s hardcore supporters.

When the owners called the party off, the group gathered at the Meidoornstraat café instead, where the banner was hung.

Threats and intimidation against Dutch public officials are a growing concern. Some 45% of local and regional political office holders, including mayors, told a 2024 home affairs ministry survey they had faced aggression in the preceding year.

World.title: Warm, dry weekend ahead as drought shows no sign of ending
World.content:
The Netherlands is set for another warm and largely cloudless weekend, with barely a drop of rain likely for the coming week, according to forecasters.

Friday will be calm and dry with temperatures of 21 to 25°, with morning cloud in the north east giving way to sunshine. Saturday will be sunny and slightly warmer, at 25 to 28°, before temperatures climb to around 30° inland on Sunday.

A brief cooler spell will push maximums down to around 25° on Tuesday, but forecasters expect the warmth to return later in the week – without any significant rain.

The dry spell means no let-up for the ongoing drought, which has pushed the Rhine to record low levels and prompted water use restrictions in several regions.

World.title: Childcare benefits falling short for most parents: CBS
World.content:
Almost two-thirds of parents who claim childcare benefits pay more than the government’s maximum hourly rate, leaving them with hundreds of euros in costs the benefit does not cover, according to national statistics agency CBS.

Parents claiming the benefit spent an average of €10,510 on childcare in 2025, of which 68% was covered, up from 65% in 2024. The benefit was raised in both years as a step towards the government plan for near-free childcare.

But childcare providers are free to set their own fees, and the benefit only applies to costs up to a ceiling fixed by the government each year. In 2025, 63% of parents paid more than the maximum rate for at least one child.

On average, parents paid €3,340 towards childcare themselves last year – €2,860 in regular contributions, plus an extra €480 to cover fees above the official maximum.

The share of parents paying over the ceiling varies widely. In Nunspeet, Bloemendaal, Houten and Midden-Delfland, almost 90% pay more than the maximum rate, compared with just 8% on the island of Ameland. The proportion is highest in the provinces of Utrecht and Noord-Holland and lowest in Friesland and Groningen.

Households in the lowest income group paid an average of €1,190 towards childcare, or 11% of the total cost, while the highest earners paid €5,950, just over half the bill.

In total, 719,000 parents claimed the benefit last year for nearly 1.1 million children. More children attended nurseries and after-school clubs, while the number looked after by registered childminders (gastouders) fell by 10,000 to around 95,000.

The cabinet plans to make childcare almost free for working parents from 2029, covering 96% of costs regardless of income – a scheme that has been repeatedly delayed.

World.title: Candidate to lead Polish state history institute rejected in rare clash between houses of parliament
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. In a rare clash between Poland’s two houses of parliament, in both of which the government has a majority, the Senate has rejected a candidate chosen by the Sejm to become the new head of the state Institute of National Remembrance (IPN). The nominee, Mateusz Szpytma, has served as deputy head of the IPN since 2016, including when it was under the leadership of Karol Nawrocki, who last year was elected president of Poland with the support of the national-conservative opposition Law and Justice (PiS) party. Szpytma’s candidacy has been opposed by most of Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s ruling coalition, who argue he helped politicise the IPN under the former PiS government. However, some more conservative elements of the coalition joined the opposition in supporting Szpytma, giving him a majority in the Sejm but not the Senate. Senatorowie nie wyrazili zgody na powołanie Mateusza Szpytmy na Prezesa Instytutu Pamięci Narodowej – Komisji Ścigania Zbrodni przeciwko Narodowi Polskiemu — Senat RP 🇵🇱 (@PolskiSenat) August 6, 2026 The IPN is a body tasked with researching, documenting and educating about Poland’s tumultuous and tragic 20th-century history. It also has the power to prosecute crimes relating to the periods when the country was under Nazi and communist rule. The institute was led by Nawrocki from 2021 until August last year, when he became president of Poland. Since then, the IPN has been without a permanent head. Last October, the IPN’s council nominated Karol Polejowski, another of the institute’s deputy heads, to be its new president. But he was rejected by the Sejm, which, along with the Senate, must approve the choice. In April, the council instead recommended Szpytma, whose candidacy was approved by the Sejm last month. He received support mainly from opposition parties, including PiS and the far-right Confederation (Konfederacja). However, in a rare split within the ruling coalition, one of its junior members, the centre-right Polish People’s Party (PSL), also backed Szpytma, as did some MPs from the centrist Poland 2050 (Polska 2050). That was enough to give him a majority. By contrast, the main ruling party, Tusk’s Civic Coalition (KO), and The Left (Lewica) opposed his nomination, citing a letter signed earlier this year by 170 academics, who described Szpytma as “one of the faces of IPN’s politicisation” under the former PiS government. However, PSL’s leader, Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, who also serves as Poland’s defence minister and deputy prime minister rejected that characterisation and said that PSL had backed Szpytma because of his work commemorating historical figures from the agrarian movement in which PSL is rooted. In a rare split in the ruling coalition, MPs from two parties, PSL and Poland 2050, voted with the opposition in the Sejm for a new head of the Institute of National Remembrance. However, PM Donald Tusk says their choice will be rejected by the Senate https://t.co/0CGmbsNp4F — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 17, 2026 However, it was widely expected that Szpytma’s candidacy would be blocked by the upper-house Senate, where even the PSL and opposition combined do not have a majority in the 100-seat chamber. That was confirmed in a vote on Thursday, when 50 senators were opposed to Szyptma and only 38 were in favour, with one abstention. “We voted against further politicisation” of IPN and “against tolerating financial irregularities”, wrote the speaker of the Senate, Małgorzata Kidawa-Błonska of KO. The latter comment was likely a reference to a report by the Supreme Audit Office (NIK) last year which found that the IPN had, between 2022 and 2025, failed to properly manage tens of millions of zloty in spending, including various violations of regulations on the use of public funds. Szpytma told journalists that he was not surprised by the result of the vote, saying he believes his connection to Nawrocki, who is an ardent opponent of the current government and has vetoed a record number of laws, is the reason why he lost. Nie zgodziliśmy się w Senacie, by człowiek Karola Nawrockiego został prezesem IPN. Zagłosowaliśmy przeciw dalszemu upolitycznianiu Instytutu. Przeciw tolerowaniu nieprawidłowości finansowych. Pan Szpytma nie wprowadziłby żadnych zmian w funkcjonowaniu IPN. — Małgorzata Kidawa-Błońska (@M_K_Blonska) August 6, 2026 The IPN plays an important role in Polish public life, including in commemorating, investigating and prosecuting crimes that took place during the Nazi-German and Soviet occupations of Poland in World War Two, as well as during the decades of communist rule afterwards. Under Nawrocki’s leadership, the IPN accelerated the process of demolishing remaining Soviet monuments in Poland, often prompting criticism from Russia. It has also been closely involved in the exhumation of victims of the Volhynia massacres, in which Ukrainian nationalists killed around 100,000 Poles during World War Two. During PiS’s time in power from 2015 to 2023, the IPN was accused of becoming increasingly politicised, using its activities to support the historical narratived promoted by the government. In 2021, Israel protested after a former far-right activist was appointed to head one of the IPN’s local branches. Russia has criticised the "sacrilegious" demolition of a Soviet monument in Poland, calling it a “flagrant violation” of a bilateral agreement. World.title: Polish state energy giant Orlen posts record half-year profit amid Middle East turmoil
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Polish state energy giant Orlen posted a record profit in the first half of 2026, as turmoil in the Middle East boosted earnings in the fuel sector, despite Polish government measures to cushion the rise in consumer prices. Orlen has also this year seen its highest ever proportion of revenue from foreign markets. The results come amid a political dispute over a government plan to impose a windfall tax on excess profits from fuel sales, aimed at recouping billions spent on consumer subsidies. Orlen would be the biggest target of the tax, but the plan has been obstructed by opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki. W pierwszym półroczu Orlen zarobił na czysto 15,8 miliarda złotych. Trzy razy więcej niż przed rokiem.https://t.co/qJS81csI0H — TVN24 BiS (@TVN24BiS) August 6, 2026 On Thursday, Orlen reported consolidated net profit of 15.9 billion zloty (€3.7 billion) for the first six months of the year, almost tripling from the 5.7 billion zloty recorded in the same period of 2025. Revenue rose to 152.2 billion zloty from 134.4 billion zloty. CEO Ireneusz Fąfara acknowledged that the figures came amid exceptional market conditions. Energy prices jumped globally in March, after the US and Israel began to attack Iran and Tehran responded by blocking the Strait of Hormuz, a key export route. Fąfara noted that, despite this, Poland had maintained some of Europe’s lowest fuel prices. He said that Orlen had prioritised fuel availability and competitive domestic prices while taking advantage of stronger margins abroad, where it brought in an “absolutely record level of revenue from foreign markets”. In the first half of 2026, foreign markets accounted for 35.7% of Orlen’s revenue, up from 33.8% a year earlier. The bulk came from Germany, the Czech Republic, Lithuania and Austria, where Orlen operates petrol stations, as well as from trading activities in markets such as the Netherlands and Switzerland. Pierwsze półrocze 2026 roku ORLEN zamyka rekordowym zyskiem z rynków zagranicznych. Wynik netto całej Grupy w II kwartale wyniósł 7,7 mld zł. Wypracowane wyniki finansowe pozwoliły na wypłatę rekordowej dywidendy dla akcjonariuszy oraz dalsze finansowanie największego programu… pic.twitter.com/ohcxksuv4G — ORLEN (@GrupaORLEN) August 6, 2026 Orlen has expanded rapidly in recent years, as it has swallowed up other state-owned energy firms and sought to diversify away from its traditional focus on oil towards gas, renewables and hydrogen. In March this year, Orlen’s market valuation rose to its highest ever level of €35.2 billion, up from €7 billion in early 2022. As a result, it overtook the market capitalisation of Russian energy giant Gazprom. Mateusz Czyżkowski, an analyst at brokerage XTB, attributed Orlen’s record profits this year to “skilful balancing between geopolitical conditions and local pressures”, including government-imposed fuel price caps that squeezed margins. “The global commodities market in the second quarter of 2026 was strongly buoyed by tensions between Iran and Israel and ongoing disruptions to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz…This significant geopolitical premium boosted profits in [Orlen’s] Upstream & Supply segment,” he wrote in a note. The announcement of record profits comes as Orlen finds itself at the centre of a political dispute over the government’s proposed windfall tax, which would introduce a 60% levy on excess profits from liquid fuel sales. The measure was expected to raise around 4 billion zloty, which would have offset most of the roughly 4.7 billion zloty the government spent on keeping fuel prices lower for consumers amid the crisis in the Middle East by, among other things, cutting VAT and introducing a maximum daily price. However, although the tax was approved by the government’s majority in parliament in July, President Nawrocki refused to sign it into law, instead referring it to the constitutional court for review – a process that has no time limit and can take years. President @NawrockiKn has obstructed a planned windfall tax on fuel companies by sending it to the constitutional court, where it could stay for years The tax aimed to offset fuel price protection costs after the Iran war surgehttps://t.co/UojVuYhvdV — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 27, 2026 According to government calculations, Orlen would account for around 60% of the tax base if the measures eventually come into force. However, at his press conference on Thursday, Fąfara emphasised that the company supports the windfall tax. “We have viewed this solution positively from the very beginning. I believe it is in the interest of the company, our customers, and the country,” he said. However, Fąfara rejected suggestions that Orlen could unilaterally reduce pump prices by sacrificing margins. “We cannot lower prices in defiance of the market and global prices…If we lowered prices below parity, there would be a shortage of fuel,” he warned, adding that artificially low prices would encourage speculative exports and fuel tourism. Prices at petrol stations jumped today in Poland after the government ended the last of the support measures introduced to cushion consumers from the energy crisis caused by the war in Iran. Some places saw prices rise by as much as 14%https://t.co/mUfWUyDMle — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 1, 2026 Prime Minister Donald Tusk used Orlen’s record profit announcement to reiterate criticism of the Nawrocki for obstructing the windfall tax. “Taxing such extraordinary profits made by oil companies, not just Orlen, was intended to bring down prices at petrol stations. That is precisely what Karol Nawrocki blocked. Remember this when you’re tanking up,” Tusk wrote on social media. Nawrocki’s office has, however, rejected the idea that an increased tax on fuel companies would somehow reduce fuel prices, arguing that, if anything, it would have the opposite effect if companies pass some of the costs onto consumers. Zysk Orlenu w pierwszym półroczu był wyższy od zeszłorocznego o 10 miliardów! Opodatkowanie takich nadzwyczajnych zysków koncernów paliwowych, nie tylko Orlenu, miały służyć obniżeniu cen na stacjach. To właśnie zablokował @NawrockiKn Pamiętajcie przy tankowaniu. — Donald Tusk (@donaldtusk) August 6, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: New Polish opposition group proposes paying parents “salary” to encourage more births
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! We cannot do what we do without your support. New Polish opposition group Development Plus (Rozwój Plus), which recently broke away from the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) party, has proposed the idea of paying a “parental salary” for the first three years of a child’s life. The idea is part of a package of proposals to tackle Poland’s dire demographic situation released on Friday by Development Plus in its first major policy announcement since leader Mateusz Morawiecki announced that the group would soon become a political party. 3600 zł miesięcznie na dziecko do 3. roku życia – jedna z wielu propozycji @RozwojPlus dla demografii! Pensja Rodzicielska wynosząca równowartość płacy minimalnej, czyli obecnie około 3600 zł netto miesięcznie przez pierwsze 3 lata życia dziecka. To ponad czterokrotnie więcej… pic.twitter.com/253pwcskNK — Mateusz Morawiecki (@MorawieckiM) August 7, 2026 The proposed parental salary would amount to 3,600 zloty (€837) per month, the equivalent of the minimum wage after taxes. It is 4.5 times more than the current child benefit payment of 800 zloty per month that all Polish parents of children under 18 receive. Development Plus says that the parental salary could be combined with income from other work that parents undertake and that it would include contributions towards their pensions. It would end once a child turns three, after which parents would have access to normal child benefit payments. The group says that, for now, the idea is just a proposal, based on expert analysis of how to tackle Poland’s demographic crisis, and that it now wants to “refine it through dialogue with Poles” rather than “imposing top-down provisions”. Poland has long been grappling with a shrinking, ageing population. Last year, the number of births fell to a new post-war low of 238,000, while deaths totalled 406,000. That marked the 13th consecutive year in which more people died than were born in Poland. The country’s fertility rate – meaning the average number of children that are born to a woman over her lifetime – fell to a new record low of 1.068 in 2025. That is one of the lowest figures anywhere in the world and well below the so-called “replacement rate” – the figure needed to ensure that the population does not decline – which is generally defined as 2.1. Poland’s fertility rate, already one of the lowest in the world, fell to a new record low of 1.07 in 2025, deepening concerns over the country's shrinking and ageing population https://t.co/OMGC1MpA5l — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 28, 2026 Successive Polish governments have introduced various measures intended to boost the birth rate, though so far without clear success. The former PiS government, with Morawiecki as finance minister and later prime minister, introduced and expanded the current child benefit programme. While there was a brief bump in births after it was launched in 2016, numbers subsequently continued their downward trend. After PiS lost power in 2023, the current government, led by Prime Minister Donald Tusk, continued the child benefit programme and also introduced new payments to support parents who return to work and restored funding for IVF treatment, which was previously cut by PiS. When announcing the proposed parental salary on Friday, Development Plus also outlined seven other proposed new policies to ease Poland’s demographic problems. One would allow workers to have a portion of their contributions go towards their parents’ pensions. Another pledged to provide better maternity care, including access to anaesthesia, a private hospital room and dedicated midwife, prenatal testing, and infertility treatment. Other policies promised more flexible working arrangements and mortgage repayments to prevent people from having to choose between a family or a career, as well as school hours and after-school care that “adapt to the lives of families, not the other way around”. Development Plus also proposed “granting parents the right to represent the voices of their minor children”. However, they provided no details of what this would mean in practice. Dzieci to nasza przyszłość! To fundament bezpieczeństwa Polski i polska racja stanu. Jak sprawić, by Polaków rodziło się coraz więcej? Oto strategia demograficzna dla Polski Stowarzyszenia @RozwojPlus🇵🇱➕. pic.twitter.com/1hiQPNuL47 — Mateusz Morawiecki (@MorawieckiM) August 7, 2026 Development Plus was founded as an association by Morawiecki in April this year. That immediately prompted criticism from some other members of the party, who saw it as a step towards creating a breakaway group. Matters came to a head last month, when PiS leader Jarosław Kaczyński demanded that all the party’s lawmakers sign a pledge of loyalty and commit to leave any political associations they are part of. Morawiecki and his allies refused to do so, prompting Kaczyński to declare that meant they had effectively resigned from the party. Last week, Development Plus announced it had formed its own separate parliamentary caucus with 40 MPs in the Sejm, the most powerful lower house of parliament. The move immediately made it the third-largest group in the parliament, while also meaning PiS was no longer the biggest. On Monday this week, Morawiecki confirmed that his group would soon form a party of its own. He laid out a vision of a more moderate, centre-right party that would focus on economic development rather than “ideological disputes”, following PiS’s shift in a more hardline direction over recent months. Mateusz Morawiecki has confirmed that his Development Plus group, which is splitting from the national-conservative opposition PiS party, will soon form a party of its own. World.title: Polish opposition calls for deportation of Ukrainian conscription-age men not working legally
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Poland’s largest opposition party, the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), has called for Ukrainian men of conscription age who are not legally working to be deported to Ukraine. The policy, which continues a recent hardening of PiS’s position towards Ukraine and Ukrainians as it competes with the far right for support, was condemned by government figures, who called it “absurd” and “disgusting”. 🇵🇱 Bezpieczeństwo obywateli powinno być priorytetem każdego rządu. Potrzebne są zdecydowane działania wobec osób przebywających w Polsce niezgodnie z prawem. 👉 Udostępnij! 🔥 Ku nowemu rządowi! pic.twitter.com/m8MctmmPXd — Prawo i Sprawiedliwość (@pisorgpl) August 6, 2026 On Thursday, PiS, which has recently been hit by falling support in the polls and the defection of a large breakaway group of more moderate MPs, held a policy convention at which it presented ideas it wants to implement if it returns to power after next year’s parliamentary elections. “One of [our] government’s first, most significant decisions will be to deport men, Ukrainians of military age, who are not legally working in Poland,” announced Tobiasz Bocheński, a deputy leader of the party. “They will have the opportunity to fight for their homeland, so that the horrors of this war can quickly end,” he continued. “Because for Central and Eastern Europe to be secure and free, Ukraine must win.” Bocheński denied that the policy was inhumane, noting that, in 2022, when PiS was in government, “Poles, like no other nation in Europe, opened their hearts, their homes and their wallets to women, children, the elderly and disabled people fleeing Putin’s bombs”. Poland was the primary destination for refugees fleeing Ukraine in 2022. Almost one million of them remain in the country, alongside hundreds of thousands of other Ukrainian immigrants, many of whom arrived before 2022. They are by far Poland’s largest foreign national group. In their announcement of the proposed policy, PiS gave no details of how it would work in practice, nor on what legal basis Ukrainians who are legally resident in Poland and have not violated any laws would be deported. News website Interia, which had reported on PiS’s plans shortly before they were officially announced, notes that data from Poland’s labour ministry show that only around 11,000 Ukrainians are registered as unemployed in Poland. The figures are not broken down by gender, but most are believed to be women. However, PiS’s policy would also apply to Ukrainians in the so-called grey economy, where people work informally without registering or paying taxes, reports Interia. Military-age Ukrainian men in other European countries should not receive social benefits, says Poland's foreign minister, @sikorskiradek. "There should be no financial incentives for avoiding the draft" https://t.co/5TcTqyDa6X — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 16, 2024 PiS’s plan was immediately criticised by government figures, with interior ministry spokeswoman Karolina Gałecka calling it “an absurd idea” and “pure demagoguery”. She noted that over 95% of Ukrainian men of conscription age in Poland are working legally and paying taxes. “Without these people, many key sectors of the Polish economy would simply grind to a halt,” wrote Gałecka. “Stop the incitement.” Deputy interior minister Maciej Duszczyk, meanwhile, told broadcaster TVN that, among the Ukrainian men not working, many are wounded soldiers in Poland for treatment and rehabilitation or fathers caring for disabled children. Deportations are a “purely political, disgusting idea”, he added. Interior minister Marcin Kierwiński wrote that, “when [PiS] was in power, they couldn’t even deport those who were breaking the law, and now they’re supposedly going to deport everyone without rhyme or reason”. Since taking power, the current government has increased deportations of foreigners who are in Poland illegally or broke the law while in the country. Last year, it carried out over 9,000 deportations, up from 7,200 in 2023, the last year that PiS was in power Absurdalny pomysł @pisorgpl ws. deportacji Ukraińców to czysta demagogia! Ponad 95% mężczyzn w wieku poborowym legalnie pracuje w 🇵🇱 i płaci podatki (dane ZUS).@OficjalnyJK zapowiada deportacje. A jak miałoby to wyglądać w praktyce? Patrole sprawdzające dokumenty na ulicach?… — Karolina Gałecka (@K_Galecka) August 6, 2026 During the conference on Thursday, PiS emphasised its tough approach to migration more broadly, saying that it would “create a new, restrictive system for foreigners” that would track each immigrant in the country. “Every foreigner will have their own individual account,” and if they commit any offences or fail to abide by any administrative obligations, “the information will be immediately entered into the system, and the deportation process will begin”, said Bocheński. “The only good migration is the return of Poles from abroad,” declared the party on social media. 🛡️ Bezpieczne granice to bezpieczna Polska. Skuteczna ochrona granic i walka z nielegalną imigracją to obowiązek każdego odpowiedzialnego państwa. 👉 Udostępnij! 🔥 Ku nowemu rządowi! pic.twitter.com/rRPZpmXi5U — Prawo i Sprawiedliwość (@pisorgpl) August 6, 2026 In fact, it was during PiS’s time in power from 2015 to 2023 that Poland saw the largest wave of immigration in its history, and one of the largest anywhere in Europe. In every year between 2017 and 2022, Poland was the EU member state that issued the highest number of first residence permits to immigrants from outside the bloc. There are now over two million foreigners registered as living in Poland, making up just 5% of the population. Around three quarters are Ukrainians (1.55 million), with the next largest groups being Belarusians (139,300), Indians (26,100), Georgians (22,200), Russians (19,500), Vietnamese (15,100) and Turks (14,500). The number of foreigners with residence permits in Poland has reached two million, making up just over 5% of the country’s population, new government data show. The largest national group by far are Ukrainians, followed by Belarusians and Indians https://t.co/SI09WtR7hR — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) April 26, 2026 While in government, PiS welcomed Ukrainian migrants and refugees and was a strong supporter of Ukraine in its defence against Russian aggression. However, since going into opposition, it has taken an increasingly tough line. That has reflected a broader shift in Polish society, with a variety of polls showing rising negative sentiment towards Ukraine and Ukrainians. Recent months have also seen a rise in reported hate crimes against Ukrainians in Poland, including a number of high-profile incidents. Meanwhile, two far-right parties that have long taken an anti-Ukrainian stance, Confederation (Konfederacja) and Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP), have soared in the polls, placing pressure on PiS to toughen its own position. One Confederation MEP, Stanisław Tyszka, mocked PiS’s latest policy announcement. “PiS wants to heroically deport hundreds of thousands of Ukrainians whom they themselves let into Poland,” he wrote. “Comedy.” The number of reported hate crimes against Ukrainians in Poland is up 30% so far this year, police data show. The figures come following recent high-profile cases of verbal and physical attacks against Ukrainians, who are Poland's largest immigrant group https://t.co/pcTsJddDz7 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 17, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Poland invokes emergency grid capacity powers for second time in three days amid heatwave
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland’s power grid operator, PSE, has, for the second time in three days and third time this summer, invoked emergency measures to ensure supply amid an ongoing heatwave. Before this summer, it had only done so twice in the eight years since such powers were introduced. However, following a meeting with PSE and other state energy officials, Prime Minister Donald Tusk has assured Poles that, despite “a very difficult period”, the “situation is under control” and power supplies are secure, thanks in part to the growth of renewables in recent years. ❗️PSE ponownie ogłaszają okresy przywołania na rynku mocy❗️ To już 3. raz w tym roku, kiedy operator sięga po to narzędzie. W historii zdarzyło się to tylko 5 razy, wliczywszy 3 przypadki tegoroczne, co pokazuje wyjątkowość roku 2026 dla energetyki. pic.twitter.com/DbCPnpyae4 — Jakub Wiech (@jakubwiech) August 6, 2026 PSE has called on contracted electricity generators to increase output and large consumers to cut use to help balance the grid on Thursday between 5:00 p.m. and 10:00 p.m., as temperatures have this week approached 40°C (104°F) in many parts of the country. The same measures were introduced on Tuesday, as the heatwave pushed up electricity consumption, partly due to increased use of air conditioning and refrigeration. Participants in Poland’s capacity market are paid for maintaining standby capacity and fulfilling their obligations when called upon by the operator. According to PSE, the mechanism is “a remedial measure” used when the generation capacity available to the operator falls significantly below the required safety level. Previously, the measures were invoked in June this year, amid another heatwave that saw Poland hit its highest-ever recorded temperature of 40.5°C. But before that, they had only been used twice since being introduced in 2018. Temperatures in Poland have reached the highest level on record, with a figure of 40.3°C (104.5°F) recorded this afternoon, as the heatwave that has hit Europe this week moves eastwards https://t.co/eRhRxiuCGq — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 28, 2026 Poland’s weather institute IMGW issued heat warnings on Thursday for 13 of the country’s 16 provinces, with daytime temperatures forecast to reach between 33C and 38C. High temperatures and prolonged drought conditions have also pushed water levels in many rivers to extremely low levels, with the Vistula, Poland’s longest river, only 5 centimetres above the historic low of 4 centimetres it fell to in Warsaw last year. Some other parts of the river have hit all-time record lows, reports Polsat News. One result has been a disruption of cooling supplies to Poland’s power sector. State energy firm Enea this week announced reduced operations at two of its coal-fired plants that are cooled by water from the Vistula. Around 1.1 gigawatts (GW) of capacity (just over 1% of Poland’s total) has gone offline. On Wednesday, Prime Minister Donald Tusk convened a meeting of a government crisis team, including PSE’s deputy president, to discuss the current heatwave and its potential impact on the power sector. However, afterwards he assured that “the situation is under control” and that the fact that Poland now has “a lot of energy from solar panels and wind turbines makes our system relatively secure”, reports the Polish Press Agency (PAP). Poland’s renewable sector has expanded rapidly over the last decade. Last year, it provided just over 29% of the country’s power, with onshore wind supplying 14% of the energy mix and solar 12%. Renewables generated 29.4% of Poland's electricity in 2025, almost exactly the same figure as in 2024, ending a period of strong growth since 2021. Coal (52.2%) remained the dominant source, though its share declined. For more, read our full report: https://t.co/XjD9hfhabo pic.twitter.com/WklP7dYL78 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) January 2, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Polish top court confirms withholding funds from opposition PiS party over campaign finance irregularities
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland’s top administrative court has upheld a decision by the finance ministry to withhold state subsidies from the national-conservative opposition Law and Justice (PiS) party due to campaign finance irregularities. The decision was welcomed by the government, with Prime Minister Donald Tusk saying that there will be “no money for grifters”. PiS, however, argues that the money is being withheld for political reasons and accuses the authorities of “Russian standards”. Naczelny Sąd Administracyjny oddalił w środę kasacje ws. dotacji i subwencji dla PiS. – Miażdżący dla PiS wyrok podtrzymany! – stwierdził szef MF Andrzej Domański https://t.co/bcL18WbiYf — OKO.press (@oko_press) August 6, 2026 The dispute dates back to August 2024, when the National Electoral Commission (PKW) rejected PiS’s financial report for the previous year’s parliamentary election campaign after identifying around 3.6 million zloty (€838,000) in unauthorised expenditure. As a result, the PKW ordered that PiS should lose 10.8 million zloty from the state subsidies that political parties in Poland receive based on their level of electoral support. The party would normally have received 25.9 million zloty based on its 2023 election result. The decision triggered months of legal wrangling, with PiS arguing that the funding should be restored after the Supreme Court upheld its complaint against the PKW’s decision. However, finance minister Andrzej Domański refused to release the money, saying there were unresolved legal doubts over the ruling. The finance minister has refused to comply with the electoral commission's decision to pay out subsidies to the opposition PiS party He says there are "legal doubts" over the issue. But PiS says he is obliged to pay and will be held criminally responsible https://t.co/ZwIZRqn5tp — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) January 9, 2025 Those doubts stem from a broader dispute over the controversial and contested judicial reforms implemented by PiS when it ruled Poland from 2015 to 2023. The chamber of the Supreme Court that ruled in PiS’s favour was created as part of those reforms. It has previously been found to not be a legitimate body by both the European Court of Justice and European Court of Human Rights because it contains improperly appointed judges. After the Supreme Court chamber’s ruling, the PKW initially said it would not recognise the decision until the chamber’s legal status was clarified. Two weeks later, however, it reversed that decision and approved PiS’s financial report. Domański still declined to restore the subsidy, arguing that the PKW’s resolution was internally contradictory. While it approved the payments, it also stated that the chamber’s ruling should come from a body recognised as a court and that it was not determining whether the chamber met that standard. PiS challenged Domański’s decision. However, its case was initially rejected by a lower court in June last year, and that decision has now been upheld by the Supreme Administrative Court (NSA), which is the final court of appeal for administrative issues. The NSA found the minister had acted lawfully in withholding the funding. It also said the Supreme Court chamber’s ruling had no legal effect because it had been issued by a body that was not a properly constituted court, reports news website OKO.press. The ruling was welcomed by Domański, who called it a “crushing blow to PiS” and said that “yet another PiS lie has been exposed”. World.title: Polish prosecutors end 10-year treason investigation into Tusk over Smolensk air disaster
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! After a ten-year-long investigation, prosecutors have concluded that Poland’s government in 2010 – which was led by current Prime Minister Donald Tusk – was not guilty of “diplomatic treason” in its response to the plane crash in Russia that killed President Lech Kaczyński. The national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) party – which ruled Poland from 2015 to 2023 and is led by Lech’s twin brother, Jarosław – has always rejected the findings of official Polish and Russian investigations into the crash, which found it to have been an accident. Instead, PiS claims that the disaster, which claimed the lives of 96 people, many of them senior Polish state officials, was caused deliberately by Russia and then covered up with the help of Tusk’s government. However, while PiS launched various investigations during its time in power, it has never substantiated its claims. And prosecutors now say that there is no evidence that diplomatic treason, a crime that carries a potential prison sentence of up to ten years, took place. Uprzednio wygrałem sprawę cywilną z posłem @OficjalnyJK, który w efekcie musiał wpłacić 50,000zł na siły zbrojne broniącej się Ukrainy. Teraz potwierdzenie @PK_GOV_PL: nie było żadnej zdrady dyplomatycznej ani żadnej intencji jej popełnienia. Oczywiście żaden z kłamców… https://t.co/VKZHlF5xkX — Radosław Sikorski 🇵🇱🇪🇺 (@sikorskiradek) August 5, 2026 Wednesday’s announcement by the National Prosecutor’s Office was welcomed by Radosław Sikorski, the current foreign minister, who held the same role in 2010. He condemned the “Smolensk liars”, such as Jarosław Kaczyński, who he suggested had exploited the tragedy for their own benefit. “They brainwashed millions of people, divided families, stirred up hatred within the nation,” he wrote. “They’ll burn in hell for it. But the power, money and satisfaction they gained from spitting on their rivals – that’s theirs.” The idea that Smolensk was an assassination of Lech Kaczyński has been a core part of PiS rhetoric. In 2022, for example, Jarosław Kaczyński said that the decision was made “at the highest level of the Kremlin” and Tusk’s government then “covered up” the incident as part of a “macabre reconciliation with Russia”. Smolensk was an “attack decided at the highest level of the Kremlin”, says Jarosław Kaczyński ahead of the 12th anniversary of the crash. Donald Tusk's government then “covered up” the incident as part of a “macabre reconciliation with Russia”, he adds https://t.co/5ae0gHJj3B — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) April 4, 2022 The investigation into diplomatic treason – a crime consisting of acting to the detriment of Poland while authorised to represent the country in relations with foreign states or organisations – was launched in August 2016, less than a year after PiS had come to power. Among the individuals who had formally notified prosecutors of a potential crime was PiS deputy leader Antoni Macierewicz, who from 2015 to 2018 served as defence minister. He has been the foremost proponent of conspiracy theories around the Smolensk air disaster. In their notifications to prosecutors, Macierewicz and the others accused Tusk and other officials of, in their relations with Russia, deliberately choosing a legal basis for an investigation into the crash that was unfavourable to Poland by giving it no real influence over how it was run. However, prosecutors now say that, after ten years in which they questioned 488 witnesses, gathered extensive documentation and requested legal assistance from several countries, they have “concluded that no crime of diplomatic treason was committed”. In a statement explaining the decision, the National Prosecutor’s Office said that the legal basis chosen for cooperating with Russia on an investigation – Annex 13 of the Convention on International Civil Aviation – was, in fact, “the most advantageous solution” for Poland. It ensured the participation of Polish representatives in the Russian-led investigation, including access to the wreckage and crash site. Other legal options would have offered no greater benefits and involved significant risks, concluded the Polish prosecutors. They acknowledged that Russia “subsequently failed to fulfil some of its obligations arising from the adopted procedure”, but said this should have no bearing on assessing the decisions that were previously made on setting up the investigation. The defence ministry will notify prosecutors of 41 suspected crimes linked to a commission established by the former PiS government to investigate the 2010 plane crash in Russia that killed President Lech Kaczyński https://t.co/aEAlmk9lDM — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 24, 2024 The prosecutors also found that, not only did Polish officials choose the best legal solution, but there was also “no evidence indicating that individuals authorised to act on behalf of Poland, including the prime minister and members of the Council of Ministers, acted with the intent to harm Poland”. Given that the crime of diplomatic treason requires intent, this finding further reinforced the decision to drop the investigation. However, the prosecutors note that their decision can still be appealed. At the time of writing, neither Kaczyński, Macierewicz, nor other senior PiS figures had commented on the prosecutors’ announcement. However, it is likely they will point to the fact that the current national prosecutor was appointed by Tusk’s government after it had removed the previous PiS-era incumbent in a legally questionable move. The Supreme Court has issued a ruling that effectively found that the government unlawfully replaced a senior prosecutor earlier this year However, the justice minister says the ruling has no legal force as it was issued by illegitimately appointed judges https://t.co/9fCE6d18uy — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 27, 2024 In 2020, in a separate civil case, a court ordered Jarosław Kaczyński to apologise for accusing Sikorski of “diplomatic treason” in relation to the Smolensk crash. Two years later, after Kaczyński had refused to comply with the ruling and Sikorski published the apology himself, Kaczyński was ordered to pay the costs. In 2024, an investigation by Tusk’s government found that the PiS administration had wasted tens of millions of zloty on a commission, headed by Macierewicz, that was tasked with re-investigating the Smolensk disaster. It notified prosecutors of dozens of suspected crimes relating to the functioning of the commission. Macierewicz, however, accused the government of spreading “lies and disinformation” designed to “protect Putin”. Poland has urged the European Union to adopt tougher measures in response to the recent migration crisis in Spain’s African exclave of Ceuta, including making migrants who enter the bloc illegally ineligible for obtaining residence rights. Among those to speak out was Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk, who on Friday called on Spain to “follow our example if Schengen is to survive”. We have invested billions of euros and engaged thousands of soldiers, police officers and border guards. Spain must follow our… — Donald Tusk (@donaldtusk) July 31, 2026 That was a reference to Poland’s response to a crisis on its eastern border, where since 2021 Belarus has encouraged and assisted tens of thousands of migrants – mainly from Asia and Africa – to try to cross irregularly into the EU. Both Poland and the EU have accused Belarus and its ally Russia of deliberately “weaponising” migration in an attempt to destabilise European societies as part of Moscow and Minsk’s broader “hybrid threats” against the EU. Tusk noted that, in response, Poland has restricted the right to asylum, invested billions in strengthening physical and electronic barriers along the border, and has deployed thousands of soldiers, police officers and border guards there (who have also been given expanded rights to use firearms).
