Giga Avaliani’s family has always maintained that those who carried out the attack were not the only people involved. They have consistently called on investigators to identify and prosecute all those who may have played a role in the crime.

The family has paid particular attention to the alleged role of the two girls. Eka Kupatadze has repeatedly said that they knew the attack was being planned.

Until recently, however, prosecutors had taken no apparent action against additional suspects, prompting repeated criticism of the investigation from Avaliani’s family.

Kupatadze even appealed for help to Ekaterine Khvedelidze, the wife of Bidzina Ivanishvili, the founder of the ruling party and widely regarded as Georgia’s “informal ruler”. Khvedelidze replied to her letter, expressing sympathy and support for the mother who had lost her son.

“As far as I am aware, the investigation has not yet been completed. I am confident that the relevant state authorities will see it through to the end and that all the circumstances will be thoroughly examined, so that no question surrounding the terrible tragedy that has befallen you remains unanswered,” Ekaterine Khvedelidze wrote in her reply.

Formal charges

On the evening of 6 August, both girls were formally charged.

Nia Imnadze at the time of her arrest

Nia Imnadze has been charged with incitement to intentionally inflict grievous bodily harm committed by a group. The offence carries a maximum sentence of 13 years’ imprisonment.

Anastasia Beruashvili has been charged with failing to report a particularly serious crime, an offence punishable by up to seven years’ imprisonment.

Under Georgian law, sentences imposed on minors are reduced by one quarter.

“The investigation conducted by the Ministry of Internal Affairs under the supervision of the Prosecutor’s Office established that, in September 2025, Nia Imnadze began taking mathematics lessons with Giga Avaliani. The accused, Nia Imnadze, told her friends Aleksandre Gabashvili and Giorgi Malania that her teacher, Giga Avaliani, had allegedly shown her excessive attention. By doing so, the accused incited Aleksandre Gabashvili to attack Giga Avaliani together with his accomplices,” the Prosecutor’s Office said in a statement.

According to the statement, Aleksandre Gabashvili, together with Giorgi Rikadze, Giorgi Malania and Demetere Chikovani, “decided to act on that incitement.”

What defence says

The defence has denied all the charges.

According to Nia Imnadze’s lawyer, Giorgi Lekishvili, there is no evidence in the case to support the allegation that she incited the attack.

The lawyer also rejected reports that prosecutors had obtained data and messages from Meta, and that the arrests followed an examination of those materials.

“Criminal proceedings cannot be based on suspicion. They must be based on lawfully obtained evidence, and no other standard can override that principle,” Lekishvili told reporters.

Ketevan Vardanashvili, the lawyer representing Anastasia Beruashvili, made similar arguments. She said Anastasia had not witnessed any crime and that she and Nia Imnadze had seen each other only once, for a few minutes.

“They had no friendship and no contact,” the lawyer said.

As for Anastasia’s relationship with the convicted defendant Giorgi Rikadze, Vardanashvili said that “even if she was his girlfriend, that does not mean she had any knowledge of the crime.”

Complaint or incitement?

The arrests of the two girls have sparked intense debate on social media. Many commentators agree that everyone responsible for Giga Avaliani’s death should be held accountable and that justice should be served. Many have also expressed sympathy for Eka Kupatadze.

At the same time, some have questioned the actions of the law enforcement authorities. They have asked whether prosecutors have sufficiently strong evidence against the two girls, particularly Nia Imnadze, who faces a lengthy prison sentence if convicted.

The Prosecutor’s Office statement says only that Nia Imnadze told her friends that Giga Avaliani had allegedly shown her excessive attention. It does not explain whether she knew an attack was being planned or whether she urged her boyfriend to take any specific action.

“Does complaining to friends amount to incitement?” some social media users have asked.

Others have also questioned why, if prosecutors had sufficient evidence, the girls were arrested only 10 months after the murder. Some have asked whether the arrests were prompted by Eka Kupatadze’s campaign, and whether political influence may have played a role.

Those questions also remain unanswered.

Timeline of Giga Avaliani's case – read more 1 October 2025 – The attack

Giga Avaliani, a 28-year-old mathematics teacher, was attacked outside his home in Tbilisi. 24 October 2025 – Death

After spending 23 days in a coma, Giga Avaliani died. November–December 2025 – First arrests

Four minors were arrested: Aleksandre Gabashvili, Giorgi Rikadze, Demetere Chikovani and Ani Naskidashvili. April 2026 – First convictions

Tbilisi City Court found Aleksandre Gabashvili and Giorgi Rikadze guilty and sentenced each to 10 years and six months’ imprisonment. Demetere Chikovani was sentenced to six years and nine months’ imprisonment. He was later convicted over separate violent offences committed at a different time, increasing his total sentence to nine years and nine months. June 2026 – Another conviction

The court sentenced Ani Naskidashvili to five years and three months’ imprisonment for failing to report the crime. July 2026 – Another arrest

Giorgi Malania was arrested. According to prosecutors, he was charged with aiding and abetting the intentional infliction of grievous bodily harm committed by a group. His trial is still under way and no verdict has yet been delivered. August 2026 – Two more arrests

Two more minor girls were arrested: Nia Imnadze, Giga Avaliani’s former student and the girlfriend of the principal convicted defendant, and Anastasia Beruashvili, described as a friend of Nia Imnadze and the girlfriend of the second convicted defendant.

Broader picture

From the outset, the Giga Avaliani case came to represent more than a single criminal investigation.

It exposed a range of systemic problems, most notably a lack of public trust in investigative authorities. The case also highlighted shortcomings in Georgia’s juvenile justice system, as well as concerns over the protection of the rights of both victims and defendants.

Many observers questioned the release of footage showing Nia Imnadze’s arrest, particularly as it was made public by her lawyer. Some argued that the video was intended to generate public sympathy for his client.

“Unfortunately, public trust in the justice system – the police, the Prosecutor’s Office, the courts and other institutions – is now so low that victims, defendants and lawyers increasingly see shaping public opinion as the only way to obtain justice. They then seek to use public pressure to their advantage,” lawyer Londa Toloraia wrote.

In her view, this reflects a profound crisis affecting both citizens and the justice system itself.

“You no longer trust the state, even when it may actually be making a lawful decision.”

Toloraia also raised a number of questions about the arrests of the two girls: What evidence were they based on? Why did they take place 10 months after the murder? And why were they carried out at night, when Georgian law restricts procedural actions during nighttime hours, particularly in cases involving minors?

“How much influence does public opinion have over the justice system? A great deal. It is extremely difficult to withstand public pressure. And where institutions are fully politicised, it becomes virtually impossible to make a decision that is unpopular with the public,” she argued.

She stressed that legal standards must be upheld even when dealing with those accused of serious crimes – especially when the defendants are minors.

The Avaliani case has also exposed a darker side of public reaction. Following Nia Imnadze’s arrest, social media was flooded with hostile comments directed at both her and her family. Many users described her as the main culprit and called for severe punishment. Others went further, posting comments about the suffering they believed awaited her in prison.

A second group of social media users expressed concern about the tone of those comments. Toloraia addressed the debate in a lengthy social media post.

“Children are not born criminals. Before demanding that they be lynched, we should first ask why they became who they are,” she wrote, adding that juvenile crime in Georgia has reached one of its highest levels in recent years. She argued that the state’s response has focused on opening a “special prison” for children rather than preventing youth crime. A state in which parents who have lost a child must seek justice through public mobilisation, while institutions make decisions according to fluctuations in public pressure, is a broken state,” Toloraia concluded.

World.title: Odesa in summer 2026: Life between sea and war. VIDEO
World.content:
Beaches, bomb-damaged homes and explosions in broad daylight. In the summer of 2026, Odesa is caught between its traditional seaside resort atmosphere and the constant threat of Russian attacks. While some people relax by the sea and stroll through the city centre, others sift through the rubble left by the latest strike.

JAMnews visited Odesa to show what life in the city looks like today.

Odesa and the surrounding region remain frequent targets of Russian strikes. Residential neighbourhoods, critical infrastructure and port facilities have all come under attack.

Russia has carried out combined attacks using drones and missiles, seeking to overwhelm Ukraine‘s air defence systems.

The impact of these attacks is visible across the city. Residential buildings have been damaged, windows blown out and flats destroyed. Strikes have also hit Odesa’s historic centre, including heritage buildings and universities.

Ports in Odesa Region, along with the logistics hubs and warehouses that support them, are also regularly targeted. Attacks on port infrastructure have disrupted Ukraine’s transport network and Black Sea export routes.

The strikes often occur in broad daylight, when the streets are busy, cafés and shops are open, and beaches are filled with residents and visitors. At any moment, the familiar sounds of the city can be interrupted by explosions, air defence fire or the buzz of attack drones.

On several occasions, missiles have been intercepted directly over the coastline while beaches were crowded with people.

Today, it is possible to spend the day at the beach and the night in a bomb shelter.

World.title: Armenia’s growing number of large families: Statistics, one couple’s story and expert insights
World.content:
Surge in large families in Armenia

In recent years, more young families in Armenia have chosen to have a third or even fourth child. According to the Ministry of Labour and Social Affairs, around 8,300 third and subsequent children were born in 2018. By 2023, that figure had risen to more than 12,400, before easing slightly to around 12,000 in 2024. Overall, the number of third and subsequent births increased by about 45% between 2018 and 2024. Full-year data for 2025 are not yet available, although figures up to September show that 8,070 third and subsequent children had been born.

Experts cite a range of reasons why families choose to have larger families. Conversations with parents of three or more children suggest there is no single explanation, but the most common responses include: “Two children didn’t feel enough“, “We wanted a child of the opposite sex“, and “We were thinking about the country’s future.”

“We planned to have a large family, regardless of state support”

Vanuհi and Tigran married in 2013. For seven years, they were unable to have children. Eventually, they turned to in vitro fertilisation (IVF). In 2021, they became parents to triplets – a girl and two boys.

“We were asked how many children we wanted. We could have chosen one or two. But we decided to take the risk and become parents of triplets, even though we knew the risks were higher,” Vanuhi says.

Parents celebrate their triplets’ birthday.

According to Vanuhi, both she and her husband grew up in large families. From the outset, they wanted a big family of their own – at least three children and, ideally, as many as six.

“I received so much love and care from my brothers and sisters that I found it hard to imagine a family with just one or two children. My parents are no longer alive, but I feel stronger and more complete because I have my brothers and sisters,” says Tigran Hovakimyan.

The couple raised the triplets on their own, without relying on grandparents or other relatives. When the children turned three, they started nursery. Then came another surprise: Vanuhi became pregnant with their fourth child.

Vanuhi says they were astonished, as doctors had told them they had virtually no chance of conceiving naturally.

“We now have four young children. We both work and can provide them with good food, clothes and opportunities for leisure. We also receive state benefits. Because we had triplets, the government counts each of them as a third child and pays 50,000 drams (about $137) per child each month. We now receive an additional 50,000 drams for our fourth child, as well as 30,000 drams (about $82) because my wife is temporarily unable to work while on maternity leave,” Tigran explains.

He says that part of the money is deposited into savings accounts opened in the children’s names, while the rest is spent on their activities and recreation. The family has bought a large inflatable swimming pool for the garden of their home, as well as bicycles, and the children also attend paid extracurricular classes and sports clubs.

Family vacation.

The couple are also setting aside modest savings to help ensure all four children can receive a good education.

“You know, many families have children because of state benefits or other government support. We don’t judge them, but our story is different. We always planned to have three or more children without relying on state assistance. It wasn’t something that influenced our decision. In the early years of our marriage, both my wife and I worked several jobs at the same time so that we could afford to buy a large house, hoping one day we’d have a big family,” Tigran says.

“If we were still paying off a mortgage, we would probably depend on the child benefits that families receive until their children turn six,” Vanuhi adds.

How state encourages higher birth rates

In 2022, Armenia introduced a state support programme under which families receive a monthly payment of 50,000 drams ($137) for a third and each subsequent child until the child reaches the age of six.

By 2025, more than 45,000 children were covered by the scheme.

Under a separate programme, the state repays part of a family’s mortgage principal following the birth of a child. The subsidy amounts to:

up to 500,000 drams ($1,377) for a second child,

for a second child, up to 1 million drams ($2,754) for a third child,

for a third child, up to 1.5 million drams ($4,132) for a fourth child.

The scheme applies to mortgages that meet certain social eligibility criteria and is regarded as one of the government’s key measures to encourage higher birth rates.

In addition, amendments to Armenia’s Labour Code that came into force in 2026 introduced new benefits for working parents. In particular, parents with children under the age of 12 are now entitled to a “parental hour” – a shorter working day without any reduction in pay:

parents with one or two children can finish work 30 minutes earlier;parents with three or more children are entitled to a one-hour reduction in their working day.

The benefit can be used by either the mother or the father.

Families also receive a one-off payment of 500,000 drams ($1,377) for every child, including their first.

More recently, the government approved a new housing programme for families raising six or more children under the age of 18, an initiative proposed by the Ministry of Labour and Social Affairs.

“Under this programme, large families will be able to purchase property or build a detached house in any regional community in Armenia with 100% state funding,” ministry spokesperson Gayane Karagezyan said.

The programme does not cover property purchases in Yerevan, however, reflecting the government’s policy of promoting balanced regional development.

“More targeted measures are needed”

Demographer Rubina Grigoryan says the government’s efforts to encourage larger families have produced some results. While the increase in births is evident, she believes it is still not enough.

“New, more targeted programmes are needed. They should be tailored separately for Yerevan and the regions. They should also go beyond financial assistance. The recently introduced ‘parental hour’ is one example of an effective incentive. I believe more should be done to expand access to nurseries and kindergartens. Just look at how many private childcare centres cater for children under the age of two. If the state increased the number of places in public childcare facilities, more women would consider having additional children.”

Grigoryan says attitudes towards large families have also become more positive in recent years. They are not only receiving greater state support but are also more valued by society.

“However, many of these families may face difficulties once their children grow older, particularly with the costs of education and other financial pressures. State support is available only until children reach the age of six. After that, families seem to be left without much assistance. This is something policymakers should also address. As for the recent rise in birth rates, I see one particularly significant factor. The increase in births between 2021 and 2023 was largely influenced by the aftermath of the Karabakh war. Many families decided to have children after the war, each for their own reasons – from a sense of responsibility towards those who died to a desire to help build a stronger country for the future,” Grigoryan says.

World.title: First digital bridge beneath Caspian Sea: How Sumqayit-Aktau cable reshapes Eurasia’s geostrategic landscape
World.content:
Sumqayit-Aktau cable reshapes Eurasia

Azerbaijan and Kazakhstan have completed a key milestone in the implementation of a Caspian Sea project, with the subsea section of the Sumqayit-Aktau Trans-Caspian fibre-optic cable now in place.

The roughly 380-km line is the first fibre-optic infrastructure to be laid on the bed of the Caspian Sea. With a capacity of more than 400 Tbps, the system is being developed by AzerTelecom International and Kazakhtelecom through their joint venture, CaspiLink B.V. The project is being financed entirely by the operators, without any state budget funding.

Offshore works began in July and were completed in early August. The connection of the onshore infrastructure and system testing are scheduled for the autumn, while commercial operations are expected to begin by the end of 2026. The project is more than a technical achievement. As one of the flagship components of Azerbaijan’s Digital Silk Way initiative, it strengthens the digital dimension of the Middle Corridor and has the potential to reshape regional data flows.

Technical and organisational aspects

The capacity of the fibre-optic cable significantly exceeds that of the existing terrestrial routes in the region. This provides the foundation for transmitting large volumes of data and supporting the development of cloud services and future artificial intelligence infrastructure.

The project is being implemented by AzerTelecom International, part of NEQSOL Holding, and Kazakhtelecom through an equal partnership under their joint venture, CaspiLink B.V. Registered in the Netherlands, the company is responsible for both the construction and future operation of the cable. The project is financed entirely with private funds, reducing its exposure to the political and bureaucratic risks associated with state funding. At the same time, its long-term success will depend on the commercial viability of the operators and the stability of the regional political environment.

Laying the cable along the Caspian seabed presented significant technical challenges, as no such operation had previously been carried out there. The route was designed to avoid anchorage areas and military exercise zones. Engineering surveys and environmental approvals were completed in 2025.

The cable was manufactured and tested in China before being shipped to Baku via Kazakhstan’s Kuryk port. Installation was carried out around the clock using a specialised vessel with a displacement of more than 20,000 tonnes. Around 70 specialists took part in the operation. The next phase will involve integrating the onshore landing stations and conducting system tests.

Although commercial operations are scheduled to begin by the end of 2026, the cable’s actual utilisation rates and transit volumes are unlikely to become clear before 2027.

Can Caspian cable provide alternative to Russia and Red Sea routes?

The answer is: to some extent, yes, but not entirely. At present, internet traffic from Central Asia and the South Caucasus largely relies on two main routes: via Russian networks to the north and via the subsea cable systems in the Red Sea and the Mediterranean to the south. In recent years, both have faced geopolitical and infrastructure-related risks, including sanctions, cable damage and network congestion. The Trans-Caspian cable helps reduce this dependence by creating an alternative route that bypasses Russia and Iran, connecting Europe via Azerbaijan, Georgia and Turkey, or linking eastwards through Kazakhstan to China.

Its impact, however, is unlikely to be immediate or comprehensive. The cable covers only the Aktau-Sumqayit section of the route. A fully functioning digital corridor will also require sufficient terrestrial network capacity in Azerbaijan, Georgia and Kazakhstan, a well-developed network of data centres, and commercial agreements between telecom operators.

From a latency perspective, the Caspian route appears competitive. According to available data, round-trip signal latency between the two shores is around 3.7 milliseconds. However, the extent to which it strengthens digital sovereignty will depend on whether substantial volumes of traffic are rerouted through the new link and whether regional operators gain greater control over traffic routing.

For Central Asian states, the project offers an opportunity to reduce, at least partially, their dependence on Russian transit infrastructure. For the South Caucasus, it strengthens the region’s position as an emerging digital hub. Full digital independence, however, remains a distant prospect, as a significant share of traffic handled by major providers, as well as data flows between China and Europe, will continue to rely on established routes.

Synergy between Middle Corridor and Digital Silk Way

Combining freight transport and digital infrastructure within a single geographic corridor offers practical advantages. The Middle Corridor, or Trans-Caspian International Transport Route, has seen container traffic grow in recent years but continues to face constraints in competing with routes through Russia and other alternative corridors.

Adding a digital dimension makes the corridor more technologically advanced by enabling real-time transmission of logistics data, digitalising customs and border procedures, and accelerating insurance and financial transactions. Azerbaijan’s ambition to become a regional digital hub is closely linked to this synergy. Complementing existing energy pipelines, railways and seaports, the fibre-optic cable enhances the country’s appeal as a transit hub for data flows.

A realistic assessment, however, is warranted. Although Azerbaijan’s geographical location is advantageous, becoming a fully fledged digital hub will require large-scale data centres, affordable electricity, a highly skilled workforce and the presence of international cloud service providers. At present, these conditions have only been partially met. Strengthening terrestrial links with Georgia and Turkey, together with laying additional subsea cables across the Black Sea, would help unlock the full potential of the Digital Silk Way.

For Kazakhstan, further development of Aktau port and the modernisation of the country’s east-west digital infrastructure will be equally important. Ultimately, the benefits of this synergy will depend on both countries developing their respective infrastructure at a comparable pace.

Private funding model and risks

The advantages of delivering the project without state funding are clear. It reduces the risk of delays linked to political decision-making, places commercial incentives at the forefront and makes the project more transparent to international investors. CaspiLink B.V.’s registration in the Netherlands also provides greater legal certainty and a well-established framework for dispute resolution. The main vulnerabilities of the model stem from the financial position of the operators themselves and their political connections.

AzerTelecom is part of NEQSOL Holding, a privately owned business group with significant regional influence. Kazakhtelecom, by contrast, is a telecommunications operator with close ties to the Kazakh state. This ownership structure helps balance political risk: it combines commercial flexibility with the prospect of state support if required. At the same time, political developments in either country, sanctions risks or sharp fluctuations in energy markets could affect the operators’ ability to finance future investment.

The project’s cost was previously estimated at around $50m. Private financing has helped keep investment at a manageable level. However, any future expansion – including a possible extension towards Turkmenistan or an increase in transmission capacity – is likely to require additional capital. Long-term transit agreements and cooperation with international telecommunications consortia will therefore be important in mitigating these risks.

Geopolitical context

For China, the project forms a practical component of the Digital Silk Way, helping diversify data flows between Central Asia and Europe. The cable was manufactured in China and supports Beijing’s broader efforts to expand digital connectivity across Eurasia. For Western countries, meanwhile, the digital dimension of the Middle Corridor is strategically significant as it offers an alternative route that bypasses Russia and Iran.

Against the backdrop of efforts to develop the Middle Corridor and establish new data links between Europe and Asia, the cable takes on added strategic importance. It does not pose direct competition to Russia. Over the longer term, however, reducing Central Asia’s reliance on Russian digital transit infrastructure could weaken Moscow’s influence in the region.

The project’s strategic significance is further enhanced by its parallel development alongside existing energy infrastructure. The Caspian region is already home to major oil and gas export routes, including the Baku-Tbilisi-Ceyhan pipeline and the Southern Gas Corridor. Running along the same geographic axis, the fibre-optic cable effectively serves as an “information pipeline”.

This helps diversify the region’s infrastructure and reinforces its role not only as an energy exporter but also as a hub for data transit. At the same time, geopolitical tensions, unresolved issues related to the legal status and security of the Caspian, military activity and sanctions risks remain potential threats to both digital and energy infrastructure.

Prospects and limitations

A possible next step would be to extend the route towards Turkmenistan. A Sumqayit-Turkmenbashi link could become an important component of a fully fledged Digital Silk Way. Its implementation, however, is likely to depend on Ashgabat’s restrictive telecommunications policies and broader strategic priorities.

As data centres and artificial intelligence infrastructure expand, Azerbaijan and Kazakhstan could benefit from relatively affordable electricity and favourable conditions for cooling equipment. More broadly, deeper regional integration will depend on agreements between telecom operators, transparent pricing and simpler cross-border procedures.

The project also faces a number of constraints. The Caspian Sea’s fragile environment, potential restrictions linked to military activity, reliance on Chinese equipment and ongoing consolidation in the global telecommunications market could all slow its development. In addition, the cable’s commercial success will ultimately depend on demand. Regional traffic alone may not be sufficient to utilise its full capacity, making it necessary to attract major international data flows.

World.title: Armenia begins shift from Russia towards EU – but finish line remains distant
World.content:
Armenia between Europe and Russia

Against this backdrop, the European Union pledged to “stand by Armenia”. EU leaders have already announced tens of millions of dollars in financial assistance and opened the bloc’s markets to Armenian goods that had suddenly ceased to meet Russian quality standards. More importantly, Brussels has expressed interest in further deepening ties with Yerevan, while Armenia’s re-elected leadership says the election results demonstrate the public’s desire to continue along the country’s European path.

Parliamentary elections in Armenia are over, but the political—and geopolitical—debate continues. Many viewed the vote as a de facto referendum on the country’s future orientation: Russia or the European Union.During the election campaign, Moscow imposed restrictions on imports of Armenian food products, a move widely interpreted in Armenia as an attempt to influence public opinion. Contrary to some expectations, Russia not only kept those trade restrictions in place after the election but tightened them.

JAMnews reviewed the latest developments and spoke to analysts with opposing views. Residents of Armenia also shared their opinions on how they believe the country should shape its future.

Yerevan residents rush to work in the morning. Photo: Arman Gharajyan/JAMnews

How Armenia’s pivot took shape

Few people remember now, but immediately after the 2018 “Velvet Revolution”, led by then-opposition figure and now Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan, he insisted that his government would not pursue any geopolitical realignment. At the time, Armenia was already a member of the Russian-led Collective Security Treaty Organization (CSTO) and the Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU). Years later, speaking from podiums in both Europe and Yerevan, the same Pashinyan has declared Armenia’s aspiration to join the European Union.

So what happened in between? Over the past several years, the entire security architecture of the South Caucasus has unraveled, triggering a snowball effect. Initially, relations between Yerevan and Moscow developed without major friction. Then came the 2020 Karabakh war. Armenia was defeated and ceased to be the guarantor of Nagorno-Karabakh’s security. Formally, Yerevan had no grounds to hold Moscow responsible in 2020. Nagorno-Karabakh was not part of Armenia, and the agreements signed between the two countries applied only to Armenia itself, not to the unrecognised entity.

However, events then took an unexpected turn.

Over the following two years, Azerbaijan launched several military operations on Armenia’s internationally recognised territory. Yerevan appealed to its allies in the CSTO for assistance, but received neither military support nor even a political assessment of the situation.

The allies responded that it was first necessary to establish where exactly the escalation had taken place, arguing that the Armenia-Azerbaijan border had not been formally delimited. Pashinyan replied sharply:

“To say that there is no border between Armenia and Azerbaijan is to claim that the Collective Security Treaty Organization has no area of responsibility. And if there is no area of responsibility, then there is no organisation.”

Since then, Yerevan, finding itself alone in the face of what it viewed as an external security threat, has frozen its participation in the CSTO and turned increasingly towards Europe. According to some analysts, the price of that shift was Armenia’s official recognition of Nagorno-Karabakh as part of Azerbaijan. In return, the European Union deployed a civilian monitoring mission to Armenia, which helped stabilise the situation along the border with Azerbaijan. Armenia also secured the EU’s political backing.

Retiree Andrey Karapetyan shares his views on European integration. Video and editing: Arman Gharajyan/JAMnews.

Shift gathered pace

These developments on the ground were inevitably followed by political change. The entire Armenia-Azerbaijan negotiation process shifted to Western platforms—an outcome few had anticipated. Since the conflict began in the 1990s, Moscow had served as the principal mediator and facilitator of the peace talks.

Following the events of September 2023, when Azerbaijan’s one-day military operation prompted the entire Armenian population to flee Nagorno-Karabakh, Russia effectively lost its influence in the region.

At the same time, Russia also lost its standing among much of Armenia’s population, no longer being viewed as a friendly state.

A park in Yerevan, where locals gather to play backgammon and discuss politics. Photo: Arman Gharajyan/JAMnews

Although Russia formally remains Armenia’s strategic ally, many Armenians have not forgotten that Russian peacekeepers effectively acted as bystanders, failing to fulfil their mission of protecting the Armenian population of Nagorno-Karabakh. Following the CSTO’s refusal to defend Armenia’s territorial integrity, relations between Moscow and Yerevan cooled even further. The Armenian leadership also adopted a more outspoken tone towards Russia, both in its rhetoric and in its actions.

At the same time, contacts between the Armenian government and its European partners intensified. Brussels allocated hundreds of millions of dollars to support political and economic reforms in Armenia, as well as strengthen the country’s borders. France also began supplying Armenia with military equipment. The culmination of these developments came on 17 October 2023, when speaking at the European Parliament in Strasbourg, Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan declared:

“The Republic of Armenia is ready to be as close to the European Union as the European Union considers possible. Our joint statement with President von der Leyen says: ‘In these difficult times, the EU and Armenia stand shoulder to shoulder.'”

In the years that followed, Pashinyan repeatedly stated that Armenia would seek EU membership. The parliamentary elections held in June and their outcome only reinforced the government’s determination.

“Last year, we adopted a law launching the process of accession to the European Union, which, I would remind you, was initiated by civil society. I believe this provides an additional incentive to give new momentum to our democratic and institutional reforms so that we can achieve EU standards as quickly as possible.

This is our main intermediate goal because we understand that no country can become a full member of the European Union without meeting its standards. Therefore, our primary task is first and foremost to comply with EU standards. […]If we are admitted to the European Union, we will be happy. If we are not, we will still benefit, because Armenia will have become a country that meets European standards, with all the positive consequences that entails,” Pashinyan said at the time.

System administrator Artak Gaboyan shares his views. Video and editing: Arman Gharajyan/JAMnews.

Russia pushes back

At the start of the crisis in Armenian-Russian relations, Moscow responded relatively cautiously to Yerevan’s efforts to move closer to Europe. The Kremlin sought to avoid further destabilising the situation, citing Armenia’s difficult historical circumstances. Even Armenia’s effective suspension of its participation in the CSTO did not result in a fundamental reassessment of bilateral relations.

However, Moscow appeared to change its approach in the run-up to the parliamentary elections held in June.

One of the defining moments came during Pashinyan’s meeting with Vladimir Putin in Moscow in April, when the Russian president openly asked him to allow pro-Russian political forces to participate in the elections. He was primarily referring to Russian-Armenian billionaire Samvel Karapetyan. However, as Karapetyan holds citizenship of several countries, not only Armenia, Armenian law bars him from serving as an MP or becoming prime minister. Pashinyan reportedly made this clear to Putin.

The Kremlin nevertheless continued to support pro-Russian political figures while also taking more concrete steps. Russian regulators began imposing restrictions on imports of Armenian products. Initially, the measures targeted specific companies and categories of goods, but they were later expanded to cover almost all agricultural produce from Armenia.

Businessman Suren Margaryan shares his views. Video and editing: Arman Gharajyan/JAMnews.

The situation continued to escalate. Armenian officials began openly accusing Moscow of attempting to interfere in the country’s internal affairs and engineer a change of government.

At the same time, international media reported on alleged hybrid attacks against Armenia. Reuters also published a report alleging that the Kremlin had devised a plan to bring 100,000 Armenian citizens into the country to vote for pro-Russian political forces.

Following the elections, Moscow has stepped up its calls for Armenia to decide, once and for all, which direction it intends to take. Russian officials have specifically called for a referendum on whether the country should pursue integration with the European Union or the Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU), arguing that choosing the EU would require Armenia to leave the EAEU.

“No one is pushing Armenia out of the EAEU. They themselves have said they want to join the European Union. They need to make a choice. And the sooner that choice is made, the better it will be for everyone,” Russian Deputy Prime Minister Aleksey Overchuk said.

This culminated in a joint statement by the EAEU member states calling for Armenia to hold a referendum on whether the country should remain in the EAEU or pursue EU membership.

Central Yerevan. Photo: Arman Gharajyan/JAMnews

Armenia says time is not right for referendum

In response to Moscow’s demands, the Armenian authorities say they have no plans to hold a referendum or withdraw from the EAEU—for now. The key word is “for now.” Yerevan intends to remain a member of the EAEU until there is a realistic prospect of joining the European Union. Moreover, under the EAEU’s founding rules, Armenia cannot be expelled from the bloc without its consent.

However, holding a referendum on EU membership appears to be a realistic prospect in the longer term. Opinion polls also suggest such a referendum could succeed. Since the 2020 war, Russia’s popularity in Armenia has declined markedly, while support for European integration has continued to grow.

According to a survey conducted by the International Republican Institute (IRI) in May 2026, 75% of Armenians support the country’s accession to the European Union, while 58% say they would vote in favour of joining the bloc in a referendum. The findings point to a sustained decline in trust in Russia and growing pro-European sentiment among the Armenian public.

Photographer Mane Sergoyan shares her views. Video and editing: Arman Gharajyan/JAMnews.

What do experts say?

Which direction should Armenia take? That is arguably the country’s defining question today. Does Armenia have the capacity to make a definitive choice in favour of the European Union? How might Russia respond if it does? And what security risks could such a shift entail?

Political analyst Robert Gevondyan says Yerevan is pursuing a diversification of its foreign policy, a goal repeatedly articulated by the country’s leadership. In his view, this aligns with the interests of Armenia’s European partners.

“Armenia is already receiving a certain level of support, particularly through its cooperation with France. It is possible that, in the future, security cooperation will expand to include other countries, although there is not yet enough information at this stage to identify them. At the same time, it should be remembered that the EU operates under NATO’s security umbrella. While Armenia is not currently seeking rapid accession to the Alliance, if it succeeds in developing close ties with individual EU member states, it could gain access to additional opportunities as an indirect beneficiary of NATO’s resources,” he said.

Is Armenia ready to become part of the European Union today? Gevondyan argues that the question itself is misplaced, as every country must go through a lengthy accession process before joining the bloc.

“No country is ever fully prepared to begin the integration process overnight. By the time Armenia is ready, it will effectively already be part of Europe. States usually go through a long period of integration, during which they implement reforms across various sectors, align with European standards, improve product quality and reach agreements on mutual trade. This process takes years. Armenia is ready to embark on that journey. At the same time, it is impossible to reconcile EU requirements and the conditions for trading with the West with the standards and requirements that exist within the EAEU. We are only at the beginning of a long road.”

Journalist Marianna Mkrtchyan shares her views. Video and editing: Arman Gharajyan/JAMnews.

“Armenia is still a long way from joining the European Union. But the current trajectory could already result in serious losses—not only economically, but also in terms of the country’s sovereignty,” argues political commentator Hayk Khalatyan, founder of the Analytical Centre for Strategic Studies and Initiatives.

Khalatyan also argues that the Armenian leadership will ultimately be unable to sustain its current course of deepening ties with the European Union while remaining a member of the EAEU:

“Pashinyan’s challenge now, after the elections, is to try to normalise relations with Moscow. He will be expected to take concrete steps demonstrating that he is abandoning his previous foreign policy course. But that would effectively mean turning his back on the powerful external actors who helped him remain in power. The question, then, is which path he will choose: to turn his back on the West and Turkey, or continue down the path of confrontation with Russia and the gradual breakdown of bilateral relations. I very much doubt that Pashinyan will abandon his Western partners and move towards normalising ties with Russia. He would like to preserve the policy he has pursued in recent years—reaping the economic benefits of EAEU membership while, in practice, steadily distancing Armenia politically from Russia. But we are now seeing that Moscow is no longer willing to tolerate that approach.”

Human rights activist and film director Hovhannes Ishkhanyan shares his views. Video and editing: Arman Gharajyan.

At the same time, relations between Brussels and Moscow remain deeply confrontational, with some political and security circles even discussing the possibility of a future conflict between Russia and the West.

Whatever the outcome, Armenia is now adapting to a new geopolitical reality while facing Russian trade restrictions. The country is seeking to redirect its exports towards European markets and diversify its trade partners. If it succeeds, Yerevan will remove what many see as its last major economic dependency on Russia.

Yasha Solomonyan, chairman of the Armenian Association of Professional Guides, shares his views. Video and editing: Arman Gharajyan/JAMnews

With the support of the Russian Language News Exchange

World.title: UK embassy in Georgia: Amaglobeli’s sentence ‘disproportionate’ and politically motivated
World.content:
UK embassy condemns Amaglobeli’s sentence

The UK embassy in Georgia has described the sentence handed down to journalist Mzia Amaglobeli as disproportionate and politically motivated, and has called for her immediate release.

“A year ago today Mzia Amaglobeli, a prominent Georgian journalist, was sentenced to two years in prison. We remain concerned that her sentence is disproportionate and politicised and call again for her immediate release,” the embassy’s post on Facebook read.

Mzia Amaglobeli was sentenced on 6 August 2025.

The journalist was arrested on 11 January 2025 on charges of assaulting Batumi police chief Irakli Dgebuadze. On 14 January, Batumi City Court granted the prosecution’s request to remand her in custody pending trial.

The defence’s requests to have the pre-trial detention measure changed were rejected by the courts. Batumi City Court ruled the request inadmissible, while on 19 February 2025 Kutaisi Court of Appeal upheld the decision to keep Amaglobeli in pre-trial detention.

According to Nona Kurdovanidze, chair of the Georgian Young Lawyers’ Association, the court relied on a falsified protocol when justifying her pre-trial detention.

Following her arrest, Mzia Amaghlobeli went on a hunger strike that lasted 38 days. On 18 February 2025, it was announced that she had ended the hunger strike and resumed eating under medical supervision.

World.title: Todd Blanche confirmed as US attorney general after divisive hearing
World.content:
US Senate Republicans have narrowly confirmed Todd Blanche to be President Donald Trump's attorney general, capping one of the most contentious cabinet fights of Trump's second term after bipartisan concerns over Mr Blanche's independence nearly derailed the nomination.

The Republican-led Senate voted 50–49 to make Mr Blanche the second confirmed attorney general since Mr Trump returned to the White House last year with a stated desire to use the law enforcement agency to investigate his political enemies.

While Mr Blanche has already been leading the department in an acting capacity, his confirmation could free him to pursue the Trump administration's agenda even more aggressively.

The vote followed a tumultuous confirmation fight that exposed deep concerns — from some Republicans as well as Democrats — about installing Mr Trump's close ally atop a Justice Department that historically prided itself on its independence from the White House.

In the end, Mr Blanche was confirmed by the narrowest of margins, opposed by two Republicans — Senator Susan Collins of Maine and Lisa Murkowski of Alaska.

On social media, Mr Blanche said he was “deeply honored by the trust and confidence President Trump has placed in me,” adding he was “grateful” to senators for working late to confirm him.

There were deep concerns about installing Donald Trump's close ally atop the US Justice Department. (Reuters: Elizabeth Frantz)

The path to confirmation for Mr Blanche was unusually rocky, due in large part to Republican concerns about a controversial settlement of Mr Trump's lawsuit against the Internal Revenue Service.

Under pressure, Mr Blanche publicly promised in writing that the department would abandon Mr Trump's proposed $US 1.8 billion ($2.5 billion) compensation fund for the president's allies, including those who attacked the Capitol on January 6, 2021, and rein in another piece of the settlement designed to shield Mr Trump and his family from IRS tax audits.

His appeals were enough to win over Republican Bill Cassidy, the decisive vote who threw his support behind Mr Blanche on Friday morning, local time.

Mr Cassidy said no other nominee may be able to run the department better under Mr Trump and suggested Mr Blanche's role as Mr Trump's former criminal defense lawyer could make him more effective at pushing back on the president's demands.

"This is not a referendum on President Trump," Senator Cassidy said, who lost his primary this year to a Trump-backed challenger.

"It is a decision regarding Mr Blanche in very specific circumstances."

Trump sued IRS for 'improper purpose', judge says US President Donald Trump's lawsuit against his own government over leaked tax records was an unparalleled exercise in self-dealing, a US judge says in a scathing ruling.

Senator Dick Durbin of Illinois, the top Democrat on the Senate Judiciary Committee, said confirming Mr Blanche would be a "serious mistake".

He begged his colleagues not to be on the "wrong side" of history.

"If there is ever a moment in history when we need an attorney general above reproach, who is clearly dedicated to ending corruption, even at the highest level of our government, it's right now," Senator Durbin said.

The vote capped off a bruising confirmation fight, with Mr Blanche's loyalty to Mr Trump at the centre of the stalemate.

Blanche elevated after Bondi firing

Mr Blanche was elevated to the top Justice Department post in an acting capacity after Mr Trump fired Pam Bondi in April.

Todd Blanche stepped in after Pam Bondi was fired. (AP: J.Scott Applewhite)

Mr Blanche moved swiftly to advance the president's interests, accelerating investigations into Mr Trump's perceived foes and announcing the settlement that created the $US1.8 billion ($2.5 billion) "Anti-Weaponization Fund" to compensate people who feel mistreated by the criminal justice system and provided Mr Trump and family members with immunity from tax audits.

The controversial settlement threatened to torpedo Mr Blanche's nomination until he formally rescinded the fund in writing under pressure from Republican Senator John Cornyn of Texas and Senator Thom Tillis of North Carolina.

The deal reached between the senators and the department unlocked a vote in the Senate Judiciary Committee, which advanced Mr Blanche's nomination earlier this week.

Even after the deal, Mr Blanche faced opposition from some Republican senators concerned with the "Anti-Weaponization Fund" and the tax audit immunity deal.

Senator Murkowski announced early Friday that she would join Senator Collins in opposing Mr Blanche's nomination, saying the country needed an attorney general "who will check the worst impulses of this administration".

Rise to fame in Trump hush money trial

A former federal prosecutor in New York, Mr Blanche rose to public prominence as a lead attorney on Mr Trump's defense team, including during the Republican's hush money trial in New York.

Tabloid boss testifies at Trump trial A former newspaper publisher outlines how he bought and buried negative stories about Donald Trump, and the former president's lawyer is chastised by a judge, as the "hush money" criminal trial continues in New York.

He also defended Mr Trump against criminal charges in the two federal cases brought by the Biden administration's Department of Justice — an experience Mr Blanche has said provided him a firsthand look at what he contends was the weaponisation of the criminal justice system against Mr Trump.

Mr Blanche entered the Justice Department last year as deputy attorney general under Ms Bondi, overseeing the agency's day-to-day operations and serving as the public face for high-profile and controversial matters, like the release of millions of investigative files related to disgraced financier Jeffrey Epstein.

Democrats have accused Mr Blanche of prioritising his loyalty to Mr Trump above all else through investigations against Mr Trump's foes such as former FBI Director James Comey and a radical reshaping of the department.

Under Ms Bondi and Mr Blanche's leadership, the department has lost thousands of employees through firings, resignations or voluntary departures.

Mr Blanche's supporters say his experience as a federal prosecutor and the trust he earned from Mr Trump in the courtroom made him better equipped than Ms Bondi to explain to the White House the legal constraints of its demands.

Republicans have also touted his efforts to bring down violent crime, tackle illegal immigration and combat violent cartels and drug trafficking.

AP

World.title: 'Really far inland': Concerns over NSW new bird flu cases in native species
World.content:
The New South Wales government has confirmed the state's first cases of H5 avian influenza in Australian native birds.

One bird was found dead near Narooma on the state's south coast and the other near Wentworth in western NSW, according to the state government.

Both birds were greater crested terns.

"[The] birds were reported by members of the public to the Emergency Animal Disease Hotline and sampled by the NSW Government's H5 response team," the government said in a statement.

The first case of H5 bird flu in NSW was found in early July. (ABC News: Carly Cook)

Surveillance in the impacted areas is continuing to "ensure early detection of any further cases".

Environment Minister Penny Sharpe said the cases were not unexpected and the state had been preparing for such an outcome.

"We remain well equipped to respond to manage further impacts," she said.

"We are using the best available data and tools to target actions for our most at-risk wildlife species and important natural places."

A total of four birds have now been infected in NSW.

In early July, the first two cases were detected in migratory petrel birds at Bennetts Beach near Port Stephens on the Mid North Coast.

Surveillance is ongoing in the areas where the birds were found. (ABC News)

The government said its preparedness measures included developing plans for 34 priority sites across the state, carrying out risk assessments and mapping, and conducting information sessions with all agencies involved.

"Governments are working closely with the poultry industry to strengthen biosecurity to mitigate the risk of outbreaks," Agriculture Minister Tara Moriarty said.

"While there have been no detections in poultry in NSW, the poultry industry has been preparing for this and is across the risks and actions required at this point.

"We are continuing to work with our industry partners including key agricultural and wildlife stakeholders, ensuring the community has up-to-date information about our surveillance and response to detections of H5 bird flu."

Location of infections 'really big development'

Jane Bennett is the state's acting chief veterinary officer. She told the ABC the area where the birds were found came "out of the blue" due to how far away it was from previous detections.

Jane Bennett described the detection at Wentworth as an "unusual sight". (ABC News)

"The one at Wentworth, which is down on the Murray, is quite some distance from the coast and these birds aren't naturally found that far from the sea," she said.

"So, an unusual sight and also the furthest inland that we've had a detection at this point.

"The one down on the south coast, down near Narooma, that's quite some distance from any previous detections."

It was a concern shared by Jack Gough, CEO of the Invasive Species Council, who described the finding at Wentworth as a "really big development" with major implications for the Murray-Darling Basin.

"It's the first time we've got [bird flu] really far inland in Australia," he said.

"This bird flu has been spreading really quickly; we've now got it in at least seven species across five states and for the first time turning up in that Murray-Darling Basin inland.

" And that's very concerning ahead of spring breeding time, in particular, and it really says the whole continent is opened up now for bird flu to be spreading. "

Birds in inland wetland colonies, he added, were now susceptible to the devastating disease.

Ms Bennett warned the spread would significantly get worse after the initial impact on coastal areas.

"Evidence from overseas tends to suggest it will slowly creep inland from there," she said.

"We certainly know that it's going to affect our native bird species; to what degree we're unsure at this point in time."

Australian cases reach 215

The total number of infections in Australia has risen to 215, including 10 new cases that were confirmed in Victoria on Saturday.

"These were all from greater crested terns in south-west Victoria and Clyde in south-east Melbourne," Australian Chief Veterinary Officer Beth Cookson said.

Bird flu 'list of doom' Thousands of Australian species have been ranked by threat level as the deadly H5 bird flu spreads.

South Australia has been hit the hardest by the virus, with Federal Agriculture Minister Julie Collins earlier in the week confirming the state's first mass mortality.

"Sadly, we do know that once the H5 bird flu is spreading in wildlife and the natural environment, it is not possible to avoid significant losses, which is what we're starting to see now," she said at the time.

On Friday, the Royal Adelaide Show announced it would go ahead in September without bird and poultry exhibits.

Anyone who sees a dead or sick bird is asked not to touch it and report it to the Emergency Animal Disease Hotline on 1800 675 888.

World.title: Gina Rinehart says ABC Ombudsman finding 'fails all Australian women'
World.content:
The company owned by Gina Rinehart AO has criticised the ABC Ombudsman after it found comments about her, which aired on an episode of Race Around the World, did not breach editorial standards.

The episode, aired on July 12, featured contestant Kate McGuinness describing a fictional scenario that involved a violent attack on Mrs Rinehart, including mixing her "guts" to "make one big sausage roll".

Mrs Rinehart's company, Hancock Prospecting, wrote to the ABC Board asking for the video to be taken down late last month, calling for a public apology and a "comprehensive investigation" into how the video came to be published by the ABC.

ABC managing director Hugh Marks this week apologised to Mrs Rinehart, saying it fell short of community expectations.

The ABC Ombudsman found that the episode did not breach the ABC Editorial Standards relating to harm and offence.

A spokesperson for Hancock Prospecting said in a statement the ABC's Editorial Standards needed "significant improvement".

"The internal ABC Ombudsman's decision that the ABC did not breach ABC Editorial Standards fails all Australian women and the millions of taxpayers who fund the ABC," the spokesperson said.

Content 'normalised violent torture'

The spokesperson criticised the "ongoing silence" from the ABC board, particularly chair Kim Williams and deputy chair Lisa Caffery.

"The buck stops with the heads of the ABC," the spokesperson said.

"We wait to see the long overdue changes to the ABC's editorial standards.

"Such editorial standards need to stop sexual violence and torture-until-death episodes being shown or depicted in any form against any woman on the ABC, including under the pretence of satire or art or any other cloak."

The spokesperson said they were waiting for a "detailed account" into how the "unacceptable piece" came to be aired and why it took 25 days for it to be removed.

"The content shown on the ABC normalised violent torture against a woman till death, and dehumanised an Australian, such that she was worthless and OK to be sexually tortured, should not be and must not be acceptable in our country," they said.

The spokesperson said it was a concept "practised by terrorists … and must never be regarded as art, or acceptable in our country, even by the ABC".

Hugh Marks says the ABC "got this wrong". (ABC News: John Gunn)

ABC Ombudsman explains decision

The matter was referred to the ABC Ombudsman following complaints about the content.

The Ombudsman said the question it considered was not "whether the remarks were offensive or in good taste but whether any likely offence was justified by the editorial context".

"Having regard to the program format, the filmmaker's established creative style, the surreal and hyperbolic nature of the film, the absence of any visual depiction of violence, and the criticism expressed by the judging panel," the Ombudsman found that a reasonable audience member "would be unlikely to interpret the remarks as a genuine call for, endorsement of, or encouragement of violence."

The ABC Ombudsman leads an investigations team that assesses, investigates and reviews complaints about specific ABC content.

While it reports to the ABC board, the ABC Ombudsman's Office "makes decisions objectively and independently from ABC content teams, ABC management and the ABC board".

ABC to change guidance

In an earlier statement, Hugh Marks said: "As part of our review of this matter, we have considered whether the guidance in the ABC Editorial Policies adequately reflects current community expectations."

"We have also considered whether the relevant guidance sufficiently distinguishes between news and non-news content."

As a result, the ABC will amend its guidance as it applies to violence.

"The change, I think, will reflect the fact that no individual should be the subject of comedy that is violent in its description in our programming, and I think the ABC has to hold itself to a higher standard and I think it's really important we make that change," Marks said.

"It's also important that we acknowledge we got this wrong.

"So, we issue the apology, and we make the relevant changes so that it doesn't happen again."

Contestant's apology

McGuinness released a statement through the ABC last week, apologising to anyone she offended and saying the sense of humour featured in her films on Race Around the World was "farcical".

"In no way was it my intention to promote violence," she said.

"My writing is cartoonish and always satirical.

"Unfortunately, jokes do not land with everyone. Its purpose was never to be taken literally."

The film has been removed from the ABC's platforms and will be replaced with an edited video without the material subject to the complaint.

World.title: Trump announces $560m critical minerals investment in tiny NSW town
World.content:
The Pentagon is investing more than half a billion dollars to expand an Australian critical mineral project poised to become the world's first scandium mine, US President Donald Trump has announced.

The $US400 million ($560m) loan to Sunrise Energy Metals' Syerston scandium project in central west NSW is expected to shore up America's supply of the "increasingly critical mineral" used in aerospace, defence and automotive sectors.

Scandium is already used widely for defence, aerospace and energy applications, but nearly all supply comes from China, Russia and Ukraine. The US has not mined scandium since 1969.

The Pentagon's Office of Strategic Capital (OSC) said while there was currently no primary mine-source scandium supply globally, it was harvested through by-products of other industrial or resource extraction processes.

Donald Trump's announcement was part of a slew of investments in critical minerals and battery projects. (Reuters: Evelyn Hockstein)

It said "foreign competitors" accounted for about 80 per cent of the world's mining production and nearly all scandium processing.

The OSC said the mine's production would "support warfighting capabilities" as well as "strategically important economic sectors" including data centres, semiconductors and automotives.

Under the proposed financing, the US Department of War would receive a right of first offer on the mine's output.

Sunrise Energy Metals said its project near Fifield, about 350 kilometres west north-west of Sydney, aimed to deliver "the world's first primary source of mine-able, high-grade scandium".

It is set to have an initial capacity of 60 tonnes a year of scandium oxide, starting production in the first half of 2028.

In February, the company's chief executive Sam Riggall said the project, backed by mining billionaire Robert Friedland, was expected to contribute to a US critical minerals stockpile worth $US12 billion ($16.9b).

Last year, the company signed a five-year deal with US defence contractor Lockheed Martin granting it to buy up to 15 tonnes of scandium oxide from its Syerston project.

The deal came days after Mr Trump and Anthony Albanese inked a critical minerals pact during the prime minister's visit to Washington.

Albanese and Trump ink deal for 'dominance' of critical minerals Donald Trump and Anthony Albanese have inked a deal for "critical mineral and energy dominance" in a new partnership that will tip billions into mining projects in the US and Australia.

Resources Minister Madeleine King welcomed the decision, calling it a "significant vote of confidence" in Australia's capacity to supply the US and its partners with the critical minerals they need.

"The Sunrise scandium project hosts the world's largest and highest-grade known scandium resource, which has a range of vital aerospace, defence and clean energy applications," she said.

"No one country alone can create secure, end-to-end supply chains in critical minerals and rare earths.

"In working together, Australian mining companies can create more jobs and investment opportunities here at home, and more jobs and investment in the United States."

Madeleine King says the Sunrise project has the world's largest and highest-grade known scandium resource. (ABC News: Kimberley Putland)

OSC's senior managing director Peter B Zuckerman said the conditional loan was a "decisive step toward creating a US-aligned scandium value chain, ensuring our warfighters and manufacturers no longer depend on adversaries".

Mr Trump announced the loan on Friday, local time, alongside a slew of other local investments in critical minerals and battery projects totalling $US3 billion ($4.2b).

Speaking at a State Department event in Washington involving more than 200 mining executives, educators and investors, Mr Trump said the US was reclaiming its place as "the minerals superpower of the world".

"Critical minerals are the raw materials of American strength that power everything from advanced weaponry to automobiles, and we want these essential products to be mined, refined and made right here in the USA," he said.

The US has burned through large numbers of precision-guided missiles and air-defence interceptors during its five-month-long war against Iran.

Defence officials and lawmakers have warned that replenishing some inventories could take years given existing production constraints, even as the Trump administration has disputed reports of significant shortages.

ABC/Reuters

World.title: Rockliff adviser, ex-minister chosen as Liberal Senate replacements
World.content:
A senior adviser to Tasmanian Premier Jeremy Rockliff has been chosen to replace outgoing Liberal Senator Wendy Askew, while a former state minister will replace Senator Jonno Duniam when he finishes up at the end of the year.

Former party president Chris Gatenby will top the Liberals Senate ticket at the next federal election, with former minister Sarah Courtney coming in second and Latrobe councillor Jacki Martin third.

Brad Stansfield, a former chief of staff to Will Hodgman, missed out on a spot on the ticket.

Senators Askew and Duniam announced earlier this year they would not be seeking preselection.

Their resignations create casual vacancies, allowing the party to appoint new senators in their place, rather than go through a by-election.

The Senate spots were determined by about 60 Liberal Senate selectors at a meeting in Launceston today.

Long-term staffer gets his chance

Mr Gatenby is a senior adviser to Premier Jeremy Rockliff and has been involved with the Liberals for years, having previously served as party president.

He was raised on a farm in northern Tasmania, and then lived in Launceston.

He has had a broad career including senior roles in policy development, advocacy and government across Australia and the UK.

The father of two ran unsuccessfully in Bass during the last election.

"I think having two attempts at the state level gives you a great grounding at the door step, understanding what people's issues are, and I'm looking forward to getting in there and making a difference," Mr Gatenby said on Saturday.

Premier Rockliff said in July 2025, during the election campaign, Mr Gatenby "brings a wealth of experience to the table, in government, in small business, in policy advocacy and in the Liberal Party, including as our previous party president.

"Chris is the next generation of the party, putting his hand up to represent his community in parliament. He already volunteers in his community, including on the board of the Launceston Harvest Market," he said.

Sarah Courtney was Tasmania's first-ever female primary industries minister, in the government of Peter Gutwein. (ABC News: Scott Ross)

Sarah Courtney was elected to the Tasmanian parliament in 2014 and appointed to cabinet in 2018.

Ms Courtney, a moderate Liberal, was viewed as a talented minister with leadership potential.

She was Tasmania's first female primary industries minister, but stepped down after starting a relationship with her department secretary, who is now her husband.

She is a trained engineer and owns a boutique vineyard in the Tamar Valley.

Ms Courtney held the health portfolio throughout the COVID pandemic, and listed the guiding of voluntary assisted dying through the parliament as a key achievement.

In 2022, Ms Courtney quit Tasmanian politics after returning from a European holiday during which she caught COVID-19.

Ms Courtney, who was education minister, was forced to isolate in France just days out from school resuming in Tasmania.

When asked on Saturday if she had learnt from that time, Ms Courtney would not comment, instead telling reporters she had a wealth of experience.

"I have enjoyed being a minister, it gave me a thorough understanding of a range of portfolios and that's the experience I bring here today," she said.

"I've got experience as a minister plus I've worked in the real world across a range of industries and that coupled together means I'm good at finding solutions.

"I'm good at working with the community and small business to make sure the policies we have here in Tasmania — and that we're advocating for in Canberra — make a meaningful difference."

Not quite for Martin, Stansfield

Jacki Martin who came third in the vote, has been a Latrobe councillor since 2022 and is currently a parliamentary adviser to Wendy Askew.

Jacki Martin has been a Latrobe councillor since 2022 and is currently a parliamentary advisor to Wendy Askew. (Facebook: Jacki Martin)

She nominated for preselection in June and said on her social media page that she would "bring energy, discipline and relentless determination" to the role.

Representing the north of the state, she has been outspoken recently on the closure of Boags Brewery in Launceston, the Liberty Bell Bay smelter and the sale of Tasmania's largest farm, Rushy Lagoon.

Ms Martin helped campaign for Education Minister Jo Palmer, Senator Claire Chandler and Health Minister Bridget Archer.

"Small business drives me, I'm the child of a small business owner … my family drives me, your family drives me, and I'll be working every day to see that this generation that's coming up underneath us isn't any worse off than what we have been," Ms Martin said.

Brad Stansfield was unsuccessful in his bid for a place high on the ticket.

Mr Stansfield was chief of staff to former Liberal premier Will Hodgman for eight years, and former Liberal senator Eric Abetz between 2007 and 2010.

Brad Stansfield has missed out on a spot. (Supplied: Font PR)

He also advised the Tasmanian Liberals through successful state election campaigns from 2014 to 2024.

Mr Stansfield was a partner in a public relations and lobbying firm before leaving to become the owner of a polling firm and co-owner in a stable of regional newspapers.

He also commentated on Tasmanian and federal politics on a podcast which he co-hosted.

Mr Stansfield has also spoken against the federal coalition doing preference deals with One Nation, and in February wrote that the "increased voter support for One Nation is a symptom of the federal coalition’s dysfunction for much of last year".

World.title: Perth man allegedly damaged 20 cars during 90-minute rampage
World.content:
A man has been charged after he allegedly went on a car-smashing spree before leading police on a wild chase through Perth's northern suburbs on Friday.

Police allege the 45-year-old began his 90-minute rampage at midday in a Toyota Camry, which was driven through several suburbs including Mount Lawley, Perth, Inglewood, East Perth, South Perth, Carine, Madeley and Duncraig.

It is alleged that after stopping and jumping out of his car, he then used a metal pole to strike at least 20 parked or stationary vehicles, causing significant damage.

Several people were inside their vehicles at the time but no injuries were reported.

Police received numerous reports from the public about the man's alleged behaviour. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

After receiving numerous reports of the destructive behaviour, police co-ordinated a cross-district response to locate the Toyota Camry, which was spotted, from the sky, in the northern suburbs.

The man allegedly failed to stop and led officers on a high-speed chase, during which he allegedly drove recklessly and on the wrong side of the road.

He was arrested when the vehicle finally came to a stop on Lilburne Road in Duncraig.

The man, from Gosnells, was due to face court on Saturday charged with a string of offences including criminal damage, being armed in a way that may cause fear, and reckless driving to escape pursuit.
