World.title: ‘Faceless’ foes to face off as Carlton and St Kilda scrap for wildcard spot
World.content:
Analysis SportAFLAFL 2026 ‘Faceless’ foes to face off as Carlton and St Kilda scrap for wildcard spot Peter Ryan August 8, 2026 — 8:36pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

There will be plenty of familiar faces on both sides when Carlton take on St Kilda at Marvel Stadium in what is arguably the most consequential clash between the two clubs since the 1972 preliminary final. Liam Stocker will be donning a Saints jumper for his 100th AFL game when he lines up alongside other ex-Blues Jack Silvagni and Tom De Koning, while former Saint Blake Acres will wear the No.13 Carlton jumper Stocker wore in his 28 matches with Carlton. Another win under interim coach Josh Fraser will kick the Blues two games clear of St Kilda in the race for a wildcard spot, while Ross Lyon’s team will leapfrog Carlton if they win – with a softer draw in their remaining two matches likely to see them home. St Kilda stars Tom De Koning and Jack Silvagni were huge names at Carlton before leaving the Blues as free agents. Getty Images It’s a huge game, particularly so for the Saints, who grabbed Carlton free agents De Koning and Silvagni during last year’s trade period to set them on a course for finals.



However, the animosity that existed between the two clubs in recent years as former Carlton list manager and club great Stephen Silvagni grabbed players from the list after an acrimonious departure from the club at the end of 2019 is said to have dissipated. Sources from both clubs, and former club officials who wanted to remain anonymous in order to speak freely, said there was no longer any angst towards each other, with the regime at Carlton now different from the one in place when Silvagni, Jack’s father, departed. While the Blues fought off an attempt to poach Brodie Kemp at the end of 2024, and weren’t happy to lose De Koning to such an outrageous offer last season, Silvagni was not a player they tried desperately to retain, despite his name being synonymous with the club. Josh Fraser has led the Blues to a 9-2 record since taking over as interim coach. AFL Photos A minor skirmish earlier this year, when the clearance of Carlton VFL player Ethan Phillips to St Kilda’s VFL list took longer than necessary, also showed the clubs were happy to play the game hard.



But when the two teams line up on Sunday evening a rivalry will be the furthest thing from their minds. “Every week it is about a faceless opponent, everyone builds up who you are playing, [but] your biggest opponent is yourself,” Lyon said after Silvagni and De Koning played against their former club for the first time in round eight. The two clubs have shared 46 players over their history, with former Blues Jack Carroll and Paddy Dow still on the Saints’ list, but they have hardly built a rivalry. The two teams have played against each other in just five finals, with the ’72 preliminary final their most recent. The Saints’ winning record of 26.75 per cent over Carlton is their lowest winning rate against any side in their history. In the late-1980s they tried to reverse that, with the Carlton crew consisting of premiership Blues Alex Marcou, Peter McConville and Ken Sheldon joining St Kilda at the end of their careers alongside other Blues Spiro Kourkoumelis, Warren Jones and Ricky Nixon.



Carlton great Alex Jesaulenko ended his playing career at the Saints The Age They had joined soon after the most famous Blue to become a Saint, Alex Jesaulenko, controversially joined the club in 1980 after coaching Carlton to a flag as captain-coach in 1979. None of the moves worked for the Saints, who spent that decade languishing at the bottom while the Blues kept playing in grand finals at winning flags. But the arrival of Carlton’s Aaron Hamill at Moorabbin in 2001 began to reverse that winning record, particularly at Marvel Stadium. The Saints now lead the head-to-head battle at that venue 22-8, with their two-point win over Carlton in the final round of 2024 tipping the Blues out of finals momentarily before Port Adelaide beat Fremantle later that day.



They defeated them comfortably earlier this season when the Blues, then coached by Michael Voss, suffered a familiar second-half collapse and Jack Silvagni showed he was on the path to an outstanding season. Sunday night is different. Lyon noted during the week Fraser has improved Carlton’s defence by six goals and jokingly nominated him for coach of the year for his effort in turning the Blues around. Fraser, for his part, was not getting caught up in any suggestions this game was anything other than business as usual – a game to win against a faceless opponent who had a talented bloke wearing No.7 (Nasiah Wanganeen-Milera) they had to worry about. “These are the games you want to play in,” Fraser said.



“These are the opportunities you want to be afforded. We’ve done enough to this point to have the opportunity to play in a game like this. We’ll lean into it, but it won’t be about the outcome – it’ll be the brand of football we want to play,” Fraser said. Nothing about the opposition. Nothing about the want to defeat the mob that contains a few of their former players. The process – that’s what Ross and Josh will focus on.

World.title: Buyer pays $2.91m for inner west semi for kids to live in while at uni
World.content:
PropertyNewsAuctions Buyer pays $2.91m for inner west semi for kids to live in while at uni Robyn Willis Updated August 8, 2026 — 8:32pm ,first published 1:08pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A two-storey Erskineville semi sold for $2.91 million at auction on Saturday to an overseas buyer who the selling agent said had purchased it for his children to live in while studying at university. About 30 people, including several neighbours, gathered in the open-plan living area at the rear of 59A Prospect Street to witness the auction of the four-bedroom, three-bathroom architecturally designed home. The property had a guide of $2.5 million and sold for $260,000 above the reserve of $2.65 million. There is no legal requirement for a vendor’s reserve to be in line with their property’s price guide.



Six parties registered to bid, with bidding opening at $2.52 million. Two parties initially battled it out in increments of $10,000, $20,000 and $30,000. When bidding reached $2.65 million, two new bidders entered the fray, with 15 bid increases of similar sizes going back and forth between the two. A final bid of $5000 ended the spectacle with the underbidders, a couple with a child who own a property further west but rent locally, quietly saying “I think we’re out”. It was socks all round for the auction of 9A Prospect Road as a crowd assembled in the compact open-plan living area. James Brickwood A lawyer acting on behalf of the successful bidder said his client was based overseas. Records show the property on the 144-square-metre site last sold in 2016 for $1.92 million. The property was one of 520 scheduled to go to auction in Sydney this week. By evening, Domain Group recorded a preliminary auction clearance rate of 50 per cent from 292 reported results throughout the week, while 94 auctions were withdrawn.





The landscaped backyard at the rear of 59A Prospect Street. Domain One of the vendors, who was present at the auction, said that while it was “very difficult to move” because her family had enjoyed the close-knit local community, an “outstanding” property closer to the city had convinced them to make a fresh start, so they bought it. In Lane Cove, a local family with a young child paid $1,463,000 for a three-bedroom apartment after it passed in at auction on Saturday. Bidding for the property at 2/15 Longueville Road opened at $1.38 million, increasing in bids of $10,000 to reach $1.45 million when things stalled and it passed in. The lead bidder was then invited to increase their offer and, after half an hour of negotiating, the property sold.



The apartment had a guide of $1.4 million and a reserve of $1.5 million. Related Article Sydney house prices ‘Fewer buyers’: The Sydney suburbs with the deepest property downturns Two bidders registered, although Raine & Horne Lower North Shore sales agent Oscar Nicholls was initially expecting only one. The underbidder was an investor who had seen the property once early in the campaign and was attracted to it for its yield potential, Nicholls said. “He got to a point [in the bidding] and said ‘at this price point it doesn’t make any sense’. He has a couple of investments which he is holding because rents are up,” Nicholls said. The vendor was a single-parent family who bought a four-bedroom home. Nicholls said market conditions were good for upsizers.



“She got a really good deal on what she bought,” he said of the new property. The three-bedroom apartment has two bathrooms, a double garage and a living area opening onto a private courtyard. Domain In Bondi Junction, negotiations continued after a two-bedroom art deco apartment passed in at $775,000. Two parties registered to bid for 2/143 Old South Head Road but just a single bid of $750,000 was placed when the auction opened. The lead bidder, a first home buyer renting in Paddington, was invited to advance on their offer with a further bid of $775,000 before the property passed in.



The apartment, sold as a deceased estate, had a guide of $800,0000 and a reserve of $850,000. It is one of nine apartments in a block positioned between Bellevue Hill and Bondi Junction and features high ornate ceilings, timber fretwork and picture rails, typical of the era. The art deco apartment is one of just nine in the boutique block. Domain A sales agent for Ray White Eastern Beaches, Angus Gorrie, expects the property to sell next week. “It takes a bit more time [to sell in this market], but we had two registered buyers, and we are getting close,” he said. “People are out there – the market is better than it was in June.”

World.title: Sheer lunacy and a coming of age: Inside the greatest Battle of Brisbane yet
World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2026 Sheer lunacy and a coming of age: Inside the greatest Battle of Brisbane yet Nick Wright August 8, 2026 — 7:55pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Jot it down and remember where you were for the craziest Battle of Brisbane yet. It may have been the Dolphins who took home the two points in a thrilling 40-32 shootout against the Broncos – securing their maiden finals appearance in the process – but the 50,000-plus fans who packed into Suncorp Stadium were arguably the biggest winners of Saturday night. Selwyn Cobbo scores for the Dolphins on Saturday. Getty Images There were moments of brilliance and sheer lunacy, contract statements and ominous reminders, injury scares and flaring tempers. As Broncos coach Michael Maguire said, “it was an unusual game”. It might be best if we just broke it down.



Mam magic and a contract statement Ezra Mam has been a man maligned for much of season 2026 – his axing at times throughout the campaign symbolic of the Broncos’ dramatic slide from defending champions to the doldrums of the competition. But the under-siege five-eighth issued a stunning reminder of just what he could produce with a first-half hat-trick that threatened to completely take the game away from the Dolphins. Loading It was fitting that in Indigenous Round Mam produced his finest performance of the year, his first highlight bouncing on the outside of Reece Walsh to take his fullback’s pass and score untouched from close range. The opportunity came from a Billy Walters 40/20, it what was the off-contract hooker’s first starting appearance since rupturing his ACL last year.



“It’s a testament to all Bill’s hard work, it would have been tough sitting in his position last year, and to fight his way through it … he’s earned his spot,” Broncos skipper Pat Carrigan said. “The Walters name is synonymous with the club, and he lives and breathes what it’s like to play for the Broncos – I’m really proud of him and a bit disappointed we couldn’t get the win for his 100th game.” For Mam’s next trick, shortly after Jamayne Isaako sent the Dolphins’ kick-off out on the full, the 23-year-old simply ran it hard and straight at the defence, before shrugging off a pair of tackles and reaching out desperately for his second. Walters was quick to issue another reminder of why he must be retained at Red Hill, slicing out of dummy half and splitting the defence, before finding Deine Mariner on his inside to score an 80-minute special. It was then Mam’s kicking game which extended Brisbane’s early lead to 24 points, his grubber twice fumbled by Jack Bostock for Xavier Willison to touch down.



And even after the Dolphins scored three straight tries, it was Mam who wrestled back the ascendancy for a moment – scoring straight from a scrum after Tom Gilbert’s knock on. Just as he was in the 2023 grand final, Mam appeared destined to add a man of the match medal to his accolades. Until one moment and a rival general flipped the script. The good fortune and little general The Dolphins needed something to go their way as Mam orchestrated a 24-0 Broncos lead. Hamiso Tabuai-Fidow was on hand to provide that. As the Broncos went on the attack again, a dropped ball by Jaiyden Hunt was swooped on by the Dolphins’ No.1 – his smile as soon as he grabbed possession a sign he knew he would not be caught on the 90-metre dash to score.



Hamiso Tabuai-Fidow scores against Brisbane. Getty Images While that try may have been in fortuitous circumstances, it appeared to awaken his side as they hunted to keep their top four hopes alive. From the following set, Max Plath – who was outstanding all night, finishing with 184 running metres – burst through the middle and into the clear to go deep into Brisbane territory. Halfback Isaiya Katoa then stood up, commanding his team into position for him to fire a perfect short pass for Connelly Lemuelu to cut the deficit to 12 points. Katoa was at it again when the Dolphins clinched the momentum, with the 22-year-old’s brilliant face pass for Bostock presenting a two-on-one, with Isaako finishing the job in the corner.



While Mam’s third briefly halted the surge, it would not be for long. Ben Talty’s dropped ball coming out of trouble opened the door, and the Dolphins turned globetrotters. Winger Selwyn Cobbo could have panicked when Katoa’s attempted long ball went behind him and crept towards the sideline, but the former Bronco’s tap-back for a supporting Farnworth was perfect. The England centre was then hardly troubled on his way to the line, the Broncos’ defence parting without hesitation. Somehow, at half-time, the Dolphins led 30-24. “Key moments are hurting us, that’s where we’re at,” Maguire lamented. “Obviously, I’m frustrated, you can’t leak or let in that many tries to put yourself in a position to really contend.”



Katoa’s masterclass and ‘The Hammer’s’ miracle He had shown signs he was about to make this game his own, but it was the way Katoa controlled the second half which ultimately proved the difference. The first-half shootout had quickly descended into an arm wrestle, with Mariner and Gilbert both sent for head injury assessments, and Farnworth seen limping regularly after an awkward tackle on his lower leg by opposite number Kotoni Staggs. Against a Broncos side missing skipper and veteran halfback Adam Reynolds, it was Katoa’s composure which guided the Dolphins home – relying on his patient kicking game while waiting for his moment to strike. That chance came when Tabuai-Fidow’s kick return, and Plath’s bulldozing carry with three defenders on his back, got the Redcliffe army on the charge – Katoa’s delicate chip over the top gifting Lemuelu his second try of the night.



Related Article NRL 2026 Storm pile on the points against Sea Eagles in Perth While Walsh would ice a penalty goal to earn Brisbane the lead back, Katoa was far from finished with the boot. His attacking bomb was miraculously taken by Tabuai-Fidow, who reached out to score his second and clinch the lead, before the Tongan maestro’s cross-field effort was reeled in by Bostock and eventually spread back the other way for Cobbo to seal the win. “It’s something I’ve been working on, and I think I can get over a couple of fullbacks. I looked at Issy and just said ‘iso’ [isolated kick] … I got the try, it’s pretty cool,” Tabuai-Fidow relived. By full-time, for all of the individual brilliance Mam and Tabuai-Fidow showcased, Katoa was the evening’s mastermind – orchestrating five of his side’s seven tries.



“You could see we had our attack on, you could see we were going to find opportunities – we were making little half breaks and linebreaks, and that gave me a lot of confidence,” Dolphins coach Kristian Woolf said. “I do love the way he steered the ship, he’s our leader and halfback, he’s got a great temperament on him, and I thought he controlled that second half really well.”

World.title: The obscure 10,000-item list of medical devices costing patients billions
World.content:
Medical devices prices are much higher in Australia than New Zealand.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Weeks before the 2022 federal election, a deal made inside then-health minister Greg Hunt’s office locked 14 million privately insured Australians into paying some of the highest prices in the world for surgical hardware. That deal, federal bureaucrats later told Mark Butler, who succeeded Hunt as health minister, went against their advice as it “predominantly benefited industry rather than providing a negotiated balance of benefits to industry and the Australian community”. Related Article Medical Malfunctions Tested on pigs, bad data but given to ambos anyway: Homegrown defibrillator’s red flags Instead of dismantling the agreement, though, Butler endorsed it – and instructed his department to enforce its terms. Four years later, it remains the foundation of Australia’s medical devices market. Last year, a review told the government that, although the system had improved in some ways, consumers still paid “significantly higher” prices than other countries. The agreement underpinned a little-known price-setting schedule called the Prescribed List. The Prescribed List dictates what private health funds must pay hospitals for more than 10,000 items – from pacemakers and artificial joints to surgical staples, sponges and glues.



These prices are often far higher than rates paid in Australia’s public hospitals, and mean privately insured Australians pay up to three times more for surgical hardware than overseas patients. In turn, critics say, the prices push up premiums. “We have a system where the government mandates a price floor for private patients that is far higher than what public hospitals pay for the exact same products,” said Stephen Duckett, a health economist and former head of the federal health department. Related Article Editorial

Medical Malfunctions Our medical devices regime is not fit for purpose The Age's View Editorial The current system isolates medical device manufacturers from normal commercial competition, forcing policyholders to subsidise corporate profits, Duckett said. “It is a legalised transfer of wealth from Australians paying private health insurance premiums straight to multinational device companies. And neither party has shown the political will to fix it,” he said. Hunt stands by the deal he made and said Labor, before the 2022 election, also supported the agreement and that its guiding principle had been to put downward pressure on insurance premiums. He also defended the consultation undertaken before his decision. A federal government review of the agreement last year found that that while it was correct that prices for medical devices had fallen after Hunt’s deal, total outlays stayed high, partly because hospitals used more devices per procedure.



Official evaluation data reveals severe price gaps between Australia and health systems in New Zealand, Britain and France across many medical devices, including defibrillators, artificial joints and pacemakers. Related Article Exclusive

Medical Malfunctions ‘Race to the bottom’: Investigation reveals toll of weak medical device laws Departmental briefs from 2022 to 2024 obtained under freedom of information (FOI) reveal the scale of local price hikes for a variety of devices. For the most popular implanted cardiac defibrillator, the private Prescribed List benefit insurance companies had to pay in 2023 was $36,500. Public hospitals paid $14,500 for an identical device. When setting prices for prescription medicines on the Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme, Commonwealth bureaucrats negotiate directly with pharmaceutical firms to secure the lowest cost for taxpayers. But for medical devices, the list dictates prices through an advisory committee that reviews the figures three times a year. In 2022, when medical technology firms were worried about a potential shake-up of the Prescribed List, Hunt built in a mandatory price floor for devices on the list, at 7 per cent above what public hospitals pay.



A Department of Health spokesman confirmed that the margin of 7 per cent above what public hospitals pay for devices remains in place. Internal Department of Health documents show public servants formally refused to endorse Hunt’s agreement in 2022. In March 2022, days before Hunt signed the agreement with the lobby group representing the device industry, the Medical Technology Association of Australia, a senior bureaucrat advised Hunt’s office that the department recommended the minister not sign the deal. The official warned of unmitigated financial risks and uncosted concessions. Greg Hunt as health minister in 2022. Alex Ellinghausen Once Labor took office, the same bureaucrats told the new government that the deal Hunt’s office agreed to “was not drafted or negotiated by the department” and “predominantly benefited industry rather than providing a negotiated balance of benefits”. Private Healthcare Australia chief executive Dr Rachel David said the Prescribed List locked in prices for medical devices in the private system that were consistently 7 to 20 per cent higher than public prices.



In some cases, the difference was far greater. David’s association provided this masthead with six examples of devices that were up to 358 per cent higher than prices paid in New Zealand for an identical product. Loading David said the Prescribed List agreement transferred hundreds of millions of dollars directly from health insurance policyholders to bolster the profit of private hospitals and device manufacturers. “Prices have been too high for too long and international medical device companies have profited at the expense of Australian consumers,” she said. Related Investigation

Medical Malfunctions Medical Malfunctions The latest figures from the Australian Prudential Regulation Authority show private health funds paid $2.52 billion for medical devices in the year to March 2026, a 3.2 per cent increase on the previous year. Over the same period, private hospital admissions grew at just 1.8 per cent. Responding to the warnings disclosed in the FOI documents, Hunt last week defended his record, and said that he and his office conducted extensive consultations with stakeholders and held numerous meetings with departmental officials throughout the reform process.

World.title: ‘Faceless’ foes to face off as Carlton and St Kilda scrap for wildcard spot
World.content:
Analysis SportAFLAFL 2026 ‘Faceless’ foes to face off as Carlton and St Kilda scrap for wildcard spot Peter Ryan August 8, 2026 — 8:36pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

There will be plenty of familiar faces on both sides when Carlton take on St Kilda at Marvel Stadium in what is arguably the most consequential clash between the two clubs since the 1972 preliminary final. Liam Stocker will be donning a Saints jumper for his 100th AFL game when he lines up alongside other ex-Blues Jack Silvagni and Tom De Koning, while former Saint Blake Acres will wear the No.13 Carlton jumper Stocker wore in his 28 matches with Carlton. Another win under interim coach Josh Fraser will kick the Blues two games clear of St Kilda in the race for a wildcard spot, while Ross Lyon’s team will leapfrog Carlton if they win – with a softer draw in their remaining two matches likely to see them home. St Kilda stars Tom De Koning and Jack Silvagni were huge names at Carlton before leaving the Blues as free agents. Getty Images It’s a huge game, particularly so for the Saints, who grabbed Carlton free agents De Koning and Silvagni during last year’s trade period to set them on a course for finals.



However, the animosity that existed between the two clubs in recent years as former Carlton list manager and club great Stephen Silvagni grabbed players from the list after an acrimonious departure from the club at the end of 2019 is said to have dissipated. Sources from both clubs, and former club officials who wanted to remain anonymous in order to speak freely, said there was no longer any angst towards each other, with the regime at Carlton now different from the one in place when Silvagni, Jack’s father, departed. While the Blues fought off an attempt to poach Brodie Kemp at the end of 2024, and weren’t happy to lose De Koning to such an outrageous offer last season, Silvagni was not a player they tried desperately to retain, despite his name being synonymous with the club. Josh Fraser has led the Blues to a 9-2 record since taking over as interim coach. AFL Photos A minor skirmish earlier this year, when the clearance of Carlton VFL player Ethan Phillips to St Kilda’s VFL list took longer than necessary, also showed the clubs were happy to play the game hard.



But when the two teams line up on Sunday evening a rivalry will be the furthest thing from their minds. “Every week it is about a faceless opponent, everyone builds up who you are playing, [but] your biggest opponent is yourself,” Lyon said after Silvagni and De Koning played against their former club for the first time in round eight. The two clubs have shared 46 players over their history, with former Blues Jack Carroll and Paddy Dow still on the Saints’ list, but they have hardly built a rivalry. The two teams have played against each other in just five finals, with the ’72 preliminary final their most recent. The Saints’ winning record of 26.75 per cent over Carlton is their lowest winning rate against any side in their history. In the late-1980s they tried to reverse that, with the Carlton crew consisting of premiership Blues Alex Marcou, Peter McConville and Ken Sheldon joining St Kilda at the end of their careers alongside other Blues Spiro Kourkoumelis, Warren Jones and Ricky Nixon.



Carlton great Alex Jesaulenko ended his playing career at the Saints The Age They had joined soon after the most famous Blue to become a Saint, Alex Jesaulenko, controversially joined the club in 1980 after coaching Carlton to a flag as captain-coach in 1979. None of the moves worked for the Saints, who spent that decade languishing at the bottom while the Blues kept playing in grand finals at winning flags. But the arrival of Carlton’s Aaron Hamill at Moorabbin in 2001 began to reverse that winning record, particularly at Marvel Stadium. The Saints now lead the head-to-head battle at that venue 22-8, with their two-point win over Carlton in the final round of 2024 tipping the Blues out of finals momentarily before Port Adelaide beat Fremantle later that day.



They defeated them comfortably earlier this season when the Blues, then coached by Michael Voss, suffered a familiar second-half collapse and Jack Silvagni showed he was on the path to an outstanding season. Sunday night is different. Lyon noted during the week Fraser has improved Carlton’s defence by six goals and jokingly nominated him for coach of the year for his effort in turning the Blues around. Fraser, for his part, was not getting caught up in any suggestions this game was anything other than business as usual – a game to win against a faceless opponent who had a talented bloke wearing No.7 (Nasiah Wanganeen-Milera) they had to worry about. “These are the games you want to play in,” Fraser said.



“These are the opportunities you want to be afforded. We’ve done enough to this point to have the opportunity to play in a game like this. We’ll lean into it, but it won’t be about the outcome – it’ll be the brand of football we want to play,” Fraser said. Nothing about the opposition. Nothing about the want to defeat the mob that contains a few of their former players. The process – that’s what Ross and Josh will focus on.

World.title: Buyer pays $2.91m for inner west semi for kids to live in while at uni
World.content:
PropertyNewsAuctions Buyer pays $2.91m for inner west semi for kids to live in while at uni Robyn Willis Updated August 8, 2026 — 8:32pm ,first published 1:08pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A two-storey Erskineville semi sold for $2.91 million at auction on Saturday to an overseas buyer who the selling agent said had purchased it for his children to live in while studying at university. About 30 people, including several neighbours, gathered in the open-plan living area at the rear of 59A Prospect Street to witness the auction of the four-bedroom, three-bathroom architecturally designed home. The property had a guide of $2.5 million and sold for $260,000 above the reserve of $2.65 million. There is no legal requirement for a vendor’s reserve to be in line with their property’s price guide.



Six parties registered to bid, with bidding opening at $2.52 million. Two parties initially battled it out in increments of $10,000, $20,000 and $30,000. When bidding reached $2.65 million, two new bidders entered the fray, with 15 bid increases of similar sizes going back and forth between the two. A final bid of $5000 ended the spectacle with the underbidders, a couple with a child who own a property further west but rent locally, quietly saying “I think we’re out”. It was socks all round for the auction of 9A Prospect Road as a crowd assembled in the compact open-plan living area. James Brickwood A lawyer acting on behalf of the successful bidder said his client was based overseas. Records show the property on the 144-square-metre site last sold in 2016 for $1.92 million. The property was one of 520 scheduled to go to auction in Sydney this week. By evening, Domain Group recorded a preliminary auction clearance rate of 50 per cent from 292 reported results throughout the week, while 94 auctions were withdrawn.





The landscaped backyard at the rear of 59A Prospect Street. Domain One of the vendors, who was present at the auction, said that while it was “very difficult to move” because her family had enjoyed the close-knit local community, an “outstanding” property closer to the city had convinced them to make a fresh start, so they bought it. In Lane Cove, a local family with a young child paid $1,463,000 for a three-bedroom apartment after it passed in at auction on Saturday. Bidding for the property at 2/15 Longueville Road opened at $1.38 million, increasing in bids of $10,000 to reach $1.45 million when things stalled and it passed in. The lead bidder was then invited to increase their offer and, after half an hour of negotiating, the property sold.



The apartment had a guide of $1.4 million and a reserve of $1.5 million. Related Article Sydney house prices ‘Fewer buyers’: The Sydney suburbs with the deepest property downturns Two bidders registered, although Raine & Horne Lower North Shore sales agent Oscar Nicholls was initially expecting only one. The underbidder was an investor who had seen the property once early in the campaign and was attracted to it for its yield potential, Nicholls said. “He got to a point [in the bidding] and said ‘at this price point it doesn’t make any sense’. He has a couple of investments which he is holding because rents are up,” Nicholls said. The vendor was a single-parent family who bought a four-bedroom home. Nicholls said market conditions were good for upsizers.



“She got a really good deal on what she bought,” he said of the new property. The three-bedroom apartment has two bathrooms, a double garage and a living area opening onto a private courtyard. Domain In Bondi Junction, negotiations continued after a two-bedroom art deco apartment passed in at $775,000. Two parties registered to bid for 2/143 Old South Head Road but just a single bid of $750,000 was placed when the auction opened. The lead bidder, a first home buyer renting in Paddington, was invited to advance on their offer with a further bid of $775,000 before the property passed in.



The apartment, sold as a deceased estate, had a guide of $800,0000 and a reserve of $850,000. It is one of nine apartments in a block positioned between Bellevue Hill and Bondi Junction and features high ornate ceilings, timber fretwork and picture rails, typical of the era. The art deco apartment is one of just nine in the boutique block. Domain A sales agent for Ray White Eastern Beaches, Angus Gorrie, expects the property to sell next week. “It takes a bit more time [to sell in this market], but we had two registered buyers, and we are getting close,” he said. “People are out there – the market is better than it was in June.”

World.title: Degrees of difference climate change makes
World.content:
Letters NationalVictoriaLetters Degrees of difference climate change makes August 8, 2026 — 8:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Photo: Matt Golding To submit a letter to The Age, email letters@theage.com.au. Please include your home address and telephone number. No attachments, please include your letter in the body of the email. See here for our rules and tips on getting your letter published. A fraction difference

Adaptation to a rapidly worsening climate is clearly important. But for many places, the answer to the question ″⁣How are we going to live here?″⁣ (Good Weekend, 8/8) is, sadly but bluntly, ″⁣We’re not.″⁣ Phrases such as ″⁣almost unbearable″⁣ are simply inadequate to describe the future we face. Numerous expert assessments have explained clearly that, within a generation, large parts of northern Australia (and many other parts of the planet) will actually be uninhabitable. No amount of adaptation will change that.

But every fraction of a degree of planetary heating will make a difference. So we must redouble our efforts to be a leader, not a laggard, on the mitigation of climate catastrophe. Beginning with a recognition that the burning of gas and coal shipped overseas from Australia has an enormous and unconscionable impact which cannot be ignored.

Richard Barnes, Fairfield Home v profit

Home owners are all on the same escalator. Some are ahead of you, some behind. If the escalator slows or even begins to reverse slowly, relative to the market nothing has changed. So those of us fortunate to own our own home are still able to trade up or down, facing the same relativity.

The only people who are disappointed are those who hope to profit by getting on and off the escalator, because they benchmark against not a replacement house but a short-term profit and loss account. As traders they should face the risk of loss as well as the crazy profits we have seen in recent years.

The motive for buying a house should be purely only for accommodation.

Adam Thomson, Collingwood Two realities

Interesting reading about ″⁣Five of the best homes in Melbourne to enjoy nature″⁣ (Domain, 7/8). It all sounds wonderful, but there is another reality – built-to-last homes with gardens that house birds and insects, sold and bulldozed to then have a McMansion built in its place. This is not progress, it is regress. And so it continues, with the added ″⁣value″⁣ of being overtaken (as if it hasn’t happened) with our councils, or community, not having a say in what happens next. So love your nature, Melbourne, but realise it can be taken away at the whim of government.

Kate Read, Canterbury



Give owner choice

Manningham Council wants to demolish someone’s house, but as in the film The Castle, ″⁣that’s not a house, it’s a home″⁣. If it happens, the owner should be relocated to a bigger and better place of their choice.

Katriona Fahey, Alphington Rethink policy changes

The article ″⁣Opponents circle Labor over delay to migration cut″⁣ (6/8) on proposed changes to immigration policy refers to “firmer controls of the migration system by stopping people taking advantage of it through manoeuvres such as ... using the family system”.

I’m curious as what this refers to, and how Australian citizens applying for family to join them here might be construed as a “manoeuvre” to “take advantage of the family system”?

The report suggests that in response the government is considering “tougher family visa rules”. But there are already extremely tight caps for family reunion visas leading to massive backlogs, with lengthy waiting times for partner visas of up to two years and 14-30 years for aged (67 years and older) parent visas.

Australians with close family overseas should have the right to bring their family to Australia in order to enjoy life together with their families like any other Australian (after security checks of course). The ALP should remember these Australians also vote.

Imposing tighter immigration controls that deny family reunions to Australian families (including the desirable skilled immigrants that we need to attract) is not the way to stop One Nation.

Miriam Faine, Hawthorn Aim for best we can be

It is hoped the Labor Party will not be panicked into a migration policy by the utterings of One Nation whose rhetoric is both disingenuous and nativist (″⁣Migration overhaul a bulwark for PM in One Nation battle″⁣, 7/8). Proposed changes to work rights and appeal processes for people seeking asylum are alarming. The government is now in a position on migration to not use people as scapegoats for political opportunism. A considered policy that encapsulates the best we can be in the framework of demonstrating an act of humanity should be at the core of any decision-making.

Judith Morrison, Nunawading Toothless in Victoria

Like so many things in Victoria, the state’s anti-corruption watchdog IBAC does not work effectively due to inadequate funding and legislative restrictions, as demonstrated by the release of IBAC’s eight-year long investigation into the Andrews government’s murky fire union deal which included some anodyne recommendations (“Secret deal exposed”, 6/8).

NSW in stark contrast has ICAC, an effective anti-corruption canine which behaves like an inquisitive, investigative terrier. Victoria has in comparison a sedated, toothless dog tethered inside its kennel.

Dennis Walker, North Melbourne The banned play on

My main sources of news are The Age, The Guardian and the ABC all of which are banned to attend news conferences by Pauline Hanson. How will I ever survive?

John Walsh, Watsonia



It’s not entertainment

There should be no surprise that the Australian Catholic Bishops Conference (″⁣Catholic Church rails against divide over values, migrants″⁣, 7/8) noted that we are facing growing social division involving incendiary language, discrimination and violence. That’s what we see and hear every day on our televisions, radio and other media.

High-rating reality TV shows highlight angry disagreements, abuse and inability to resolve issues in sensible adult ways. Movies with anger and violence are being promoted as must-see events.

While we continue to promote these types of behaviour as “entertainment” we will continue to see such behaviour played out in other aspects of life to the detriment of maintaining a civil society.

The younger generation are being taught that all of this normal. Their living out of such behaviours is not their fault. It’s what we’ve allowed to be promoted as normal and so-called “entertaining”. Political rhetoric re adult crime/adult time is classic “ambulance at the bottom of the cliff” approach. We older generations need to take responsibility that such promoted behaviours are not appropriate or even entertaining.

Frank O’Connor, Albert Park Pack of memories

Brian Johnston’s Comment piece (2/8) on the demise of the real backpacker rings true. Travelling in the late ’70s across Australia, Asia and up through Europe, our packs contained all our worldly possessions. We lived sometimes literally on $2 a day. In our packs we carried a tent, cooking gear and threadbare clothes. There was no souvenir shopping – if it didn’t fit in the pack, it was left behind.

We slept on beaches and showered in nearby resorts. We picked up cash work wherever possible. Countries were changing then, with the desire for wealthy tourists over travellers. An eviction from Sri Lanka due to lack of funds sealed the deal. I can’t say I miss the backpack but I certainly have some fabulous memories.

Wendy Daniels, Hawthorn Came to my census

Whew, I filled in the census with the help of a younger neighbour (she is only 90) and posted it off. I didn’t lie about my age or income. I hope we did it to the authorities’ satisfaction.

Myra Fisher, Brighton East

World.title: Sheer lunacy and a coming of age: Inside the greatest Battle of Brisbane yet
World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2026 Sheer lunacy and a coming of age: Inside the greatest Battle of Brisbane yet Nick Wright August 8, 2026 — 7:55pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Jot it down and remember where you were for the craziest Battle of Brisbane yet. It may have been the Dolphins who took home the two points in a thrilling 40-32 shootout against the Broncos – securing their maiden finals appearance in the process – but the 50,000-plus fans who packed into Suncorp Stadium were arguably the biggest winners of Saturday night. Selwyn Cobbo scores for the Dolphins on Saturday. Getty Images There were moments of brilliance and sheer lunacy, contract statements and ominous reminders, injury scares and flaring tempers. As Broncos coach Michael Maguire said, “it was an unusual game”. It might be best if we just broke it down.



Mam magic and a contract statement Ezra Mam has been a man maligned for much of season 2026 – his axing at times throughout the campaign symbolic of the Broncos’ dramatic slide from defending champions to the doldrums of the competition. But the under-siege five-eighth issued a stunning reminder of just what he could produce with a first-half hat-trick that threatened to completely take the game away from the Dolphins. Loading It was fitting that in Indigenous Round Mam produced his finest performance of the year, his first highlight bouncing on the outside of Reece Walsh to take his fullback’s pass and score untouched from close range. The opportunity came from a Billy Walters 40/20, it what was the off-contract hooker’s first starting appearance since rupturing his ACL last year.



“It’s a testament to all Bill’s hard work, it would have been tough sitting in his position last year, and to fight his way through it … he’s earned his spot,” Broncos skipper Pat Carrigan said. “The Walters name is synonymous with the club, and he lives and breathes what it’s like to play for the Broncos – I’m really proud of him and a bit disappointed we couldn’t get the win for his 100th game.” For Mam’s next trick, shortly after Jamayne Isaako sent the Dolphins’ kick-off out on the full, the 23-year-old simply ran it hard and straight at the defence, before shrugging off a pair of tackles and reaching out desperately for his second. Walters was quick to issue another reminder of why he must be retained at Red Hill, slicing out of dummy half and splitting the defence, before finding Deine Mariner on his inside to score an 80-minute special. It was then Mam’s kicking game which extended Brisbane’s early lead to 24 points, his grubber twice fumbled by Jack Bostock for Xavier Willison to touch down.



And even after the Dolphins scored three straight tries, it was Mam who wrestled back the ascendancy for a moment – scoring straight from a scrum after Tom Gilbert’s knock on. Just as he was in the 2023 grand final, Mam appeared destined to add a man of the match medal to his accolades. Until one moment and a rival general flipped the script. The good fortune and little general The Dolphins needed something to go their way as Mam orchestrated a 24-0 Broncos lead. Hamiso Tabuai-Fidow was on hand to provide that. As the Broncos went on the attack again, a dropped ball by Jaiyden Hunt was swooped on by the Dolphins’ No.1 – his smile as soon as he grabbed possession a sign he knew he would not be caught on the 90-metre dash to score.



Hamiso Tabuai-Fidow scores against Brisbane. Getty Images While that try may have been in fortuitous circumstances, it appeared to awaken his side as they hunted to keep their top four hopes alive. From the following set, Max Plath – who was outstanding all night, finishing with 184 running metres – burst through the middle and into the clear to go deep into Brisbane territory. Halfback Isaiya Katoa then stood up, commanding his team into position for him to fire a perfect short pass for Connelly Lemuelu to cut the deficit to 12 points. Katoa was at it again when the Dolphins clinched the momentum, with the 22-year-old’s brilliant face pass for Bostock presenting a two-on-one, with Isaako finishing the job in the corner.



While Mam’s third briefly halted the surge, it would not be for long. Ben Talty’s dropped ball coming out of trouble opened the door, and the Dolphins turned globetrotters. Winger Selwyn Cobbo could have panicked when Katoa’s attempted long ball went behind him and crept towards the sideline, but the former Bronco’s tap-back for a supporting Farnworth was perfect. The England centre was then hardly troubled on his way to the line, the Broncos’ defence parting without hesitation. Somehow, at half-time, the Dolphins led 30-24. “Key moments are hurting us, that’s where we’re at,” Maguire lamented. “Obviously, I’m frustrated, you can’t leak or let in that many tries to put yourself in a position to really contend.”



Katoa’s masterclass and ‘The Hammer’s’ miracle He had shown signs he was about to make this game his own, but it was the way Katoa controlled the second half which ultimately proved the difference. The first-half shootout had quickly descended into an arm wrestle, with Mariner and Gilbert both sent for head injury assessments, and Farnworth seen limping regularly after an awkward tackle on his lower leg by opposite number Kotoni Staggs. Against a Broncos side missing skipper and veteran halfback Adam Reynolds, it was Katoa’s composure which guided the Dolphins home – relying on his patient kicking game while waiting for his moment to strike. That chance came when Tabuai-Fidow’s kick return, and Plath’s bulldozing carry with three defenders on his back, got the Redcliffe army on the charge – Katoa’s delicate chip over the top gifting Lemuelu his second try of the night.



Related Article NRL 2026 Storm pile on the points against Sea Eagles in Perth While Walsh would ice a penalty goal to earn Brisbane the lead back, Katoa was far from finished with the boot. His attacking bomb was miraculously taken by Tabuai-Fidow, who reached out to score his second and clinch the lead, before the Tongan maestro’s cross-field effort was reeled in by Bostock and eventually spread back the other way for Cobbo to seal the win. “It’s something I’ve been working on, and I think I can get over a couple of fullbacks. I looked at Issy and just said ‘iso’ [isolated kick] … I got the try, it’s pretty cool,” Tabuai-Fidow relived. By full-time, for all of the individual brilliance Mam and Tabuai-Fidow showcased, Katoa was the evening’s mastermind – orchestrating five of his side’s seven tries.



“You could see we had our attack on, you could see we were going to find opportunities – we were making little half breaks and linebreaks, and that gave me a lot of confidence,” Dolphins coach Kristian Woolf said. “I do love the way he steered the ship, he’s our leader and halfback, he’s got a great temperament on him, and I thought he controlled that second half really well.”

World.title: Mistake to omit creative arts technologies from new school subjects, drama teachers say
World.content:
The drama teachers' association says the government has made a mistake by omitting technologies that support the creative arts from its list of new industry-led school subjects.

The nine subjects would be developed by industry skills boards to provide clear pathways to further training and jobs for secondary school students in Years 12-13.

Whakaari Aotearoa Drama New Zealand said it should have included a subject that covered areas like lighting, sound, staging, costume, and set design.

The organisation's president Annette Thomson said failing to do so would sever students' pathway into industries such as film and television that had critical skill shortages.

Whakaari Aotearoa Drama president Annette Thomson. Supplied / Whakaari Aotearoa Drama NZ

She said currently teens could earn credits toward an NCEA qualification while they participated in backstage roles like lighting or sound for school productions, but that would not be possible under the new qualification being introduced in 2029 because students would have to study entire subjects and there was no subject that covered those skills.

Thomson said the decision endangered the government's plan to grow the creative sector's economic contribution to $22 billion a year by 2030.

"We feel like they're not really thinking about some of these things that are actually important. They do actively contribute to GDP and to our students," she said.

"All we're seeing is a cutting, a reducing, a narrowing of subjects in the arts."

World.title: What's gone wrong for Milford's Active Growth Fund?
World.content:
Milford's Active Growth Fund has long been one of the success stories of KiwiSaver, reliably at the top of performance tables in its category and delivering strong returns year after year.

But in recent times, it's started to slip - and quickly.

While it's still the best performing growth fund over 10 years, with a return of 10.2 percent a year, it was the worst performer over the most recent three months according to research firm Morningstar, returning 5 percent compared to 12.5 percent for the best performer.

It was 28th over one year, with a return of 7.8 percent, compared to 21.5 percent for the top fund.

Steven Le, associate director at Morningstar, said Milford had taken a deliberate step back to a "somewhat defensive" position relative to other fund managers in terms of its allocation to technology and the US, both of which have been strong performers recently.

But he said Milford was still a strong manager. "They do a lot of good things, robust research, they cover a lot of ground. They have boots on the ground in several regions including Australia and the research they conduct is quite comprehensive. We think they're doing good things and we have a positive view of them as a business as well as a positive view of the strategy."

Do I have to buy that extended warranty? No Stupid Questions with Susan Edmunds Download MP3 12m

There have been concerns that the fund has become too big. Le said those were legitimate because as funds grew larger investment managers were forced to extend their reach.

Since 2020, New Zealand equities exposure in the fund had more than halved. He said that trend was likely to continue as Milford tried to manage capacity in smaller local markets.

"Milford is undoubtedly a major player in the New Zealand market. The scale and growth of the business have enabled ongoing investment in its research and investment capabilities over time, which are key contributors to our positive view of the business and a number of its strategies.

"That said, the considerable growth of the business and several of its strategies does come with associated risks. In particular, the firm has expanded into new segments, such as global equities, and when a fund manager broadens its capabilities beyond its traditional areas of expertise, it is something we pay close attention to. To date, we have not identified any issues that we think would materially impact investors, but it's an area we are actively monitoring."

He noted that Milford's wide-ranging mandate for the fund allowed it to change its split between growth and income assets with discretion.

The allocation to equities fell as low as 60 percent in December 2022, while it sat at 76.3 percent as of November 2025. Le said although reduced US equities exposure could dent returns, as in recent times, it was beneficial during the April period last year when the fund returned 0.1 percent when the category index fell 1.6 percent.

Milford head of KiwiSaver Murray Harris. Supplied / Milford

Milford recently held a webinar for financial advisers about the fund, at which they were told that Milford intended to stick with its strategy, which aimed to deliver 10 percent annual returns over a seven-year period.

Milford head of KiwiSaver Murray Harris said the session was an opportunity for advisers to hear directly from and ask questions of the investment team about recent performance, portfolio positioning, the market environment and the outlook for the strategy. "Advisers place significant trust in us when recommending our funds to clients, and it is important that we are open, accessible and transparent about performance, investment decisions and portfolio positioning."

Milford said it had seen some movement of investment funds into higher-risk categories, such as people moving from growth to aggressive, and balanced to growth.

World.title: Charities raise money for Kaimanawa muster, save horses from culling
World.content:
Kaimanawa wild horse charities have raised enough money for a fourth muster of the year, and found enough homes for a small group of animals living in an ecologically sensitive area of the North Island's central plateau.

The fourth muster was required because a group of about 15 horses is living away from the main herd, on Defence Force land near Waiouru.

Three musters have taken place earlier this year to help limit herd numbers, which current sit at about 500.

The Kaimanawa Wild Horse Advisory Group - including the Department of Conservation and the charities, Kaimanawa Heritage Horses and the Kaimanawa Legacy Foundation - recently decided that a muster of those horses could take place if the charities raised the money for it.

If they didn't it was possible aerial culling would have been used.

Legacy Foundation founder Kelly Wilson said the charities had raised about $60,000, which was enough, although the cost for the latest muster had since increased by about $19,000.

The charities would have to cover that cost.

Legacy Foundation founder Kelly Wilson. Nick Monro

Eighteen homes had agreed to take wild horses if needed. Wilson said no one knew the exact number that would be taken from the site, so it was good to have flexibility.

"It's a huge relief," Wilson said.

"Our fundraising to do the muster would be pointless if we didn't have homes for them to go to."

She said it would be interesting to see how easily the horses could be trained as, unlike horses from the main herd, they'd had little contact with people.

Trainer Morgan Chandler-Bruce would work with six or seven of the horses at Wilson's sanctuary, near Taupō.

Wilson said a week before applications for horses had closed, the charities had only received one for the five stallions likely to be mustered, and they were short of homes for mature mares.

However, private sponsors put up the money for eight horses, to cover most of the costs of training them. Applications then followed.

"We are hugely appreciate of the public for the donations received to enable the muster to go ahead, as well as the homes that have stepped forward to offer these special Kaimanawa horses homes," she said.

DOC project lead Sarah Tunnicliffe. Dan Jones

DOC project lead Sarah Tunnicliffe said the department was finalising logistics of the muster and setting up temporary yards for it.

World.title: Whanganui opts out of Head Start pathway ahead of deadline
World.content:
Whanganui District Council has voted not to submit a proposal on local government reform ahead of the Head Start deadline on Sunday.

It has instead signed a regional Memorandum of Understanding with its neighbours - Rangitīkei and Ruapehu - committing to working proactively towards locally-led reform.

Mayor Andrew Tripe said Whanganui needed more time to consider its options.

"We need robust modelling to help us understand the implications, opportunities and long-term outcomes. That work, alongside continued conversations with our communities and partners, will help shape the next phase of this process," he said.

"For our council, the priority is making sure decisions deliver the best outcomes for Whanganui and the region and we'll continue working constructively with our regional partners while keeping the community involved as the picture becomes clearer."

The government would decide next month which Head Start proposals should move on to a detailed design phase, before final decisions were made in 2027.

Whanganui, meanwhile, would now fall into the group of Back Stop councils for whom reform would begin after the 2028 elections.

Tripe said continuing to work with interested councils didn't predetermine any outcome or limit councils from exploring alternatives.

"What it does do is give us a structured way to continue to work together, build a stronger evidence base and consider different options before any decisions are made."

Tripe said over the past three months, mayors and council chief executives in the region and nearby had met regularly to discuss opportunities and challenges presented by the government's Simplifying Local Government reforms.

The council had also commissioned and considered data and technical analysis, engaged with iwi and hapū partners, and asked the community for its initial thoughts.

"We've had many productive discussions and begun to build up an information base," he said.

"That work has strengthened our understanding of the issues and, in particular, the opportunities. It's shown there's more work to do before any structural changes can be properly considered. In addition, it gives us the opportunity to think bigger than the Head Start pathway to reimagine local government in and for the future."

Tripe said for some councils change was more straightforward because amalgamation discussions were well advanced and Head Start was primarily for those councils.

"But for most, it makes sense to take the time to build a robust evidence base and work carefully through it so we can make the best decision for our communities now and in years to come."

World.title: Privacy experts warn of gaps in NZ law, as camera glasses hit Kmart shelves
World.content:
Privacy experts are warning that wearable camera technology, dubbed by some as "pervert glasses", expose significant gaps in New Zealand's laws.

University of Canterbury professor Annette Mills said the devices, which were often marketed as smart glasses, were "essentially a computer on your face", combining cameras, microphones, speakers and AI-powered functions in everyday wearable technology.

The Anko Camera Glasses. Supplied / Kmart

Her warning comes as Kmart begins selling its Anko Camera Glasses for just $99, a price point expected to make the technology far more accessible than premium smart glasses such as Meta's Ray-Ban range.

She said that while the glasses offered some benefits, especially as assistive technology for people with disabilities, the technology's growing popularity raised serious privacy concerns.

"We expect to be recorded in some places, such as by CCTV cameras in supermarkets," Mills said.

"But we certainly don't expect to have that everywhere we go."

Mills said that unlike smartphones, which required users to visibly raise a device before taking a photo or recording video, smart glasses could capture footage far more discreetly, making it difficult for bystanders to know whether they were being filmed.

She said overseas cases had already shown how wearable cameras could be misused, including secret recordings in bathrooms and people approaching women in public before uploading the footage to social media without their consent.

Mills said future developments, including facial recognition technology, could make the privacy implications even more significant.

"You could literally look at someone and say, 'Tell me everything there is about this person'. That can make someone feel very vulnerable."

Laws designed for organisations, not individuals

Mills believed New Zealand's privacy framework had a fundamental weakness when it came to wearable technology.

"Our privacy regulations are primarily aimed at protecting individuals, but they are targeted at organisations and what organisations do," she said.

"They are not set up to deal with personal information collected by individuals."

While existing laws could apply to intimate recordings, harmful digital communications and some forms of stalking, Mills said many everyday uses of camera glasses may fall outside current legal protections.

Her concern extended beyond what people record.

Once footage was uploaded to cloud services, it could be processed, analysed and potentially shared in ways many users - and the people they record may not fully understand.

"I think we need to come up with not just regulations that deal with the use, but also controls that deal with the deployment of these devices," she said.

University of Canterbury professor Annette Mills. Supplied / University of Canterbury

Minister of Justice Paul Goldsmith said the government may consider "taking advice on the matter" in the next parliamentary term.

'Serious privacy harms'

The Office of the Privacy Commissioner said the Privacy Act was largely focused on regulating the actions of businesses and organisations, not individuals and it applied regardless of what technology was used.

"Tools like CCTV, drones, and smart glasses make it easier for individuals to record each other. If individuals do not use them in a responsible manner, that can lead to serious privacy harms," a spokesperson said.

It said that individuals using glasses to film covertly should be aware that their actions might breach the Privacy Act if the collection, use or disclosure of the personal information was highly offensive to a reasonable person.

"Other laws are also likely to be relevant, such as the Harmful Digital Communications Act, stalking offences or other crimes under the Crimes Act."

Surveillance concerns extend beyond the wearer

Meanwhile, University of Auckland commercial law professor Gehan Gunasekara raised questions about the companies behind the devices.

University of Auckland commercial law professor Gehan Gunasekara. RNZ / Phil Pennington

His concern was not simply that individuals may misuse camera glasses, but that platforms operating the technology could collect vast amounts of information about where people went, what they looked at and how communities behaved.

"The platform also knows all of that information," he said.

"They can map trends, see where people travel and the kinds of stores they shop at."

Even where companies anonymised data before using it to improve artificial intelligence systems, Gunasekara said the aggregated information remained commercially valuable and raised broader questions about privacy and data sovereignty.

A 'game-changing' technology for blind New Zealanders

However, not everyone saw the technology as a threat.

Blind Low Vision New Zealand chief executive Andrea Midgen described AI-enabled smart glasses as the most significant technological advancement her community had seen.

Blind Low Vision chief executive Andrea Midgen. Supplied / Blind Low Vision NZ

The glasses could read street signs, restaurant menus and other visual information aloud while allowing users to keep both hands free for a white cane or guide dog.

"This is the most exciting game changer thing that we've had in technology for our community ever," Midgen said.

She acknowledged privacy concerns but said they stemmed from how people chose to use technology, rather than the technology itself.

"This is just a different form of what already happens with smartphones," she said.

'Use responsibly' - Kmart

A Kmart Group spokesperson confirmed that its Anko Camera Glasses were available to buy in New Zealand.

"The Anko Camera Glasses are part of an established and increasingly mainstream category of wearable technology, with similar products available globally from major technology and eyewear brands. Like other products in this category, they allow users to capture photos and video while also providing audio and connectivity features," the spokesperson said.

"As with any device capable of recording images, we expect customers to use the product responsibly, respectfully and in accordance with applicable laws and community expectations around privacy."
